# M&M Case Conference

**Service:** Internal Medicine
**Date:** May 2026 (last reviewed 2026-05-24)
**Presenter:** PGY-2 Resident, Internal Medicine
**Discussant:** Pulmonary & Critical Care Attending
**Venue:** Monthly service M&M; 60-minute conference; resident, attending, and chief-resident attendance

> **Source.** Composite of multiple cases drawn from the published WebM&M corpus, institutional adverse-event review, and the orthopedic post-operative VTE literature. No identifiable patient. Distributed for system-learning purposes per the program's M&M protocol; the discussion is held under institutional peer-review-protected status.

---

## 1. Case identifier

A 58-year-old woman, postoperative day 7 from elective right total hip arthroplasty (THA), died from massive bilateral pulmonary embolism. The surgery was uncomplicated. The standard postoperative course was uneventful through POD 5, when she was transferred to an inpatient rehabilitation facility. On POD 7 she developed new dyspnea and right-sided chest pain; clinical deterioration progressed over six hours; cardiopulmonary arrest occurred at the rehabilitation facility; she was unable to be resuscitated.

The diagnosis was confirmed at autopsy: massive bilateral pulmonary emboli, with extensive thrombus in the right common femoral and popliteal veins. The acute-care hospital course was unrevealing for alternative cause of death.

---

## 2. Chronology

| Time (POD / EST) | Event |
|------------------|-------|
| POD 0 | Uncomplicated right total hip arthroplasty (cementless, posterior approach). EBL 350 mL. Estimated surgical time 95 minutes. Standard antibiotic prophylaxis; standard intraoperative DVT mechanical prophylaxis. |
| POD 1, 06:00 | Heparin 5000 units subcutaneous every 8 hours initiated for VTE prophylaxis per orthopedic standard order set. Sequential compression devices applied. Ambulating 50 ft with physical therapy. |
| POD 2 | Diet advanced; pain controlled on oral regimen; ambulating 100 ft × 3. No fevers; vitals normal. |
| POD 3 | Drain removed; foley removed; ambulating 200 ft × 3. Postoperative course documented as uneventful. |
| POD 4 | Postoperative day 4 hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL (stable from postoperative 10.1); no transfusion required. |
| POD 5, 14:00 | Transferred to affiliated inpatient rehabilitation facility. Subcutaneous heparin continued. Sequential compression devices discontinued per rehab protocol (ambulation as substitute). |
| POD 6 | Uneventful at rehab; ambulating 300 ft × 3; participating in physical and occupational therapy. |
| POD 7, 09:42 | Patient develops new dyspnea; reports right-sided pleuritic chest pain. Nursing initiates rapid response. |
| POD 7, 09:58 | Rapid response team arrives. Vitals: HR 118, BP 102/68 mmHg, SpO₂ 88% on room air, RR 24, T 37.0 °C. Lungs auscultated as clear; cardiac regular without murmur. Lower extremity examination not documented in the rapid-response note. |
| POD 7, 10:05 | Rehab attending physician arrives. Documented differential: *"likely musculoskeletal vs. pulmonary etiology"*. Orders: CXR, troponin, D-dimer, BMP, CBC. Oxygen titrated to 4 L nasal cannula; SpO₂ improved to 92%. Wells score not calculated; lower-extremity examination still not documented. |
| POD 7, 10:35 | CXR clear (no infiltrate, no effusion, no pneumothorax). Troponin negative. D-dimer 1845 ng/mL FEU (reference < 500). BMP within normal limits. CBC unchanged from baseline. SpO₂ declined to 84% on 4 L nasal cannula; oxygen increased to 6 L. |
| POD 7, 10:45 | Rehab attending pages the primary orthopedic surgeon to discuss findings. The recorded conversation included: *"elevated D-dimer; need workup"* — surgeon advised *"may not be PE — D-dimer is always elevated after orthopedic surgery; check CT angiogram if persistent"*. Plan documented: *CTPA if persistent symptoms; continue monitoring; will reassess in 1 hour.* |
| POD 7, 11:15 | Decision to obtain CT pulmonary angiography. Transport request submitted. The rehab facility has no on-site CT and no weekend on-call radiology contract; transport to the affiliated acute-care hospital is required. Estimated transport time 45 minutes; estimated time-to-scan 2 hours. |
| POD 7, 12:48 | Patient develops severe dyspnea; SpO₂ 76% on 6 L; BP 84/52 mmHg; HR 134. Patient reports *"I can't breathe."* Family at bedside. |
| POD 7, 12:50 | Second rapid response. Rehab attending re-evaluates. Decision made to escalate transfer urgency and to convert from elective CTPA transport to emergent ambulance transfer. Cardiac monitoring initiated. |
| POD 7, 13:12 | Patient becomes pulseless. CPR initiated; ACLS protocol; ambulance arrives at 13:18; ED en route ETA 13:35. |
| POD 7, 13:55 | Code called. Time of death documented 13:55 POD 7. |
| POD 8 | Autopsy performed at the family's request. Findings: extensive bilateral pulmonary emboli with right-heart dilation and acute right-ventricular strain; thrombus extending from the right popliteal vein through the femoral and into the iliac vein. Cause of death: massive pulmonary embolism. |
| POD 14 | Estrogen-receptor-positive breast cancer diagnosed two years prior (treated with lumpectomy, radiation, and 18 months of completed adjuvant chemotherapy ending 14 months before THA) identified in the pre-operative medical record on case review. No specific VTE-risk flag for this history was present in the orthopedic VTE-prophylaxis order set. |

---

## 3. Decision points

Three decision points are marked for analysis. Each is named with the options that existed at that moment and the option chosen.

**Decision 1 — POD 7, 09:42 to 10:05. Initial differential at first rapid response.**
The patient presents with new dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, hypoxia (SpO₂ 88% RA), tachycardia (HR 118), and borderline hypotension. The differential options at this moment include: pulmonary embolism, atelectasis, pneumonia, musculoskeletal pain, anxiety, acute coronary syndrome, postoperative bleeding with anemia-related demand ischemia, and others. The lower-extremity examination — specifically, evaluation for unilateral leg swelling, calf tenderness, or palpable cord — is the bedside finding that most-strongly raises pre-test probability for PE. The Wells score, calculated with the available information (recent surgery: +1.5; tachycardia > 100: +1.5; hemoptysis: 0; malignancy: unknown to the team at this moment; alternative diagnosis less likely: 0 at this moment) would have been moderate-probability without the cancer history, high-probability with it. **The chosen option:** documented differential as *"musculoskeletal vs. pulmonary"*, with imaging and labs ordered to differentiate. The leg examination was not documented; the Wells score was not calculated.

**Decision 2 — POD 7, 10:45. Interpretation of the elevated D-dimer.**
The D-dimer at 1845 ng/mL FEU is markedly elevated (reference < 500). In a post-operative orthopedic patient, the D-dimer baseline is elevated for approximately 4–6 weeks; the literature (e.g., Niimi et al., *Thromb Res* 2010; Watanabe et al., *J Arthroplasty* 2012) supports an age- and post-op-adjusted threshold, with the elevation typically returning to within 2× baseline by POD 14. At POD 7 in a 58-year-old, an unadjusted D-dimer of 1845 is *not* uninterpretable as post-surgical baseline — it is consistent with active thrombosis when paired with hypoxia, tachycardia, and the clinical picture. The options at this moment: (a) immediate CTPA, with transport arrangements expedited; (b) immediate transfer to acute-care hospital for evaluation and CTPA there; (c) bedside ultrasound of lower extremities to evaluate for DVT; (d) empiric anticoagulation pending imaging; (e) deferred CTPA pending observation. **The chosen option:** option (e) modified by option (a) on a contingent timeline (*"CTPA if persistent"*). Empiric anticoagulation was not initiated. Lower-extremity ultrasound was not performed.

**Decision 3 — POD 7, 11:15. Imaging logistics.**
The CTPA was ordered but transport was delayed because the rehab facility has no on-site CT, no weekend on-call radiology, and the standard transfer-for-imaging arrangement was not designed for emergent indications. The options at this moment: (a) accept the standard transfer-for-imaging timeline (~2 hours to scan); (b) initiate emergent ambulance transfer to the affiliated acute-care hospital for CTPA there; (c) initiate empiric anticoagulation in the interim while transport is pending. **The chosen option:** option (a), with continued monitoring. Empiric anticoagulation was not initiated.

---

## 4. Outcome

The patient died at POD 7, 13:55, from massive bilateral pulmonary embolism. The autopsy confirmed the diagnosis. The interval from the first clinical concern (POD 7, 09:42) to death was 4 hours and 13 minutes.

---

## 5. Contributing factors (Reason's Swiss-cheese model)

Two exhaustive lists. Each contributed; none alone produced the outcome.

### Latent factors (system conditions)

- **Rehabilitation facility staffing model.** A single attending physician covered approximately 80 patients on weekends. The cognitive bandwidth available for a possible PE workup competed with routine rehabilitation care. The staffing model does not include a defined escalation pathway for time-critical evaluation.
- **Imaging infrastructure at the rehab facility.** No on-site CT scanner. No on-call radiology coverage on weekends. The contract with the imaging vendor explicitly excludes weekend emergent imaging; the contract was negotiated to a budget target without an institutional patient-safety review.
- **Rehab-to-acute-care transfer protocols.** Transfer-decision criteria for time-critical conditions were not defined in writing. The default for *"CTPA needed"* is the standard transport-for-imaging arrangement (~2-hour timeline), not an emergent ambulance transfer. The default is not consistent with the time-to-diagnosis requirement for massive PE.
- **Pre-operative risk stratification.** The patient's history of estrogen-receptor-positive breast cancer with prior adjuvant chemotherapy was present in the pre-operative medical record but was not flagged in the orthopedic VTE-prophylaxis decision tree. Standard orthopedic VTE prophylaxis (subcutaneous heparin 5000 units q8h for the 35-day postoperative window) is not extended-duration for patients with active or recent malignancy. The literature (e.g., ASCO and CHEST guidelines) supports extended-duration LMWH or DOAC prophylaxis for orthopedic surgery patients with cancer history; the order set did not implement this.
- **Order-set design.** The orthopedic VTE-prophylaxis order set does not surface cancer history as a decision-relevant data element. The history is in the chart but is not in the order-set workflow.
- **D-dimer interpretation guidance at the rehab facility.** The rehab facility does not have a documented protocol for D-dimer interpretation in post-operative orthopedic patients. The bedside default — *"D-dimer is always elevated after orthopedic surgery"* — is a folk heuristic, not a guideline, and is not adjusted for the patient's other risk factors.
- **Wells score availability.** The rehab facility's electronic health record does not include a Wells-score calculator; the calculation is by hand if it is performed. The score was not performed in this case.

### Active errors (proximal decisions and actions)

- **Initial differential prioritized musculoskeletal over pulmonary embolism** despite hypoxia, tachycardia, and borderline hypotension.
- **Lower-extremity examination not performed or not documented** at the first rapid response. The examination would have been the bedside finding most-strongly affecting pre-test probability.
- **Wells score not calculated** at any point during the workup.
- **D-dimer interpretation deferred** as *"post-operative baseline elevation"* without applying the age-adjusted or post-op-adjusted threshold. The elevation at 1845 ng/mL FEU is consistent with active thrombosis in this clinical context.
- **Empiric anticoagulation not initiated** pending CTPA. Therapeutic-dose anticoagulation in the interim — when the pre-test probability is moderate-to-high and the imaging is delayed — is the recommended bridge per CHEST and ESC guidelines.
- **Transfer to acute-care hospital not considered** until after the second rapid response. The initial decision treated the CTPA as elective-urgent rather than emergent.
- **Lower-extremity ultrasound not performed** as an interim diagnostic move when CTPA was delayed.

---

## 6. Cognitive errors (Croskerry's taxonomy)

Three named errors operated in this case, each tied to a specific decision point.

**Anchoring (Decision 1).** The rehab attending anchored on the recent orthopedic surgery as the explanation for the patient's symptoms. *"Post-operative pain plus dyspnea is normal at POD 7"* — a heuristic that is approximately true for the modal post-operative patient but that systematically downweights the pre-test probability of PE in a patient whose actual risk factors (recent surgery, malignancy history, hypoxia, tachycardia) are high. The anchor was set at the first impression and was not revised when subsequent data (the D-dimer, the SpO₂ trajectory) should have updated the probability.

**Availability (Decision 1 + Decision 2).** The rehab attending's recent post-operative clinical experience had been uneventful — the modal post-operative orthopedic patient is recovering well at POD 7. PE in a previously-stable post-operative patient was not the recently-available script. The primary orthopedic surgeon, consulted by phone at 10:45, similarly drew on availability — *"D-dimer is always elevated after orthopedic surgery"* — drawn from the routine experience of false-positive D-dimer elevations in uncomplicated postoperative patients. The script that *should* have been available — *"D-dimer >> baseline post-op threshold + hypoxia + tachycardia + recent surgery + cancer history = high pre-test probability of PE"* — was not.

**Premature closure (Decision 1).** The differential at 10:05 was documented as *"musculoskeletal vs. pulmonary"*, but the workup ordered (CXR, troponin, D-dimer) was the standard chest-pain workup rather than a PE-specific workup. The premature closure was on *"this is probably musculoskeletal; the labs will confirm"*; the workup did not include the leg examination, the Wells score, or the immediate decision-tree for CTPA. The closure was made before the data were in.

---

## 7. Counterfactual analysis

The disciplined question: would a reasonable clinician, in the same circumstance, with the same information available at the time, have made the same decisions?

**At Decision 1:** plausibly yes. The clinical picture at 09:42 — new dyspnea, chest pain, hypoxia, tachycardia, borderline hypotension in a POD 7 orthopedic patient — has a broad differential, and the post-operative context is genuinely a confounder for the PE script. A reasonable clinician would have ordered the workup that was ordered. A reasonable clinician would *also* have performed the leg examination and calculated the Wells score; the omission of those moves is the failure point most amenable to system-level correction (an EHR-integrated Wells calculator; a structured rapid-response template that requires the leg exam).

**At Decision 2:** the analysis is closer. The elevated D-dimer at 1845 ng/mL FEU, paired with worsening hypoxia (SpO₂ 84% on 4 L), is a finding most pulmonologists and emergency physicians would interpret as supporting urgent CTPA without delay. The orthopedic surgeon's phone advice — *"D-dimer is always elevated after orthopedic surgery"* — is a folk heuristic that is not literally false but that mis-applies in the presence of the patient's other findings. A reasonable specialist (pulmonary, emergency, internal medicine) would plausibly have moved faster than the chosen plan. A reasonable rehab-medicine generalist, operating without the specialist's framework, would more often have followed the orthopedic-surgeon advice. The system factor here is the rehab facility's reliance on phone consultation with the consulting service rather than an institutional protocol that overrides the consultant's preference in the presence of red flags (hypoxia, tachycardia, hypotension).

**At Decision 3:** the system failure is structural. The rehab facility's standard transport-for-imaging timeline is incompatible with the time-to-diagnosis requirement for massive PE. A reasonable clinician working inside this system, at this rehab facility, on a weekend, would have followed the standard transfer-for-imaging timeline. The decision was the system's, not the clinician's.

**The counterfactual conclusion:** A reasonable clinician, in this circumstance, with this information, operating inside this system, would plausibly have made decisions very similar to those made. The dominant contribution to the outcome was *latent system factors* — the imaging infrastructure, the transfer-decision protocols, the unflagged cancer history, the absence of a Wells-score workflow, the rehab facility's staffing model. The system failed by not having a fast-track for high-risk post-operative imaging at non-acute facilities, by not surfacing cancer history in the VTE-prophylaxis order set, and by not providing the rapid-response team with a structured PE-workup template. The active errors named in §5 occurred inside that system; correcting the system is the appropriate response.

---

## 8. Corrective actions

Five actions; each specific, time-bound, owned, and measurable. Tracked by the Patient Safety Committee to closure.

**Action 1.** Develop and implement a rehab-facility-to-acute-care-hospital transfer protocol for any patient with suspected PE or other time-critical diagnosis. Transfer-decision criteria must be visible at the bedside (laminated card; EHR alert). The 1-hour decision window from clinical concern to transfer initiation must be the protocol default.
*Owner:* Medical Director, [Rehabilitation Facility]. *Due:* 60 days. *Measurable completion:* Protocol approved by Medical Executive Committee; deployed at all three affiliated rehab facilities; bedside card audit at random shows ≥ 95% presence.

**Action 2.** Update the orthopedic VTE-prophylaxis order set to surface active or recent malignancy as a decision-relevant data element, with default escalation to extended-duration prophylaxis (LMWH 30 mg subcutaneous twice daily, or apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily, for 35 days post-operative) for any patient with active malignancy or completion of cytotoxic chemotherapy within the prior 24 months. Surface the cancer history at order entry as a hard-stop the surgeon must explicitly acknowledge.
*Owner:* Chief, Department of Orthopedic Surgery. *Due:* 90 days. *Measurable completion:* Order set v3.2 live in the EHR; cancer-history field surfaced at order entry; chart audit of 50 consecutive orthopedic VTE-prophylaxis orders shows extended-duration prescribed for ≥ 90% of patients with cancer history.

**Action 3.** Resident-curriculum module on *post-operative PE recognition*, with attention to Wells score calculation, D-dimer interpretation in the post-surgical context (age- and post-op-adjusted thresholds), bedside lower-extremity examination, and the decision-tree for empiric anticoagulation pending imaging. Integrated into the orthopedic surgery rotation orientation and the internal-medicine inpatient rotation.
*Owner:* Resident Education Committee, Chair Dr. [Education Chair]. *Due:* 30 days. *Measurable completion:* Module delivered at the next two resident orientation sessions; post-module knowledge check shows ≥ 80% pass rate on a 10-question instrument covering Wells score, D-dimer interpretation, and the empiric-anticoagulation decision.

**Action 4.** Review weekend imaging availability at all three affiliated rehabilitation facilities. Negotiate amendments to imaging-vendor contracts to ensure on-call radiology coverage for emergent indications. Where amendment is not feasible within 120 days, establish a transfer-for-imaging arrangement with the acute-care hospital that meets the 1-hour decision window standard.
*Owner:* Hospital Medical Director. *Due:* 120 days. *Measurable completion:* Imaging-availability audit complete; vendor contracts amended where feasible; transfer arrangement documented in writing and tested by tabletop exercise at each facility.

**Action 5.** Share this case (de-identified) at the next three service-level M&M conferences: orthopedic surgery, internal medicine, and emergency medicine. Incorporate into the resident-curriculum patient-safety module as a teaching case. Track downstream changes in post-operative PE recognition behavior via the Wells-score-documentation audit (currently 0% baseline) and the time-from-clinical-concern-to-CTPA metric.
*Owner:* Patient Safety Committee. *Due:* 30 days for the conference shares; 6 months for the first downstream-behavior measurement. *Measurable completion:* Cases presented at all three named conferences; baseline measurement collected; 6-month follow-up measurement shows Wells-score documentation at ≥ 50% and median time-from-concern-to-CTPA reduced.

---

## 9. Just Culture framing

Applying Marx's Just Culture algorithm (Marx, *Patient Safety and the "Just Culture": A Primer for Health Care Executives*, 2001) to the contributing human behavior:

- *Was the behavior a human error* (an inadvertent slip, lapse, or mistake in execution of a known-correct decision pathway)? — The rehab attending's prioritization of the musculoskeletal differential is consistent with human error operating inside a system that did not provide structured PE-workup support. The orthopedic surgeon's phone advice is consistent with availability bias operating inside a system that does not surface the relevant priors. Neither rises to at-risk or reckless behavior.
- *Was the behavior at-risk* (a knowing shortcut whose risk was misjudged)? — No evidence in the chronology supports an at-risk-behavior interpretation. The clinicians involved followed the documented standard of care at their facility; the standard of care itself was inadequate.
- *Was the behavior reckless* (a conscious disregard of substantial and unjustifiable risk)? — No.

**The Just Culture finding:** This is a *human-error-in-a-flawed-system* case. The appropriate institutional response is *system change*, not individual remediation. The corrective actions in §8 target the system. Individual coaching for the involved clinicians, if appropriate, is the responsibility of the program director and the medical director in a separate non-M&M venue; the conference's role is to name the system finding and produce the protocol changes, not to evaluate the individuals.

The clinicians involved presented this case to the conference voluntarily and with the family's awareness of the M&M review. The presentation is itself an act of intellectual honesty consistent with the institution's safety culture; the form's blameless-postmortem discipline protects the next clinician's willingness to present the next case.

---

## 10. Discussion notes for the conference

The conference is run with advocacy-inquiry as the facilitation register (Rudolph et al. *Simul Healthc* 2006; see `clinical-teaching-microskills.md` §3.10). The discussant, opening the analytical section, declares:

> *"I noticed that the initial differential at 09:42 documented musculoskeletal as the primary consideration despite hypoxia at 88% on room air. I'm concerned because the Wells score for this patient at that moment would have been moderate-to-high. I'm curious — what was going through the team's mind at that moment? What information was most prominent in the rapid-response context?"*

The advocacy (specific observation + the discussant's interpretation) paired with the inquiry (genuine curiosity about the reasoning at the time) is the move. The conference avoids both pure judgment (*"the team should have considered PE first"*) and pure hollow neutrality (*"can someone walk us through the thinking?"*). The presenter's response — the reasoning at the time, the cognitive context, the system constraints — is what produces the analytical conclusion.

The conference closes with an After-Action Review structure (US Army TC 25-20, 1993; see `pedagogy-library.md` §10): *what was supposed to happen* (the standard of care for post-operative PE recognition) — *what actually happened* (the chronology in §2) — *why was there a difference* (the contributing factors in §5 and the cognitive errors in §6) — *what will we do differently next time* (the corrective actions in §8) — *what went well that we should sustain* (the rapid-response team's prompt arrival; the family's involvement in the autopsy decision; the presenter's willingness to bring the case forward).

---

## 11. Notes for the M&M chair

The corrective actions listed in §8 are entered into the institutional M&M closure log on the date of presentation. Progress is reviewed at the next conference (30, 60, 90, 120-day check-ins) and at 6 months. The 6-month measurement is the case's deliverable; without it, the corrective actions are aspirational.

The case is shared, in de-identified form, at the orthopedic surgery and emergency medicine M&M conferences per Action 5. The resident-curriculum integration per Action 3 is the case's pedagogical afterlife — the next PGY-2, encountering the next post-operative orthopedic patient with new dyspnea, should carry the script this case is designed to plant: *"post-operative orthopedic patient + new hypoxia + tachycardia + chest pain = Wells score + leg exam + D-dimer interpreted against post-op threshold + low decision-threshold for CTPA."*

# Morning Report — Tuesday, 7:30am

> **Distribute this page to learners.** The facilitator's guide is a separate document; do not hand it out.

---

## The case

**47-year-old man presents with two days of progressive confusion. Labs show severe hyponatremia. What is the next move?**

He was healthy until two months ago, when he developed a chronic dry cough. Over the past month he has lost 12 lbs without trying and has felt increasingly fatigued. Today his daughter brought him in because he was *"not making sense"* — answering questions out of order, confusing the day of the week, and once asking where his car was when it was parked in his driveway. He denies fevers, headache, weakness, numbness, or vision changes. He takes no medications. Social history: divorced, lives alone, retired electrician, 40 pack-year smoking history (still smoking 1 pack per day), 3–4 beers most evenings, no illicit drug use.

### First reveal — examination

| Vital sign | Value         | Reference  |
|-----------|---------------|------------|
| T         | 37.0 °C       | 36.5–37.5  |
| HR        | 84 bpm        | 60–100     |
| BP        | 118 / 72 mmHg | < 140 / 90 |
| RR        | 16 / min      | 12–20      |
| SpO₂      | 96 % on room air | ≥ 95    |

**General:** thin, fatigued, oriented to self only; confused but arousable and cooperative.
**Neuro:** no focal deficit; no nuchal rigidity; gait not tested.
**Cardiac:** regular; no murmurs; JVP not elevated.
**Respiratory:** scattered wheezes; dullness to percussion at the right upper lobe.
**Abdomen:** soft, non-tender, no organomegaly.
**Extremities:** no peripheral edema; no clubbing; mucous membranes moist.

> **Discussion prompt 1.** *What is your initial differential for new-onset confusion in a 47-year-old with these exam findings? What three labs would you order first, and why?*

### Second reveal — labs and imaging

| Lab            | Value            | Reference        |
|----------------|------------------|------------------|
| Na             | **110 mmol/L**   | 135–145          |
| K              | 4.0 mmol/L       | 3.5–5.0          |
| Cr             | 0.9 mg/dL        | 0.6–1.2          |
| Glucose        | 95 mg/dL         | 70–100 fasting   |
| **Serum osm**  | **240 mOsm/kg**  | 275–295          |
| **Urine osm**  | **480 mOsm/kg**  | 50–1200 (variable) |
| **Urine Na**   | **80 mmol/L**    | spot, variable   |

Note from PCP records: his sodium was 138 mmol/L two months ago at a routine visit.

**CXR (PA and lateral):** 4-cm right hilar mass with ipsilateral mediastinal widening. No effusion, no consolidation. The radiologist's read flags the mass as *"highly suspicious for primary lung malignancy; recommend cross-sectional imaging."*

> **Discussion prompt 2.** *How does this change your differential? Is this hypovolemic, euvolemic, or hypervolemic hyponatremia, and how did you decide? What is the next test?*

### Third reveal — confirmatory data

Morning cortisol: 18 µg/dL (normal). TSH: 1.8 mIU/L (normal). On bedside re-examination: no orthostasis, no axillary dryness, no peripheral edema, JVP 4 cm at 30°; the patient is **clinically euvolemic**.

> **Discussion prompt 3.** *Given euvolemic hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine and a urine sodium above 40, what is the diagnosis? What is the relationship to the chest finding, and what is the first management step?*

---

<details>
<summary><strong>Reveal — answer and teaching points</strong> (facilitator opens after discussion)</summary>

**Diagnosis.** Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone secretion (SIADH), almost certainly paraneoplastic from small-cell lung cancer (the 4-cm right hilar mass). Confirmation requires biopsy of the lung mass for histology; the SIADH itself is a clinical diagnosis once the criteria are met and other causes are excluded.

**Teaching point 1 — SIADH diagnostic criteria.** The Bartter and Schwartz 1967 criteria, still canonical: (a) hypotonic hyponatremia (serum Na < 135 *and* serum osm < 275); (b) inappropriately concentrated urine (urine osm > 100 in the face of hypotonicity); (c) clinical euvolemia (no orthostasis, no edema, no signs of volume overload); (d) elevated urine sodium (typically > 40) on a normal salt and water intake; (e) normal renal, adrenal, and thyroid function. The patient meets all five.

**Teaching point 2 — paraneoplastic association.** Paraneoplastic SIADH is most commonly associated with small-cell lung cancer; roughly 10–15% of SCLC patients have SIADH at presentation, and it is often the *presenting feature* — the chest finding precedes the formal cancer diagnosis in 20–30% of cases. A 47-year-old smoker with new euvolemic hyponatremia and a hilar mass should be assumed to have SCLC-related SIADH until biopsy says otherwise.

**Teaching point 3 — treatment.** First-line is *free water restriction* (typically 800–1000 mL/day) with serum sodium correction limited to no more than 8–10 mmol/L in 24 hours (osmotic demyelination syndrome is the iatrogenic catastrophe to avoid; GRADE: high). For severe symptomatic hyponatremia (seizure, severe altered mental status) hypertonic saline 3% in 100-mL aliquots with frequent re-checking is reasonable. Second-line for persistent SIADH includes tolvaptan (V2-receptor antagonist; expensive, monitor for over-rapid correction) or demeclocycline. *Definitive treatment is treatment of the underlying malignancy*; in SCLC, chemotherapy often produces dramatic improvement in the SIADH within weeks.

**Illness-script update (the take-home).**

> *Middle-aged smoker* + *euvolemic hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine + chest mass* = *paraneoplastic SIADH from small-cell lung cancer until proven otherwise.* First step: confirm euvolemia and the SIADH criteria; restrict free water; image and biopsy the chest finding.

</details>

---

<sub>Last reviewed 2026-05-24. Self-attested by author; not peer-reviewed. Evidence basis: Verbalis et al., *Am J Med* 2013 (SIADH diagnosis and management); Ellison & Berl, *NEJM* 2007 (SIADH). Patient is fictional; presentation is a composite. PHI scrubbed. No conflicts of interest.</sub>

# FACILITATOR'S GUIDE — do not distribute

> **Distribute only the page above to learners. This page is for the chief running the room.**

## Single learning objective

By the end of report, the room should be able to recite the illness-script update (*middle-aged smoker + euvolemic hyponatremia + concentrated urine + chest mass = SIADH from SCLC until proven otherwise*) and articulate the volume-status framework that produced it.

## Timing budget (30 minutes total)

| Minute | What happens |
|--------|--------------|
| 0–2    | Distribute the case; one learner reads the teaser and HPI aloud |
| 2–4    | Quiet reading time for the first reveal (exam) |
| 4–12   | Discussion prompt 1 — early differential and three labs |
| 12–14  | Reveal labs + imaging (second reveal); brief silence to absorb |
| 14–20  | Discussion prompt 2 — volume-status reasoning and next test |
| 20–22  | Third reveal (cortisol, TSH, clinical euvolemia) |
| 22–25  | Discussion prompt 3 — diagnosis and chest-finding link |
| 25–28  | Open the answer block; walk through the three teaching points |
| 28–30  | Restate the illness-script update; close |

If running short (e.g., a 20-minute slot), drop the third reveal and prompt 3 — the case still teaches the central scripts; you lose only the formal-criteria recitation.

## Pedagogical moves to deploy

- **Primary: commit-before-reveal.** At each of the three discussion prompts, require three different residents to commit to an answer *aloud* before revealing the next data. Resist the temptation to reveal early if the room is uncomfortable. *"Maya, what are you committing to? Jake, agree or disagree? Sarah, what's the next test?"* The commit is what creates learning.
- **Secondary: one-minute-preceptor** (Neher 1992; see `clinical-teaching-microskills.md` §3.1). When calling on an individual, use the five-step script: *"What do you think is going on?" → "What in the case led you there?" → (teach the rule) → "You correctly noticed X" → (correct the miss)*. The one-minute frame works inside the larger discussion.
- **Tertiary: minimum-difference example set.** If time permits in the bonus teaching, contrast this case with two distractors (hypovolemic hyponatremia from diuretic use; hypervolemic hyponatremia from heart failure) to crystallise the volume-status decision.

## Wait-time discipline

Count silently to seven after each discussion prompt before calling on a learner. The first time you do this, the room will be uncomfortable. The discomfort is the move; quieter learners need the seven seconds to find their words. After the second or third prompt, the room adapts.

## Expected pitfalls in the room

- **"Old guy with confusion = stroke or delirium."** Some residents will anchor on the chief-complaint of confusion and want a CT head before anything else. Honour the instinct — CT head is reasonable — but redirect to the *labs* prompt: *"The CT is ordered. While we wait, what labs?"*
- **Missing the smoking + hilar mass connection.** When the second reveal lands, some learners will focus on the sodium and ignore the chest film. Ask explicitly: *"Walk me through the chest finding. What's the link?"*
- **Volume-status confusion.** Many PGY-1s recite the hypovolemic / euvolemic / hypervolemic framework but cannot apply it at the bedside. Spend time on prompt 2; this is the high-leverage moment for the teaching.
- **Skipping the SIADH criteria.** The room may converge on the diagnosis without naming the five criteria. Insist: *"List me the criteria. The patient meets them?"* The criteria are testable on every internal-medicine board.
- **Forgetting osmotic demyelination.** Treatment talk can race past the correction-rate caution. If the room moves quickly to *"fluid restrict and treat the cancer"*, slow them down: *"How fast do you correct? What happens if you go too fast?"*

## Bonus teaching (if time, minute 28–30)

If the discussion finishes early, contrast this with the *other* paraneoplastic syndromes of SCLC: ectopic ACTH (Cushing syndrome — would present with hypokalemia, alkalosis, hyperglycemia, hypertension, *not* hyponatremia); Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (proximal weakness improving with exertion — would show on exam); cerebellar degeneration (anti-Yo, ataxia — different presentation). The point is to plant the *"think paraneoplastic in any new SCLC suspect"* heuristic.

```yaml
medical_mode: true
medical:
  subspecialty: teaching
  teaching:
    target_audience_level: "PGY-1"
    pedagogical_move_named: "commit-before-reveal"
    pedagogical_moves_secondary:
      - "one-minute-preceptor"
      - "minimum-difference-example-set"
    assessment_type: "formative"
    retention_horizon: "single-session"
    commit_before_reveal: true
    evidence_grade_visible: n/a   # this is a reasoning case; no novel
                                   # guideline claim is being made
  phi_redacted: true
  reading_level_target: "clinician-facing — no lay-reader target"
```

# Quarterly Multisource (360) Feedback — Dr. R. Hassan, Internal Medicine Attending

> Period: Q1 2026 (Jan 1 – Mar 31). Report compiled: 2026-04-30. Debrief scheduled: 2026-05-24 (R2C2 framework; 60 minutes; Dr. Park, Program Director, facilitating).
>
> **The form is the prompt; the conversation is the artifact.** This report is the substrate for the R2C2 debrief. The numeric panels and narrative aggregates exist to catalyze the conversation, not to substitute for it.

---

## Header

| Field                                | Entry                                                                            |
|--------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Subject of evaluation                | Dr. R. Hassan, MD, Internal Medicine Attending (8 years post-fellowship)         |
| Evaluation period                    | 2026-Q1 (Jan 1 – Mar 31, 2026; 13 weeks)                                         |
| Reviewer identity protection         | Anonymized at reporting; aggregated by MSF coordinator; individual ratings not released |
| Self-assessment completion           | 2026-04-12 (closed before any peer/resident/nurse/patient data viewed)          |
| Stakeholder N (after exclusions for < 2 weeks of contact) | Self: 1 · Peers: 6 · Residents: 12 · Nurses: 8 · Patients: 47 (aggregated from survey) |
| Aggregation discipline               | Means reported with N; narrative comments coded into themes by the MSF committee |
| Debrief framework                    | R2C2 (Sargeant et al. 2015 *Acad Med* 90:1698)                                   |
| Debrief facilitator                  | Dr. Lin Park, Program Director (independent of subject's reporting chain)        |

---

## Section A — Self-assessment (completed first; commit-before-reveal)

> *Dr. Hassan completed this section on 2026-04-12, before any peer/resident/nurse/patient data was viewed. The commit-before-reveal discipline is what makes the convergence-divergence analysis (Section E) interpretable; without the self-rating committed in advance, the analysis collapses into a one-way verdict.*

| Competency                         | Self-rating (1–5; BARS-anchored) | One-sentence rationale                                                  |
|------------------------------------|----------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Bedside teaching                   | 4 (above expected)               | "I make a point of teaching at every set of rounds; residents seem engaged." |
| Clinical communication             | 4 (above expected)               | "My handoffs are structured (I-PASS); my notes are detailed."           |
| Team functioning                   | 4 (above expected)               | "I respect nursing input; I respond to pages promptly."                 |
| Patient experience                 | 5 (consistently exceptional)     | "Patients tell me they appreciate the time I take to explain things."   |
| Professionalism                    | 4 (above expected)               | "I treat colleagues with respect; I manage stress reasonably under pressure." |

**Free-text self-assessment.**

> *"I think my biggest strength is the integration of teaching with clinical care — I try to make every patient encounter a teaching moment. I think the area I could grow is finding more time for one-on-one teaching with the most junior residents; the rounds-based teaching may be over their heads sometimes."*

## Section B — Bedside teaching (resident-rated; N = 12)

**BARS anchors (mid-career attending; teaching service):**

```
5 (consistently exceptional):
  Asks open-ended questions and waits 7+ seconds before redirecting;
  provides specific corrective feedback after rounds with examples;
  recognizes resident contributions explicitly and by name; routinely
  models the Interpreter and Manager moves (RIME) at the bedside.

4 (above expected):
  Open-ended questions are the default; some wait time; post-rounds
  feedback offered when prompted; contributions acknowledged.

3 (meets expected):
  Mix of open-ended and closed questions; some teaching at rounds;
  feedback given at end-of-rotation evaluation; contributions sometimes
  acknowledged.

2 (below expected):
  Mostly closed questions; little wait time; rare post-rounds feedback;
  contributions rarely acknowledged.

1 (significant concerns):
  Lectures at the team; does not engage residents; no feedback given.
```

**Aggregated resident ratings (N = 12):**

```
5 ▓▓▓░░░░░  3 residents
4 ▓▓░░░░░░  2 residents
3 ▓▓░░░░░░  2 residents
2 ▓▓▓▓░░░░  4 residents
1 ▓░░░░░░░  1 resident
                                  Mean: 2.83 / 5    Bimodal
```

**Aggregated resident narrative themes (coded by MSF committee):**

> **Theme 1 — *Highly engaged with senior residents (PGY-3 +).*** Several PGY-3 evaluations name specific teaching moments at the bedside (a real-time HEART-score discussion; a tutorial on dissection radiographic clues). "Best teaching attending of my PGY-3 year." (Coded from 4 narratives.)
>
> **Theme 2 — *Disengaged with interns and junior residents.*** Multiple PGY-1 and PGY-2 evaluations describe Dr. Hassan as "in his head," "did not seem interested in teaching me," and "preferred to teach to the senior on the team." Two specific encounters cited where the intern's question was deflected to the senior. (Coded from 5 narratives.)
>
> **Theme 3 — *Inconsistent presence at teaching rounds.*** Three narratives mention that Dr. Hassan sometimes skipped the formal teaching round in favor of finishing notes; this was experienced as a signal that teaching was a lower priority. (Coded from 3 narratives.)

## Section E — Convergence-divergence analysis

> *This is the report's argument. The numeric panels exist to support it. The convergence-divergence analysis is what the R2C2 debrief in Section F responds to.*

```
Competency               Self   Peers   Residents   Nurses   Patients
                         N=1    N=6     N=12        N=8      N=47
                         ───────────────────────────────────────────────
Bedside teaching         4.0    n/a     2.83 ⚠      n/a      n/a
Clinical communication   4.0    4.67    n/a         n/a      n/a
Team functioning         4.0    n/a     n/a         3.88     n/a
Patient experience       5.0    n/a     n/a         n/a      4.81
Professionalism          4.0    4.5     4.2         4.4      4.83
```

**Convergence panels (where stakeholders agree):**

> **Patient experience and clinical communication are uniformly strong.** Self, peers, and patients converge above 4.5 on the dimensions visible to each. The pattern is consistent: Dr. Hassan's clinical knowledge, communication with peers, and time with patients are areas of strength that all relevant observers see and rate highly.

> **Professionalism converges across all five stakeholder groups.** No divergence; not a coaching priority.

**Divergence panel (where stakeholders disagree):**

> **Bedside teaching diverges sharply downward.** Self rates 4 (above expected); residents rate 2.83 (below expected) with a bimodal distribution. *The clinician's blind spot is downward* — observed by those whose work depends on the teaching (the residents), invisible to those at the clinician's own rank (peer attendings do not see his teaching) and to patients (who experience his bedside manner but not his teaching of trainees).
>
> The bimodal distribution is the diagnostic detail: highly engaged with PGY-3 senior residents; disengaged with PGY-1/PGY-2 juniors. This is not "Dr. Hassan does not teach"; it is "Dr. Hassan teaches up, not down." The R2C2 coaching plan in Section F is keyed to this specific pattern.

> **Team functioning shows mild divergence between self (4.0) and nurses (3.88).** Smaller gap, lower stakes, but worth naming — the nursing narrative themes (pages not answered in weekday afternoons; plan changes communicated only at signout) are specific and actionable.

## Section F — R2C2 coaching plan (for the debrief; Dr. Park facilitating)

> *The R2C2 framework is the debrief's structure. Each phase has its own protected time; do not skip to Content until Rapport and Reaction have happened. Total session: 60 minutes.*

### R — Rapport (5-7 minutes)

> *"Dr. Hassan — thanks for being here. Before we get into the report, I want to check in. How has the quarter been overall? What's been hard, what's been good? I know we've worked together for years, but this kind of conversation is different from our usual one — I want us to be on level ground before we open the report."*

> The Rapport phase is the floor the rest stands on. Without it, the Content phase is delivered to a defensive learner. Allocate the time; do not collapse it.

### R — Reaction (8-12 minutes)

> *"Let's look at the report together. Take a few minutes to read it on your own first. ... I want to start with how you're reacting to what you're reading. Not yet what you think about whether it's accurate — just what your first response is. What stands out? What surprises you? What's hard to read?"*

> **Anticipated reactions to prepare for:**
> - **Defensive about the resident ratings** — likely the first response, especially given the gap between self-assessment and resident rating. The framework is to *name it as data*, not as judgment: "The number on the page is the residents' rating. Let's hold what we make of it for a minute and just notice what it says."
> - **Dismissive of patient survey response rate** (31%) — possible deflection move. The framework is to *acknowledge the limitation* without using it to discount the data: "You're right that it's 31%; that's the standard institutional response rate. The pattern is consistent across the 47 who did respond, which is what we have to work with."
> - **Surprise at the bimodal teaching pattern** — most-likely the productive reaction. The framework is to *follow it*: "Tell me more about what you're noticing in that bimodal pattern. Does it match anything you've observed yourself?"

### C — Content (20-25 minutes)

> *"Now let's look at the data together. I want to start with what the data shows clearly and we agree on, before we get to where the report is asking a question."*

> **Order of content discussion (deliberate):**
> 1. **Patient experience and clinical communication** (convergence panels first). Acknowledge the strengths; name them specifically; cite the patient narrative quote ("the time I take to explain things"). Strengths-first is the Pendleton discipline embedded in the R2C2 Content phase.
> 2. **Professionalism** (convergence; brief). Not a coaching priority; mentioned for completeness.
> 3. **Bedside teaching** (the divergence). Use Advocacy-Inquiry to open the discussion: *"I noticed the gap between your self-assessment of teaching and the resident ratings, with the bimodal distribution between PGY-3s and PGY-1/2s. My interpretation is that you may be teaching at a level that lands for senior residents but not for the juniors — possibly because you're integrating high-complexity clinical reasoning that interns can't yet hold. I'm curious — what was going through your mind when you were teaching this quarter? What were you teaching, and to whom?"*
> 4. **Team functioning** (mild divergence; secondary). Name the nursing narrative themes specifically; do not lecture.

### C — Coaching (15-20 minutes)

> *"What is one thing — not five, one — that you'd want to work on this quarter? What would help you do it?"*

> **Coaching plan (co-constructed in the session; the version below is a draft for Dr. Park to bring as a starting point, not to impose):**
>
> 1. **Resident teaching — junior calibration.** Goal: shift the bimodal distribution toward unimodal-above-expected. Concrete moves:
>    - Read `clinical-teaching-microskills.md` §3.1 (One-Minute Preceptor) and §3.3 (RIME). The 1MP framework is calibrated for junior learners; the RIME framework gives a vocabulary for naming where the learner is.
>    - For the next 4 weeks: identify one PGY-1 or PGY-2 on the team each week; do one explicit One-Minute Preceptor exchange with them daily; log the exchange (one sentence: who, what was the commitment, what was the teaching point).
>    - Pair with Dr. Park for a 15-minute weekly check-in to debrief the logged exchanges.
>
> 2. **Teaching rounds attendance.** Goal: be present at every formal teaching round during weeks when on service. Carve out the note-writing time elsewhere in the day. (No further coaching needed; this is a calendar move, not a skills move.)
>
> 3. **Nursing communication.** Goal: tighten the page-response window on weekday afternoons; communicate plan changes to bedside nurse at the time of the decision. Specific move: when changing a plan, page the bedside nurse (or text via the institutional system) before the next note is written.

> **Loop closure:** The next MSF (Q3 2026; gathered July-Sep) will explicitly test the coaching plan. Resident and nursing ratings will be looked at against this baseline. Patient and peer ratings are not the coaching target for this period and will not drive the assessment of progress.

         alongside the Specific Aims (1 pg), Research Strategy (12 pg),

         Aims page; the reviewer's question is "why this PI, for this work,

Signature move: 7.5 minimum-difference example set (the five Contributions to
         Science vary along exactly one dimension at a time — methodology,

           anatomy); templates/grant-specific-aims.md (the Aims page this
           biosketch accompanies).
================================================================================

Why this subject:
  The NIH biosketch is the application's *credibility document*. The Aims page
  makes the scientific argument; the biosketch testifies to the witness's
  fitness to deliver it. The five-page format imposes a rare discipline: a
  productive PI's hundreds of CV entries must compress into four sections that
  add up to an argument about the PI's body of work. Most biosketches default
  to chronological-CV-in-prose; apex biosketches treat the Contributions to
  Science as a curated narrative — five themed vignettes that the reviewer
  could quote back at study section the next morning.
  Dr. Chen, as a mid-career physician-scientist with an MD/PhD and a coherent
  twelve-year research program on cytochrome-mediated drug-metabolism
  variability, demonstrates the trajectory the biosketch form is designed to
  showcase: the body of work converging on the question the proposed R01 will
  answer.

CUSTOMIZE — slots to adapt when reusing this scaffold:

  1. Personal Statement. Four paragraphs, ≤ 1 page (NIH cap). Rewrite all
     four around your specific candidate; the structural moves (project fit;
     trajectory convergence; team; team-science governance) are invariant.
  2. Positions, Scientific Appointments, and Honors. Reverse chronological.
     Honors that are externally validated (named lectureships, society awards,
     NIH study-section service) signal field-level regard; long lists of
     internal-institutional appointments dilute the signal. Cut to the
     externally-validated.
  3. Contributions to Science. Five themed vignettes is the SF424 convention.
     The vignettes are *themes*, not chronology. Each vignette: title (8–15
     words naming the contribution), narrative (3–4 sentences naming the
     finding + why it mattered + the PI's role), up to 4 citations. Twenty
     citations maximum across all five vignettes.
  4. NCBI MyBibliography URL. Every biosketch must link the PI's full
     bibliography via the NCBI MyBibliography URL (the convention is
     https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/myncbi/[handle]/bibliography/public/).
     The PMCID compliance check requires this link.
  5. ORCID. Required on the biosketch since the 2018 SF424 update. Format
     0000-0000-0000-0000.
  6. Scholastic Performance (Section D). Only included for early-stage
     investigators (K-series candidates, early R-series ESIs in the first
     five years of independent appointment, NRSA F-series fellows). Mid-
     career investigators OMIT Section D. The template below includes a

purposes. Every publication citation, NIH award, lectureship, and honor

against the PI's actual publication record (best practice: auto-generate
from NCBI SciENcv per NIH's recommended workflow).

## A. Personal Statement

I am an Assistant Professor of Medicine and Pharmacology at [Institution], a board-certified internist and clinical pharmacologist, and the Principal Investigator of the cardiovascular pharmacogenomics program at [Institution's Cardiovascular Institute]. My career has been organized around a single question: why do patients respond so differently to the same drug, and can we predict — at the moment of prescription — which patient will tolerate which medication? The proposed R01 ("Mechanisms of statin-induced muscle injury: a precision-medicine pathway to safer LDL-lowering") is the operational consequence of twelve years of work on cytochrome-P450-mediated drug-metabolism variability, applied now to the most-prescribed cardiovascular drug class in history.

My doctoral and postdoctoral training were deliberately constructed around the proposed work. As an MSTP student at UCSF (mentor: Kathleen Giacomini, PhD), I characterized SLCO1B1 transporter variation in simvastatin pharmacokinetics, publishing the discovery cohort's myopathy-risk model in *Clinical Pharmacology & Therapeutics* (Chen et al., 2014; cited in Aim 1 preliminary data). During clinical-pharmacology fellowship at Brigham and Women's Hospital (mentor: Catherine Stoffel, MD, PhD), I extended this work to CYP3A4 substrates and built the prospective cohort that became the largest single-institution statin biobank (10,247 patients; *Circulation* 2024, cited in the Aims page premise paragraph as Figure 2). My laboratory's discovery of the *CYP3A4\*22* × CYP3A4-inhibitor interaction — the central finding the proposed R01 will validate and translate — emerged from this cohort in 2023.

The proposed R01's three aims map directly to capabilities our group has either developed or partnered to acquire: the discovery analytics (Aim 1) use Mendelian-randomization methods I co-developed with Dr. Andrew Lin's biostatistics group (NIH R01 GM131142, co-investigator); the prospective validation cohort (Aim 2) extends the recruitment infrastructure of our currently-funded K23 study (K23 HL148746, PI, ending 2026-11); and the EHR-integrated clinical-decision-support deployment (Aim 3) leverages the institutional informatics partnership with [Health-System Informatics Director], whose letter of support is in the application. The eMERGE-IV consortium membership (Collaborator A on this application) extends the Aim 1 validation set to ~50,000 additional statin-exposed patients across seven academic medical centers.

I take seriously the team-science governance that makes work like this possible: I have chaired the institutional Translational Cardiovascular Pharmacogenomics Working Group since 2023, served on the NIH NHLBI's Pharmacogenomics Network Steering Committee since 2024, and mentor four PhD students and two postdoctoral fellows in cardiovascular pharmacogenomics. Three of my mentees have been first authors on the manuscripts cited as preliminary data for this application; one (Dr. Maria Velasquez) holds a K99 award and is now an Assistant Professor at [Institution Y]. I commit, on this application, to the same mentorship density and team-science discipline that have produced the preliminary data the R01 builds upon.

PMID: 38271546. PMCID: PMC11048321. DOI: 10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.123.067821.

## C. Contributions to Science

The five contributions below are themed, not chronological. Each names a coherent line of investigation, the finding, why it mattered, and my role. Up to four citations per contribution; full bibliography at the NCBI MyBibliography URL above. Total citations across the five contributions: nineteen.

### Contribution 1 — Established the SLCO1B1-mediated transporter pathway as a quantitative predictor of simvastatin-induced myopathy in a discovery + validation cohort.

My doctoral and early-postdoctoral work characterized the SLCO1B1 *c.521T>C* (*rs4149056*) polymorphism's quantitative effect on simvastatin pharmacokinetics and downstream myopathy risk, validating in two independent cohorts (Stanford-UCSF discovery, n = 1,847; Boston-Brigham validation, n = 2,103) the dose-dependent risk gradient — homozygous variant carriers had a 4.5-fold higher 12-month myopathy incidence on simvastatin 80 mg than wild-type (95% CI 2.8–7.2; p < 0.001) — and showed that the effect was specific to OATP1B1-substrate statins (simvastatin, atorvastatin). The work established the *single-gene* discovery template that the proposed R01 generalizes to *gene-by-environment* interactions; methodologically, the discovery + validation + drug-class-specificity triad recurs in the proposed Aims 1 and 2.

1. **Chen SW**, Stoffel CL, Giacomini KM. *SLCO1B1 c.521T>C and simvastatin myopathy: discovery-cohort validation and clinical-decision-support implications.* **Clinical Pharmacology & Therapeutics**. 2014;96(2):198–207. PMID: 24798458. PMCID: PMC4124067.
2. **Chen SW**, Park RJ, Giacomini KM. *Drug-class specificity of OATP1B1 polymorphisms in statin pharmacokinetics: a four-statin within-subject crossover study.* **Clinical Pharmacology & Therapeutics**. 2016;100(4):412–423. PMID: 27341212. PMCID: PMC5024829.
3. Park RJ, **Chen SW**, Stoffel CL. *SLCO1B1-guided statin prescribing: a cost-effectiveness analysis in two US health systems.* **Annals of Internal Medicine**. 2018;169(8):547–556. PMID: 30242396.
4. **Chen SW**, Velasquez MR, Lin AK. *The SLCO1B1 myopathy-risk model at five years: prospective discrimination in 4,201 statin starters.* **JAMA Cardiology**. 2019;4(11):1108–1116. PMID: 31532459. PMCID: PMC6824277.

### Contribution 2 — Discovered the CYP3A4\*22 × CYP3A4-inhibitor interaction underlying a major fraction of statin-associated muscle symptoms in CYP3A4-substrate statins.

Building on the single-gene template above, my laboratory at [Institution] assembled a 10,247-patient biobank with prospective muscle-outcome phenotyping (linked whole-exome sequencing, complete medication histories, serial CK, validated SAMS-Clinical-Index scores) and demonstrated that the combination of a *CYP3A4\*22* reduced-function variant and a concomitant CYP3A4-inhibitor medication (amiodarone, diltiazem, macrolide antibiotics, others) was associated with a 4.7-fold increased risk of SAMS within 12 months of simvastatin or atorvastatin initiation (95% CI 3.1–7.2; p < 0.001), with the interaction absent for pravastatin and rosuvastatin (non-CYP3A4 substrates). This is the central preliminary finding the proposed R01 will validate prospectively (Aim 2) and translate to clinical decision support (Aim 3); the *Circulation* paper has been cited 142 times since publication.

1. **Chen SW**, Lin AK, Velasquez MR, Park RJ, Giacomini KM. *CYP3A4\*22 and concomitant CYP3A4 inhibitors predict statin-associated muscle symptoms in a single-institution biobank cohort.* **Circulation**. 2024;149(14):1102–1115. PMID: 38271546. PMCID: PMC11048321. *(Aim 1 anchoring publication.)*
2. **Chen SW**, Velasquez MR, Lin AK. *Gene-by-environment interactions in statin pharmacogenomics: a methodological framework.* **Clinical Pharmacology & Therapeutics**. 2023;114(3):611–624. PMID: 37214592. PMCID: PMC10428764.
3. Velasquez MR, **Chen SW**, Park RJ. *Replication of the CYP3A4\*22 × CYP3A4-inhibitor SAMS interaction in the eMERGE-III network: a 14,892-patient analysis.* **Pharmacogenomics Journal**. 2025;25(2):88–101. PMID: 39604721. PMCID: PMC12183047.
4. **Chen SW**. *From single-gene pharmacogenomics to gene-by-environment risk prediction: a precision-medicine framework for statin tolerability.* **Nature Reviews Cardiology**. 2025;22(4):245–260. *(invited review)* PMID: 40012883.

### Contribution 3 — Co-developed Mendelian-randomization methods for gene-by-environment interaction estimation in pharmacogenomic observational cohorts.

In collaboration with Dr. Andrew Lin's biostatistics group (Co-Investigator on this R01), I co-developed an extension of two-sample Mendelian randomization that accommodates a multiplicative interaction term between a genetic instrument and a continuous or categorical environmental exposure, with closed-form variance estimators and sensitivity analyses for instrument-exposure violations and unmeasured confounding. The method is now adopted across the eMERGE-IV consortium for gene-by-co-medication analyses; the software implementation (R package `mr.gxe`) has > 6,000 CRAN downloads since release. This methodology underlies the proposed Aim 1 discovery analytics.

1. Velasquez MR, Lin AK, Park RJ, Stoffel CL, **Chen SW**. *Mendelian randomization for gene-by-environment interaction estimation in pharmacogenomic cohorts.* **Statistics in Medicine**. 2022;41(28):5601–5618. PMID: 36110293. PMCID: PMC9742116.
2. Lin AK, **Chen SW**, Velasquez MR. *Sensitivity analysis for gene-by-environment Mendelian randomization under pleiotropic instrument violations.* **Biostatistics**. 2024;25(1):112–129. PMID: 37789214.
3. **Chen SW**, Lin AK. *Open-source software for gene-by-environment Mendelian randomization (mr.gxe).* **Bioinformatics**. 2023;39(8):btad482. PMID: 37498217. PMCID: PMC10421843. *(software RRID: SCR_024118)*

### Contribution 4 — Demonstrated the population-level cardiovascular consequences of statin discontinuation driven by perceived muscle symptoms, using linked EHR + claims + mortality data.

To establish the public-health stakes of SAMS-driven non-adherence — the *why this matters* paragraph the R01 inherits from this contribution — my group conducted a retrospective cohort study (n = 89,412 statin initiators across three US health systems) linking statin discontinuation within 12 months to subsequent major-adverse-cardiovascular-event (MACE) incidence over five years. Statin discontinuation within 12 months was associated with a 1.42-fold increased 5-year MACE rate (95% CI 1.31–1.54), adjusted for baseline cardiovascular risk; among discontinuers, 67% cited muscle symptoms as the reason. The work provides the quantitative public-health stakes the proposed R01 Aim 3 deployment will address.

1. Park RJ, **Chen SW**, Velasquez MR, Lin AK. *Statin discontinuation within 12 months and 5-year major adverse cardiovascular event incidence: a multi-system retrospective cohort.* **Lancet Public Health**. 2024;9(7):e489–e499. PMID: 38876421. PMCID: PMC11423019.
2. **Chen SW**, Park RJ. *Preventable cardiovascular events attributable to statin discontinuation: a population-attributable-fraction analysis.* **JAMA Cardiology**. 2025;10(2):182–191. PMID: 39612847.
3. Velasquez MR, **Chen SW**. *Patient-reported muscle symptoms versus objectively measured myopathy: discordance and clinical-decision implications.* **Annals of Internal Medicine**. 2023;176(11):1481–1490. PMID: 37844319.
4. **Chen SW**, Park RJ, Stoffel CL. *Statin adherence and cardiovascular mortality: a target-trial-emulation analysis in the Veterans Affairs cohort.* **JAMA Internal Medicine**. 2024;184(8):901–909. PMID: 38856712. PMCID: PMC11267548.

### Contribution 5 — Translated pharmacogenomic discovery to EHR-integrated clinical decision support: a deployment-evaluation paradigm.

To anchor the R01 Aim 3 deployment science, my group conducted the first prospective evaluation of EHR-integrated pharmacogenomic clinical decision support at point-of-prescription for SLCO1B1-guided statin selection. In a stepped-wedge cluster-randomized trial across 12 primary-care clinics (NCT04XXXXXXX), the CDS alert reduced inappropriate high-dose simvastatin prescribing by 41% (95% CI 28% to 52%) and was associated with a 23% reduction in 12-month myopathy incidence (95% CI 8% to 36%). The deployment-evaluation paradigm — pre-specified primary outcome, stepped-wedge design, EHR-native alert integration, qualitative implementation study running in parallel — is the template the proposed R01 Aim 3 inherits and extends.

1. **Chen SW**, Velasquez MR, [Informatics-Director], Park RJ. *EHR-integrated SLCO1B1-guided statin clinical decision support: a stepped-wedge cluster-randomized trial.* **Nature Medicine**. 2024;30(5):1342–1353. PMID: 38734281. PMCID: PMC11198432.
2. Velasquez MR, **Chen SW**. *Implementation outcomes of pharmacogenomic clinical decision support: a mixed-methods study.* **Implementation Science**. 2024;19:42. PMID: 38869117. PMCID: PMC11201938.
3. **Chen SW**, [Informatics-Director], Park RJ. *Alert-fatigue calibration for pharmacogenomic CDS: a framework with quantitative thresholds.* **JAMIA**. 2025;32(3):548–559. PMID: 39798241.
4. **Chen SW**. *Pharmacogenomic clinical decision support: from proof-of-concept to scaled deployment.* **Annual Review of Pharmacology and Toxicology**. 2026;66:[in press]. *(invited review; manuscript ID ARPT-2025-0412)*
