# Operative note — Right primary total hip arthroplasty

**Patient:** Eleanor Martinez · MRN-4516 · 67yo F · DOB redacted
**Date of operation:** 2026-05-24
**Operating room:** OR 7
**Anaesthesia start:** 07:42 · **Incision:** 08:14 · **Closure complete:** 09:58 · **Patient out of room:** 10:08
**Length of procedure:** 1 h 44 min (incision to closure)

**Surgeon:** Dr. Marcus Wei, MD — Adult Reconstruction, Attending of record
**Assistant:** Dr. Theo Ramirez, MD — PGY-3 Orthopaedic Surgery (under direct supervision throughout)
**Scrub nurse:** RN Janet Park, BSN, CNOR
**Circulating nurse:** RN Daniel Cho, BSN
**Anaesthesia:** Dr. Priya Khanna, MD — Anaesthesiology Attending (general endotracheal anaesthesia)
**Implant rep present:** Yes — DePuy Synthes representative scrubbed at the back table

---

## PRE-OPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS

Severe right hip osteoarthritis (Kellgren–Lawrence grade 4), refractory to 18 months of nonoperative management (physiotherapy, NSAIDs, weight management, single intra-articular corticosteroid injection in March 2026 with transient benefit only).

## POST-OPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS

Same. Intra-operative findings confirmed the pre-operative diagnosis: complete loss of articular cartilage on both the femoral head and the acetabular surface, circumferential osteophyte formation, eburnated subchondral bone. No evidence of inflammatory or infectious arthropathy intra-operatively.

## PROCEDURE PERFORMED

Primary right total hip arthroplasty via posterior (Moore / Southern) approach, cementless press-fit acetabular and femoral components, 36 mm ceramic-on-highly-crosslinked-polyethylene bearing. CPT 27130.

## ANAESTHESIA

General endotracheal anaesthesia, induced by Dr. Khanna. Anaesthetic course uncomplicated. Intra-operative tranexamic acid 1 g IV at incision and 1 g IV at closure (per institutional ERAS-arthroplasty protocol). Antibiotic prophylaxis: cefazolin 2 g IV at 07:35 (30 min prior to incision; re-dosed at 11:00 per duration protocol if patient remained intubated; not re-dosed as case was completed within window).

## ESTIMATED BLOOD LOSS

350 mL.

## SPECIMENS

The native right femoral head was sent to pathology in formalin (labelled: *"Right femoral head, primary THA"*); requested examination for any unexpected pathology (inflammatory arthropathy, occult tumour, avascular necrosis). No frozen-section requested; permanent-section evaluation only.

## DRAINS

**None.** No subfascial or subcutaneous drain placed. (Per current arthroplasty evidence and institutional ERAS protocol; routine drain placement has not demonstrated benefit in primary THA and is associated with higher transfusion rates.)

## IMPLANTS

All implants documented at the time of placement by the circulating nurse with confirmation of catalog number and lot number against the manufacturer packaging.

| Component | Manufacturer | Model | Size / specification | Catalog # | Lot # |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Acetabular cup** | DePuy Synthes | Pinnacle Gription 100 (multi-hole, HA-coated, cementless) | 56 mm outer diameter | 1101-56-000 | (documented in EHR implant log) |
| **Acetabular liner** | DePuy Synthes | Marathon HXLPE (highly cross-linked polyethylene), neutral profile | 36 mm inner diameter | 1106-3656-N | (documented in EHR implant log) |
| **Femoral stem** | DePuy Synthes | Corail (cementless, collared, tapered wedge, HA-coated, fully porous) | Size 5 standard offset | 1110-05-S00 | (documented in EHR implant log) |
| **Femoral head** | DePuy Synthes | Biolox Delta (ceramic) | 36 mm diameter, +0 (neutral) neck length | 1120-3600-N | (documented in EHR implant log) |
| **Acetabular screws** | None placed | — | — | — | — |
| **Cement** | None used | — | — | — | — |

## INDICATIONS

The patient is a 67-year-old woman with end-stage right hip osteoarthritis (Kellgren–Lawrence grade 4 on the 2026-04-12 AP pelvis radiograph) and 4 years of progressive hip pain limiting her function. She has failed 18 months of structured nonoperative management including: physiotherapy (12-week structured course completed 2025-09 with no durable benefit); NSAIDs (naproxen, then meloxicam, both with partial benefit and GI intolerance); weight management (BMI reduced from 32 to 29 over 12 months); a single intra-articular corticosteroid injection (March 2026) with transient benefit lasting six weeks only.

Pre-operative medical clearance was obtained from her primary care physician on 2026-04-28 and from cardiology (consultation for known well-controlled HTN and HLD) on 2026-05-05. She was cleared for general anaesthesia and surgery. Anticoagulation was held appropriately (last home aspirin 81 mg on 2026-05-17).

Risks, benefits, and alternatives were discussed in detail at the pre-operative visit on 2026-05-10 and again on the morning of surgery in the pre-operative holding area. Procedure-specific risks named: surgical-site infection (1–2 %); dislocation (1–3 % via posterior approach; mitigated by capsular repair); intra-operative or peri-operative fracture (< 1 %); leg-length inequality perceptible to the patient (5–10 %); sciatic-nerve injury (~ 1 %, mostly neuropraxia with full recovery; rare complete laceration with foot-drop); thromboembolic disease (DVT / PE; mitigated by chemical and mechanical prophylaxis); cardiac, pulmonary, urinary, and renal complications related to anaesthesia and immobility; implant-related complications including aseptic loosening and the eventual need for revision surgery (median time to revision in modern cementless THA exceeds 20 years per registry data). Alternatives explicitly named and declined by the patient: continued nonoperative management; alternative surgical approaches (direct anterior, anterolateral, direct lateral, each with its own structures-at-risk profile); hip resurfacing (not a candidate given age and bone quality). Written informed consent was obtained, signed, and is on file in the chart.

## FINDINGS

The right hip joint showed end-stage osteoarthritis as expected: complete loss of articular cartilage on the femoral head with eburnation of the subchondral bone (the dome of the femoral head was bare cortical bone); complete loss of acetabular cartilage with similar eburnation; circumferential acetabular osteophyte formation (most prominent at the posterior-inferior rim, ~ 8 mm thick); femoral osteophyte formation at the head-neck junction. The labrum was attenuated and was excised. No evidence of inflammatory arthropathy (no synovial hypertrophy beyond what is typical of OA; no pannus formation); no evidence of infection (clear synovial fluid, normal-appearing capsule); no evidence of avascular necrosis or occult tumour (the femoral head trabecular architecture was preserved beneath the eburnation). Bone quality was good throughout (cancellous bone of normal density on broaching; cortical rim of the acetabulum intact). The medial femoral circumflex artery was identified deep to the quadratus femoris and was preserved during the approach.

## TECHNIQUE

The patient was identified in the pre-operative holding area and the surgical site (right hip) was marked with a sterile surgical marker by the surgeon (Dr. Wei) and witnessed by the patient and the circulating nurse. The patient was transported to OR 7. General endotracheal anaesthesia was induced by Dr. Khanna with the patient supine on the gurney. Following intubation, the patient was transferred to a radiolucent operating table and positioned in the **left lateral decubitus position with the right hip up**, secured with well-padded anterior (over the ASIS) and posterior (over the sacrum) pegs; an axillary roll was placed; the well leg (left) was padded with the hip and knee in slight flexion for stability; the dependent peroneal nerve was padded at the fibular neck; the dependent eye and ear were protected with foam. The pelvis was confirmed perpendicular to the table by palpation of both anterior superior iliac spines.

A pre-incision **time-out** was performed at 08:08 with all personnel present (surgeon, assistant, anaesthesiologist, scrub nurse, circulating nurse, implant rep). The time-out confirmed: patient identification (name + MRN + DOB); procedure (right primary THA, posterior approach); site (right hip, marked); operative consent on file; allergies (none); antibiotic prophylaxis (cefazolin 2 g IV given at 07:35); availability of all required implants (Pinnacle Gription 54/56/58 mm; Marathon liners; Corail 4/5/6; Biolox Delta heads -3.5/+0/+5/+8.5 mm); availability of backup cemented implants on the back table; availability of blood (type and screen on file; no cross-matched units requested).

The right hip was prepped with two 30-second applications of 2 % chlorhexidine gluconate in 70 % isopropyl alcohol, allowed to dry, and draped in the usual sterile fashion. Iodine-impregnated adhesive incise drape was applied.

A 10 cm incision was made centred over the greater trochanter, curving slightly posteriorly toward the PSIS proximally and extending distally along the femoral shaft axis. The subcutaneous tissue was divided with electrocautery, with haemostasis achieved at each layer. The fascia lata was incised in line with its fibres distally; the gluteus maximus was split bluntly in the fibre direction proximally with finger dissection (preserving the inferior gluteal nerve, which enters the muscle from the deep surface medially). The trochanteric bursa was incised, exposing the deep posterior structures.

**The sciatic nerve was identified** under the inferior border of the piriformis muscle by palpation and visualisation; the nerve was protected by a soft-tissue retractor throughout the remainder of the case. The short external rotators were divided sequentially at their trochanteric insertions, each tagged with a #2 non-absorbable suture for later anatomic repair: the **piriformis** tendon first (most superior), then the **conjoint tendon** of obturator internus and the gemelli (middle), then the **quadratus femoris** (most inferior; preserving the medial femoral circumflex artery on its deep surface). A T-shaped capsulotomy was performed with the longitudinal limb along the femoral neck axis and the transverse limb at the acetabular rim; the capsular flaps were tagged with #2 non-absorbable stay sutures for later repair.

The hip was dislocated posteriorly by flexing to 90°, adducting, and internally rotating. The femoral head delivered without resistance. The femoral neck osteotomy was made with an oscillating saw at 10 mm proximal to the lesser trochanter (per pre-operative templating; reference point confirmed by palpation), angled per the Corail stem-specific guide; irrigation was continuous to prevent thermal necrosis. The native femoral head was extracted with a corkscrew extractor and passed to the back table for pathology (measured at 48 mm diameter at the back table; consistent with the 56 mm planned cup).

**Acetabular preparation.** Self-retaining retractors were placed: a curved Hohmann anteriorly over the anterior wall (psoas displaced; retractor tip on bone to protect the femoral nerve and external iliac vessels); a Hohmann posteriorly over the ischium; a Hohmann inferiorly under the transverse acetabular ligament. The acetabular labrum was excised circumferentially. The pulvinar was removed from the cotyloid fossa. Sequential acetabular reaming was performed with the reamer oriented at 45° abduction and 20° anteversion relative to the perpendicular-to-floor pelvic reference established at positioning: 52 mm reamer, then 54 mm reamer, then 55 mm reamer (1 mm under the planned 56 mm cup, per Pinnacle Gription press-fit protocol). Medial-wall integrity was confirmed by palpation after each reaming pass. The reamed bed showed dense cancellous bone with haematic ooze and an intact cortical rim — bone quality criteria for press-fit were satisfied; the case proceeded to press-fit cup (cement backup not required).

A 56 mm trial cup was placed and confirmed good seating against the medial wall and circumferential cortical contact. The final **DePuy Pinnacle Gription 56 mm cup** was inserted with the cup impactor at 45° abduction / 20° anteversion. Seating was confirmed by direct visualisation and by feel. No acetabular screws were required (cup achieved primary press-fit stability without supplementary fixation). The **Marathon HXLPE 36 mm inner-diameter liner** was inserted and locked in place; locking mechanism confirmed by direct inspection.

**Femoral preparation.** The leg was repositioned in flexion, adduction, and external rotation to deliver the proximal femur into the operative field; a Hohmann was placed anterior to the femur to elevate. The piriformis fossa was identified; a box-osteotome was used to open the canal at the piriformis fossa, removing the lateral 'shoulder' of bone that obstructs straight-line broach entry. A canal-finder was passed and confirmed the canal axis without resistance.

Sequential broaching was performed with controlled mallet blows: size 3 broach, then size 4, then size 5 (the planned final size per templating). The size 5 broach achieved full seating to the calcar collar, rotational stability (could not be rotated by hand), circumferential metaphyseal fit, and no distal canal tightening — broaching endpoints all satisfied.

A trial reduction was performed with the +0 (neutral) neck length and the 36 mm trial head. Stability was assessed: flexion to 90° with adduction and internal rotation to 30° was stable without subluxation; extension with external rotation to 30° was stable. Range of motion was confirmed: flexion to 110°, abduction to 45°, internal rotation in flexion to 30°. Leg length was measured by direct medial-malleoli comparison with the hips squared; the operative leg matched the contralateral leg within 2 mm. Soft-tissue tension (shuck test) was 3 mm of distraction — appropriate. The trial result supported proceeding with +0 neck length and standard offset stem.

The trial broach was removed. The final **DePuy Corail size 5 cementless tapered-wedge stem** (collared, HA-coated, fully porous) was inserted with the stem impactor and seated to the calcar collar with controlled mallet blows. Stem version was confirmed at approximately 15° anteversion relative to the posterior condyles of the distal femur. The stem trunnion was cleaned thoroughly with a sterile dry sponge and inspected for any debris. The **Biolox Delta ceramic 36 mm head with +0 neck length** was placed on the trunnion and seated with a soft (plastic-tipped) impactor to engage the Morse taper.

The hip was reduced by traction and gentle internal rotation; a satisfying 'clunk' confirmed reduction. Range of motion and stability were re-assessed and were consistent with the trial result.

## CLOSURE

The wound was thoroughly irrigated with 3 L of normal saline. The posterior capsule was repaired with the previously-placed #2 non-absorbable stay sutures, restoring the T-shaped capsulotomy to its native anatomy. The short external rotators (piriformis, conjoint tendon, quadratus femoris) were reattached at their trochanteric insertions through transosseous bone tunnels drilled in the posterior greater trochanter, using the previously-placed #2 non-absorbable tags (Pellicci-style capsular and rotator repair to minimise dislocation risk).

The fascia lata was closed with #1 Vicryl interrupted sutures, tension-free. The subcutaneous tissue was closed with 2-0 Vicryl interrupted sutures. The skin was closed with surgical staples per the patient's request and surgeon preference. Sterile dressing applied (Aquacel Ag over the incision; tegaderm overlay).

## COUNTS

**Correct, x2.** Sponge, needle, and instrument counts were correct at the start of closure (08:35) and again at completion of skin closure (09:58). Confirmed by the scrub nurse (Janet Park, BSN, CNOR) and the circulating nurse (Daniel Cho, BSN).

## CONDITION

The patient tolerated the procedure well. She was extubated by Dr. Khanna at 10:02 without complication. She was transferred to PACU in stable haemodynamic condition (BP 124/76, HR 78, SpO2 99 % on 4 L NC, T 36.4 °C) and remained Full Code throughout the procedure.

## POST-OPERATIVE PLAN

- **Weight-bearing:** weight-bearing as tolerated (WBAT) on the right lower extremity from POD#1, with walker; modern cementless press-fit implants tolerate immediate WBAT (AAOS CPG 2023; GRADE: high).
- **Posterior hip precautions for 6 weeks:** no hip flexion past 90°; no hip adduction past midline; no hip internal rotation past neutral; no combining the above (the dislocation moment is *flexion + adduction + internal rotation*); elevated toilet seat; abduction pillow when supine; chair with raised seat.
- **DVT prophylaxis:** aspirin 81 mg PO BID × 35 days post-op (low-risk patient per institutional protocol); sequential compression devices on the contralateral leg in hospital.
- **Pain management:** multimodal analgesia — acetaminophen 1 g PO q6h scheduled; celecoxib 200 mg PO BID × 14 days; oxycodone 5 mg PO q4h PRN breakthrough (limited quantity).
- **Antibiotic prophylaxis:** cefazolin 2 g IV q8h × 3 doses total post-operatively (per institutional protocol).
- **Pulmonary:** incentive spirometry q1h while awake.
- **Mobility:** physiotherapy POD#1; sit-to-stand and transfers; ambulation with walker.
- **Foley:** removed POD#1 if placed; will not be placed routinely.
- **Diet:** advance as tolerated POD#0.
- **Labs:** CBC POD#1 (haemoglobin trend); BMP POD#1 if any clinical concern.
- **Follow-up:** wound check POD#10–14 (staples removed if used); radiographic follow-up (AP pelvis + lateral hip) at 6 weeks; clinic appointment at 6 weeks.
- **Discharge planning:** anticipated discharge home POD#2 with home health physiotherapy; case manager (Robin Vaughn) notified pre-operatively; family-support arrangements confirmed.

## ATTENDING SURGEON PRESENCE

**Dr. Marcus Wei** (attending surgeon of record) was present and scrubbed for the entire procedure from time-out through skin closure. CMS billing requirement: attending presence for the entire critical and key portions of the procedure was satisfied.

## RESIDENT PARTICIPATION

**Dr. Theo Ramirez** (PGY-3 Orthopaedic Surgery) participated under direct supervision throughout the case, performing the femoral broaching, the cup-trial confirmation, and assisting throughout the approach, exposure, and closure. Resident participation in operative steps was at a level appropriate to PGY-3 training and was directly supervised by the attending surgeon throughout.

```markdown
<!--
================================================================================
Template: osce-station.md
Subject: Breaking bad news — communicating a new diagnosis of pancreatic cancer
Audience: PGY-1 internal medicine / late MS4 / family medicine residency
Signature move: 6.2 dual-substrate artifact (one encounter, four scored documents)
Register: Technical for examiner docs; warm-familiar (in-character) for SP script
Pair with: references/medium-playbooks/assessment-artifact.md

================================================================================

Why this subject:
  Breaking-bad-news stations are among the highest-stakes OSCE genres — the
  technical content (the diagnosis, the next steps) is easier than the
  communication discipline (sit at eye level, fire a warning shot, allow
  silence, respond to affect first). Pancreatic cancer is dense enough that
  the candidate cannot recite their way through; the SP is in distress, which
  forces the candidate to *attend to the patient*, not deliver a speech. The
  station discriminates between candidates who can sit with discomfort and
  those who cannot. Calibration: PGY-1 IM / late MS4 / FM residency entry.

CUSTOMIZE — slots to adapt when reusing this scaffold:

  1. Subject + scenario. The diagnosis, the patient, the setting. Adapt to
     other communication-skills genres (informed consent; goals-of-care
     conversation; disclosing a medical error; agitation de-escalation).
  2. Length and station type. The station ships as 14 minutes (10 candidate +
     2 SP feedback + 2 examiner viva). Adjust for shorter circuits (10 min)
     or longer (20-minute integrated stations).
  3. Checklist. Behavioural items only; rewritten for any change in clinical
     content. Each item is observable; "demonstrated empathy" is not.
  4. Global rating scale. Anchored at 1 (clear fail), 4 (pass), 7 (exceptional).
     Re-anchor if rating range differs (some institutions use 5-point).
  5. Patient script. Backstory rich enough that the SP can adlib answers; the
     opening line and the "trigger" facts (the cue the candidate misses or
     catches) are scripted exactly.
  6. Feedback rubric. For the post-station debrief, structured by SPIKES
     (Setting / Perception / Invitation / Knowledge / Empathy / Strategy).

# OSCE Station: Breaking bad news — new diagnosis of pancreatic cancer

**Station length:** 14 minutes (10 min candidate encounter + 2 min SP feedback + 2 min examiner viva)
**Candidate level:** PGY-1 internal medicine / late MS4 / family medicine residency
**Last reviewed:** 2026-05-24 — self-attested by author
**Construct measured:** Communication of serious news (SPIKES protocol); response to patient affect; integration of next clinical steps

---

## Document 1 — Candidate brief

> *To be posted on the station door. Candidate has 1 minute to read before entering.*

**You are an FY1 / intern in the outpatient gastroenterology clinic.**

Mrs. Eleanor Whitmore is a 62-year-old woman who was investigated for two months of progressive epigastric pain, 8 kg unintentional weight loss, and new-onset painless jaundice. A CT abdomen and pancreas-protocol MRI showed a 3.2 cm mass in the head of the pancreas with regional lymph-node involvement; endoscopic ultrasound with fine-needle aspiration returned cytology positive for pancreatic adenocarcinoma. Staging is consistent with locally advanced disease (likely T3 N1 M0; resectability to be determined at MDT).

She is here today, with her daughter Hannah waiting in the corridor, for the results conversation. She knows tests were done. She has not been told the result.

**Your task (10 minutes):**

- Disclose the diagnosis using a structured approach.
- Respond to the patient's emotional reactions.
- Outline the immediate next steps (MDT referral, oncology, supportive care).
- The daughter will not be in the room unless the patient asks.

**At minute 9, the examiner will pause the encounter and ask one question.**

---

## Document 2 — Standardised-patient script (Mrs. Eleanor Whitmore)

> *For the SP. Trained role; the SP should have rehearsed this script with the examiner team and be familiar with the affect cues below.*

### Backstory (the SP knows this; the candidate is not told)

You are Eleanor Whitmore, 62. You worked as a secondary-school English teacher until you retired three years ago. Your husband Tom died of cardiac arrest 18 months ago; you live alone in the house you raised your children in. Your daughter Hannah, 36, is an A&E nurse at a different hospital; she has driven you here today and is waiting in the corridor. Your son David lives in Australia and you speak to him on Sundays.

For two months you have had a *gnawing* pain in your upper abdomen, worse after eating, radiating to your back. You have lost 8 kg without trying. Three weeks ago you noticed your skin was yellow and your urine was the colour of strong tea. Your GP referred you urgently; you have had blood tests, a CT scan, an MRI, and an endoscopic procedure where they took a sample. You have been worried but have tried not to let on to Hannah; you have not allowed yourself to look up your symptoms online. You have suspected something is seriously wrong but have not allowed yourself to name it.

You trust doctors but you are also frightened. You will read the candidate's face the moment they sit down.

### Opening line (delivered exactly)

> *"Doctor. Thank you for seeing me. My daughter Hannah is outside — should I have her come in? I wasn't sure if she should be here for whatever this is."*

### Affect cues by phase

| Encounter phase | Expected candidate move | Your response |
|-----------------|------------------------|---------------|
| Greeting + setting | Introduces self by name + role; offers seat; checks who else should be present | You answer: *"I'm a bit nervous. Yes, this is fine."* If the candidate asks about Hannah, say: *"She wanted to be in. I told her I would come in first and call her if I needed her. I'll see how this goes."* |
| Perception check (*"What have you been told so far?"*) | Asks what you know | You give the truthful summary: *"They said they were looking for what's causing the weight loss and the jaundice. The GP said there was something on the scan. I don't know more than that."* |
| Invitation (*"How much would you like to know?"*) | Asks how much information you want | You answer: *"I want to know everything. I'd rather know than not know."* If the candidate does not ask this and goes straight to diagnosis, *do not stop them* — but rate this on the feedback. |
| Warning shot (*"I'm afraid the news isn't good"*) | Fires a warning shot before the diagnosis | You take a breath. Nod slowly. *"Go on."* |
| Diagnosis delivered | States the diagnosis in plain language | You go quiet. **Pause for at least 8 seconds.** Look down at your hands. If the candidate fills the silence, do not interrupt — let them — but rate this on the feedback. |
| First question | Allows you to ask | You ask: *"Is it cancer?"* (if not already stated using the word). Then: *"How long?"* (about prognosis). |
| Prognosis question | Acknowledges uncertainty; gives honest range | You ask: *"What about Hannah — can she come in now?"* This is your cue that you have heard enough for the moment and need your support person. |
| Closing | Outlines next steps; offers contact | You say: *"What do I tell my son in Australia? He'll want to fly back."* |

### Specific responses if asked

| Candidate asks | You say |
|----------------|---------|
| About your work / hobbies | *"I taught English for thirty-two years. Retired three years ago. I read. I garden. I have a book club on Thursdays."* |
| About your husband | *"Tom died eighteen months ago. Cardiac arrest. It was very sudden."* |
| Whether you have considered the possibility of cancer | *"I think — I knew. I didn't want to know. Does that make sense?"* |
| About finances / will | *"My will is up to date. Tom and I sorted it after his diagnosis."* |
| If they ask whether you have spiritual or faith support | *"I'm not religious. My book group is, though. They will help."* |

### Trigger facts (the candidate may or may not surface these)

- You drink a glass of wine most evenings; the candidate should not lecture you about this today.
- You smoked from age 18 to 42; quit twenty years ago.
- You have *not* discussed end-of-life preferences with anyone. If the candidate gently raises this in the context of "having the conversation with your family," respond: *"I haven't. I should, shouldn't I."*
- If the candidate asks about your support network, you mention Hannah, the book club, your neighbour Margaret.

### Empathy / safety cues

- If the candidate moves too fast (delivers diagnosis in the first two minutes, before perception or invitation), allow them to continue but show distress through body language: hand to mouth, looking away, eyes filling.
- If the candidate uses medical jargon without translating (*"adenocarcinoma"*, *"locally advanced"*, *"resectable"*), look puzzled and ask: *"I'm sorry, what does that mean?"*
- If the candidate becomes visibly distressed themselves, do not rescue them. Hold the silence. The examiner will rate the candidate's recovery.
- If at any point the candidate makes a clearly inappropriate statement (false reassurance, *"it'll be fine"*; minimisation, *"these things happen"*; presumption, *"you'll want chemo"*), look up sharply and say: *"I don't think that's quite right, is it?"* The candidate's recovery is part of the assessment.

---

## Document 3 — Examiner checklist

> *Examiner marks each item 1 (observed) or 0 (not observed) during the encounter. Total possible: 18 checklist points.*

### Setting and opening (3 items)

- [ ] Introduced self by full name **and** role
- [ ] Checked the patient's preferred name and used it
- [ ] Asked / addressed the question of whether daughter should be present

### Perception and invitation (3 items)

- [ ] Asked the patient what she had been told already (*"What have you understood so far?"*)
- [ ] Asked how much information she wanted to receive (*"How much detail would you like?"*)
- [ ] Used plain language in the perception check (no jargon)

### Warning shot (1 item)

- [ ] Fired a warning shot before the diagnosis (*"I'm afraid the news isn't what we hoped"* or equivalent)

### Knowledge delivery (4 items)

- [ ] Stated the diagnosis using a recognisable term (*cancer*, not only *adenocarcinoma*)
- [ ] Translated any medical jargon used (*"locally advanced means …"*)
- [ ] Paused for ≥ 5 seconds after the diagnosis was delivered
- [ ] Did *not* present a treatment plan in the same breath as the diagnosis

### Empathy and emotion (4 items)

- [ ] Acknowledged the patient's distress (verbal or non-verbal, named)
- [ ] Did not offer false reassurance (*"it'll be fine"*; *"we caught it early"*; *"don't worry"*)
- [ ] Tolerated silence (≥ 8 seconds without filling)
- [ ] Did not lecture about lifestyle factors (alcohol, smoking) during this encounter

### Strategy and next steps (3 items)

- [ ] Outlined the next clinical step (MDT referral / oncology appointment)
- [ ] Offered to bring the daughter into the room when the patient asked
- [ ] Provided a contact point for questions before the next appointment

### Critical-failure items (any one triggers automatic global rating ≤ 2)

- [ ] Delivered the diagnosis in the first 2 minutes without any perception or invitation step
- [ ] Used the phrase *"there's nothing we can do"* or equivalent terminal-pessimism statement
- [ ] Failed to use the word *cancer* when asked directly

---

## Document 4 — Global rating scale and feedback rubric

> *Examiner records a global rating after the checklist; rationale below the rating. The SP gives the candidate two minutes of structured feedback after the encounter.*

### Global rating scale (Royal College–style 7-point)

| Rating | Anchor | Brief description |
|--------|--------|-------------------|
| 7 | Exceptional | Performance indistinguishable from a senior who breaks news regularly. Pacing, empathy, and clinical content all integrated. The patient feels heard *and* informed. |
| 6 | Above competent | All elements present; one or two minor refinements possible. The patient is well-served. |
| 5 | Competent | All major elements present; some clumsiness or missed cues; the patient is informed but the empathy is procedural rather than felt. |
| 4 | **Pass** | The diagnosis is delivered; the patient is not harmed; major elements present but several missed cues or jargon lapses. |
| 3 | Borderline fail | Several major missed elements (e.g., no warning shot; jargon untranslated; rushed); the patient is informed but feels unheard. |
| 2 | Clear fail | A critical-failure item occurred, or multiple major elements missed; the encounter caused additional distress beyond the diagnosis itself. |
| 1 | Egregious | The candidate is unsafe in communication; remediation required. False reassurance, minimisation, terminal pessimism, or refusal to use the word *cancer* when asked. |

### SPIKES-based feedback rubric (post-station debrief)

> *Two minutes; structured by SPIKES. The SP and examiner each contribute.*

| SPIKES element | What the SP felt | What the examiner noted | Suggested move for next time |
|----------------|------------------|------------------------|-----------------------------|
| **S** etting | Was the room appropriate? Were you seated? Did the candidate manage the daughter question? | (examiner records) | (one specific suggestion) |
| **P** erception | Did the candidate ask what you knew? Did they listen? | | |
| **I** nvitation | Did the candidate ask how much you wanted to know? | | |
| **K** nowledge | Was the diagnosis delivered clearly? Plain language? Pause? | | |
| **E** mpathy | Did the candidate respond to your distress? Did they tolerate silence? | | |
| **S** trategy | Did you leave with clear next steps and a contact? | | |

The candidate writes one sentence in response: *"The single change I would make next time is …"* The exercise is the close of the station.

---

## Examiner viva (minute 9 interruption — 1 minute)

> *Examiner asks one of the following, chosen at random.*

1. *"You have 30 seconds. What is your immediate plan for this patient's care after this clinic visit?"*
   - Expected answer: MDT discussion within 7 days for resectability; oncology referral; supportive care / pain management; nutrition; social-work involvement.

2. *"Mrs. Whitmore asks you, 'How long do I have?' What do you say?"*
   - Expected answer: Honest acknowledgment of uncertainty; range-not-point (median survival for locally advanced pancreatic cancer 6–12 months without treatment, longer with effective therapy); offer to discuss in detail once MDT plan is known.

3. *"Mrs. Whitmore's daughter is a nurse. Does that change anything about how you communicate?"*
   - Expected answer: Slight adjustment of jargon level if the patient consents; daughter does not become the primary recipient of information; the patient remains the focus.

---

## Station administration notes

- **Room setup:** Two chairs at a 90° angle (not directly opposite — confrontational; not side-by-side — too intimate). Box of tissues visible. Door closable. No desk between the candidate and the patient.
- **SP training:** Minimum 4 hours; rehearsal of the script with the examiner team; standardised reactions; debrief after each candidate.
- **Inter-rater reliability:** Two examiners trained on the same rubric should agree within 1 point on the global rating in at least 80% of cases. Calibration sessions before each circuit.
- **Bias review:** The candidate's accent, gender, and apparent age should not influence the rating. Examiners are trained to mark the *behaviours observed*, not the *impression formed*.

<sub>OSCE station prepared for residency-entry communication-skills assessment. Last reviewed 2026-05-24. Self-attested by author. No conflicts of interest. Patient is fictional; the encounter draws on common breaking-bad-news training scenarios in UK and US residency curricula.</sub>
```

# Pre-Participation Evaluation — soccer clearance

> **Athlete.** Adolescent female, age 16, varsity school + club soccer (midfielder). Pre-season clearance for fall season; first PPE at this practice.
>
> **Date of evaluation.** 2026-05-24. **Evaluator.** primary-care physician (self-attested). **Form derived from:** PPE 5th edition (AAP / AAFP / ACSM / AMSSM / AOSSM / AOASM consensus monograph, 2019); AHA 14-element cardiovascular screen (Maron BJ et al., *Circulation* 2014;130:1303-1334). **Sport-load classification:** Mitchell IIIB high-dynamic moderate-static (Mitchell 2005, 36th Bethesda Conference).
>
> **Mandatory pre-read for the parent and athlete.** Complete History section at home; bring to the visit. Any **YES** answer on the AHA 14 history items routes to a branched follow-up question that the physician will work through with you at the visit. The form will *not* issue clearance until every YES is resolved.

---

## Section 1 — Demographic and contact

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **Athlete name** | A. R. (initials only on this template; full name on production form) |
| **Date of birth** | 2010-02-14 (age 16 at evaluation) |
| **Sex assigned at birth / gender** | Female / cisgender female |
| **Sport(s) and level** | Soccer (varsity school team + competitive club, U17) |
| **Position** | Midfielder |
| **Prior PPE date** | None at this practice; prior PPE 2024 at an outside clinic (records requested but not received at time of visit) |
| **Primary-care physician** | this office |
| **Pediatric cardiologist (if any)** | none currently |
| **Emergency contact** | mother (cell on file) |
| **Insurance / consent on file** | yes |

---

## Section 2 — Past medical, surgical, and medication history

The PPE 5th ed. monograph standard items. Athlete/parent completes at home; physician confirms at visit.

| Item | Athlete response | Physician confirmation |
|---|---|---|
| Hospitalisations (lifetime) | none | confirmed |
| Surgeries (lifetime) | none | confirmed |
| Chronic medical conditions | none | confirmed; no asthma, no diabetes, no inflammatory or rheumatologic disease |
| Daily prescription medications | none | confirmed |
| Daily over-the-counter or supplement use | none | confirmed; no creatine, no protein powder beyond food-equivalent, no pre-workout |
| Allergies (food, drug, environmental) | none known | confirmed |
| Immunisations current per CDC schedule | yes | confirmed; HPV series complete; influenza this season; COVID booster current; meningococcal current (school requirement) |
| Last menstrual period (LMP) | 2026-05-12 (12 days prior to visit) | confirmed; menarche age 13; cycles 28–30 days, regular; no concern for relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S) |

> **Female-athlete-triad / RED-S screen.** Three questions per IOC consensus (Mountjoy et al., *Br J Sports Med* 2018;52:687-697): (a) intentional weight loss in the past year — *no*; (b) menstrual irregularity (oligomenorrhea, amenorrhea > 3 months, or primary amenorrhea) — *no*; (c) stress fracture or bone-stress injury history — *no*. **Screen negative.** If any *yes*, route to nutrition + endocrine consultation before clearance.

---

## Section 3 — AHA 14-element cardiovascular screen

The American Heart Association recommends 12 personal-history and 2 physical-exam items as the screening floor for pre-participation cardiovascular evaluation in young athletes (Maron BJ et al., *Circulation* 2014;130:1303-1334). The 14 items appear below in canonical numeric order. **Each YES routes to a branched follow-up the physician resolves before clearance.**

### Personal history (items 1–7)

| # | Item | A. R. response | Branched follow-up if YES |
|---|------|----------------|---------------------------|
| **1** | Chest pain, discomfort, tightness, or pressure related to exertion | **NO** | (none required) |
| **2** | Unexplained syncope or near-syncope, *especially exertional* | **NO** | If YES: characterise as vasovagal vs cardiogenic (timing relative to exertion, prodrome, witness account, post-event recovery). **Exertional syncope is a HOLD-AND-REFER item** regardless of other findings (Maron 2014; Class I, LoE C). |
| **3** | Excessive exertional and unexplained dyspnea, fatigue, or palpitations | **NO** | If YES: characterise pattern, frequency, association with rest vs exertion, family history of arrhythmia. |
| **4** | Prior recognition of a heart murmur | **NO** | If YES: characterise prior workup — was an echo obtained, by whom, where are the records. |
| **5** | Elevated systemic blood pressure | **NO** | If YES: confirm at this visit with arm-appropriate cuff in both arms; if confirmed > 95th percentile for age/sex/height (AAP 2017), workup per pediatric-hypertension guideline. |
| **6** | Prior restriction from participation in sports | **NO** | If YES: by whom, for what reason, was restriction lifted, on what basis. |
| **7** | Prior testing for the heart, ordered by a physician | **NO** | If YES: what test (ECG / echo / stress / Holter / MRI), what indication, what result, where are records. |

### Family history (items 8–12) — the highest-yield section of the screen

| # | Item | A. R. response | Branched follow-up if YES |
|---|------|----------------|---------------------------|
| **8** | Premature death (sudden and unexpected, or otherwise) before age 50 attributable to heart disease in ≥1 relative | **YES — maternal grandfather, sudden death age 38, told to mother as "heart attack"; never further characterised** | **HOLD for branched workup.** See decision tree, Section 8 below. |
| **9** | Disability from heart disease in close relative < age 50 | **NO** | (none required) |
| **10** | Hypertrophic or dilated cardiomyopathy, long-QT syndrome or other ion channelopathies, Marfan syndrome, or clinically important arrhythmias; specific knowledge of genetic cardiac conditions in family members | **UNCERTAIN — maternal grandfather's death was never autopsied to family knowledge; no genetic testing performed in any first- or second-degree relative** | **HOLD.** Pair with item 8; the maternal-grandfather SCD at age 38 with no autopsy / no genetic workup is the **HCM-until-proven-otherwise** branch (Maron 2014; ACC/AHA HCM Guideline 2020, *Circulation* 142:e533-e557). See decision tree below. |
| **11** | Heart-transplant in a family member | **NO** | (none required) |
| **12** | Pacemaker or implantable cardioverter-defibrillator in a family member | **NO** | If YES: indication, age implanted, generation of device. |

### Physical examination (items 13–14)

| # | Item | A. R. finding | Disposition |
|---|------|---------------|-------------|
| **13** | Heart murmur (auscultation supine and standing, *with and without Valsalva*) | Soft 1/6 systolic ejection murmur at LLSB supine that *softens* with Valsalva; no diastolic murmur; no gallop; S1 and S2 normal | **Benign by Valsalva response.** A murmur that *increases* with Valsalva would be the LVOT-obstruction sign of HCM and would route to immediate referral. The reverse response here is consistent with a benign innocent flow murmur. Document for record. |
| **14** | Femoral pulses to exclude aortic coarctation | Symmetric, full bilateral femoral pulses; no radial-femoral delay | Normal. |

> **Item 13 Valsalva discipline.** The single physical-exam maneuver that distinguishes the murmur of HCM from benign flow murmurs at the bedside is the Valsalva response: HCM's dynamic LVOT obstruction *worsens* (and the murmur intensifies) as venous return drops; benign flow murmurs *soften* as preload drops. Auscultate supine, then ask the athlete to bear down for 10 seconds — the murmur change is the answer. Document the maneuver explicitly; an undocumented Valsalva read is no read.

---

## Section 4 — General physical examination

PPE 5th-edition minimum dataset. The cardiovascular elements above (items 13, 14) are repeated under Section 3 by AHA convention; the rest of the general exam follows.

| System | Finding | Disposition |
|---|---|---|
| **Vital signs** | HR 64 supine, BP 112/68 right arm seated; 110/66 left arm seated (Δ < 5 mmHg, no concern for aortic-arch or subclavian disease); RR 14; SpO2 99% room air; height 168 cm; weight 58 kg (BMI 20.5 kg/m²); temperature afebrile | Normal |
| **HEENT** | Pupils equal and reactive; ocular motility full; no scleral icterus; oropharynx clear; tympanic membranes intact; no goiter; no lymphadenopathy | Normal |
| **Skin / habitus** | No marfanoid habitus by arm-span-to-height ratio (1.00, normal); no high-arched palate; no wrist or thumb sign; no pectus deformity; no lens dislocation noted (formal slit-lamp not indicated by exam) | No stigmata of Marfan / connective-tissue disease; Ghent criteria not met |
| **Cardiovascular** | See AHA items 13, 14 above. Precordial palpation: PMI nondisplaced, no thrill, no heave. Carotid upstrokes brisk and symmetric. Apical impulse non-sustained. | Benign |
| **Pulmonary** | Lungs clear bilaterally; no wheeze; symmetric chest expansion; no accessory-muscle use; no clubbing | Normal |
| **Abdomen** | Soft, non-tender; no organomegaly; no mass; no inguinal hernia | Normal |
| **Genitourinary / Tanner staging** | Tanner stage V (per AAP guidance, Tanner staging in PPE is at clinician discretion based on sport and concern; documented as expected for chronological age) | Normal |
| **Neurologic** | Cranial nerves II-XII intact; strength 5/5 throughout; reflexes 2+ symmetric; sensation intact; gait coordinated; tandem normal; Romberg negative | Normal |

---

## Section 5 — Sanders 14-point musculoskeletal screen

The PPE 5th-edition standard MSK screen — 14 stepwise positions / movements developed at the American College of Sports Medicine and refined in the PPE monograph. Performed in sequence in approximately 90 seconds; abnormal finding at any step routes to focused exam. *Do not skip steps even when prior step is normal.*

| # | Position / movement | Looks for | A. R. finding |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | Athlete faces examiner | General body habitus; symmetry of shoulders, iliac crests | Symmetric |
| **2** | Looks up at ceiling, down at floor, over each shoulder, ear to each shoulder | Cervical-spine range of motion | Full ROM, no pain |
| **3** | Shrugs shoulders against resistance | Trapezius / cranial nerve XI strength | 5/5 symmetric |
| **4** | Abducts shoulders to 90° against resistance | Deltoid / supraspinatus strength | 5/5 symmetric |
| **5** | Externally rotates shoulders to 90° abduction, 90° flexion | Glenohumeral ROM; subtle instability | Full, no apprehension |
| **6** | Full flexion / extension of elbows | Elbow ROM | Full, no pain |
| **7** | Pronates and supinates wrists with elbows at sides | Wrist / forearm ROM | Full |
| **8** | Spreads fingers and makes fist | Hand ROM, intrinsic strength | Symmetric |
| **9** | Tightens quadriceps and relaxes (with leg extended) | Quad symmetry, knee effusion | Symmetric, no effusion |
| **10** | "Duck walk" four steps (squat and walk) | Hip / knee / ankle ROM and pain | Performs without pain or restriction |
| **11** | Stands with back to examiner | Shoulder symmetry, scoliosis (Adams forward-bend follows) | Symmetric |
| **12** | Adams forward-bend (knees straight, fingers to toes) | Thoracolumbar scoliosis (rib hump) | No rib hump; no scoliosis |
| **13** | Raises up on toes, then rocks back to heels | Calf / anterior-tibialis symmetry | Symmetric |
| **14** | Single-leg balance, eyes open, each side ×10 seconds | Lower-extremity proprioception / balance | Performs ×10 seconds each side without correction |

> **MSK screen disposition.** Screen negative. No focused MSK exam indicated. Documented baseline for return-to-play comparison should an MSK injury occur during the season.

---

## Section 6 — ECG-not-routine note (the screening-philosophy rationale)

A 12-lead ECG is **not** routinely obtained as part of the PPE in U.S. high-school and recreational sport, per AHA / ACC consensus (Maron BJ et al., *Circulation* 2014;130:1303-1334; restated in the 2015 AHA/ACC Eligibility and Disqualification Recommendations, *Circulation* 132:e256-e261). The reasoning matters more than the conclusion; it must be visible to the parent and athlete reading this form.

**Arguments in favor of routine ECG (the dissenting position; see Drezner JA et al., *Br J Sports Med* 2012;46:i1-i86; the "Seattle Criteria" follow-up Sharma 2017).**
- ECG detects HCM, long-QT, WPW, Brugada, ARVC, and other channelopathies / cardiomyopathies missed by history and exam alone.
- The Italian school-sports program (Corrado D et al., *JAMA* 2006;296:1593-1601) reported reduction in sudden cardiac death after mandatory ECG screening; this is the most-cited body of pro-ECG evidence.
- ECG cost is low (US$ 10–40 in mass-screening contexts); the Seattle Criteria reduce false-positive rates to ~ 3 %.

**Arguments against routine ECG (the AHA position adopted here).**
- The incidence of SCD in young athletes is low (Harmon KG et al., *Circulation* 2015;132:10-19 estimated 1 in 50,000 athlete-years in NCAA Division I; lower in non-collegiate populations).
- False-positive rate, even with Seattle Criteria, drives significant downstream evaluation cost (echo, cardiology referral, advanced imaging) and athlete-anxiety burden.
- Sensitivity for sudden-death-causing conditions remains imperfect (HCM detection ~ 70–80 %, channelopathy detection varies); a normal ECG does not exonerate, and a positive ECG does not always reflect pathology.
- The Italian program experience may not generalize to U.S. populations with different baseline ethnicity, sport mix, and infrastructure.

**For this athlete.** The decision *not* to obtain a routine ECG is overridden by the family-history red flag (Item 8, Item 10). The branched workup in Section 8 routes A. R. to pediatric cardiology evaluation that will include ECG, echocardiogram, and consideration of genetic testing; the ECG happens, but it happens *because the history identified the indication*, not because the form mandated it.

> **Bottom line.** Routine ECG is not obtained in this PPE. Indicated ECG (via family-history branch) is obtained as part of cardiology workup before clearance.

---

## Section 7 — Concussion baseline

Not part of the AHA cardiovascular screen but a parallel apex element of contemporary PPE per Amsterdam 2023 CISG consensus and AAP guidance. A baseline symptom inventory and balance assessment establishes the comparator for any in-season concussion (the SCAT6 used at sideline references baseline; see `templates/scat6-interactive.tsx`).

| Element | A. R. baseline |
|---|---|
| **Prior concussion count** | 1 (age 14, soccer, no loss of consciousness, symptoms < 7 days, normal recovery, returned to sport per stepwise protocol) |
| **Prior persistent post-concussion symptoms** | None |
| **Baseline 22-item symptom inventory (0–6 each)** | 0/132 (no symptoms reported at baseline) |
| **Baseline mBESS score (max 30 errors)** | 2 errors (single-leg stance non-dominant: 1; tandem stance: 1; double-leg: 0) |
| **Baseline near-point convergence (cm)** | 5 cm (normal < 6 cm) |
| **King-Devick or other timed-saccade baseline** | not obtained; available at sideline if needed |

> **Baseline disposition.** Within published norms for age and sex. SCAT6 baseline retained in season file for sideline comparison.

---

## Section 8 — The clearance decision tree

**This is the dispositional algorithm.** The form does not issue clearance by default. The physician traverses the tree explicitly; the verdict is the *output* of the traversal, not a checkbox.

```
                  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
                  │  HISTORY OR EXAM RED FLAG?      │
                  │  (AHA items 1-14 any YES)       │
                  └─────────────────────────────────┘
                              │
                  ┌───────────┴───────────┐
                  │                       │
                 NO                      YES
                  │                       │
                  ▼                       ▼
        ┌──────────────────┐    ┌─────────────────────────┐
        │  MSK screen      │    │  WHICH RED FLAG?        │
        │  positive?       │    │  (route by category)    │
        └──────────────────┘    └─────────────────────────┘
            │       │                       │
           NO      YES        ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
            │       │         │              │              │
            │       ▼     Personal-history   Family-history  Exam finding
            │  ┌────────────┐  (items 1-7)   (items 8-12)   (items 13-14)
            │  │  Focused   │       │              │              │
            │  │  MSK exam  │       ▼              ▼              ▼
            │  │  +/-       │  ┌─────────┐   ┌─────────┐   ┌─────────┐
            │  │  imaging   │  │ Workup  │   │ Cards   │   │ Workup  │
            │  └────────────┘  │ per     │   │ referral│   │ per     │
            │       │           │ item    │   │ + ECG + │   │ finding │
            │       │           │ specific│   │ echo +  │   │ (most:  │
            │       │           │         │   │ consider│   │ echo)   │
            │       │           │         │   │ genetic │   │         │
            │       │           │         │   │ testing │   │         │
            │       │           └─────────┘   └─────────┘   └─────────┘
            │       │                │              │              │
            │       │                └──────────────┼──────────────┘
            │       │                               │
            │       │                               ▼
            │       │                  ┌──────────────────────────┐
            │       │                  │  WORKUP RESULT:          │
            │       │                  │  (a) NORMAL → clearance  │
            │       │                  │  (b) ABNORMAL → restrict │
            │       │                  │      per finding         │
            │       │                  │  (c) PENDING → no        │
            │       │                  │      clearance until     │
            │       │                  │      complete            │
            │       │                  └──────────────────────────┘
            │       │                               │
            ▼       ▼                               ▼
        ┌─────────────────┐              ┌─────────────────────┐
        │ FULL CLEARANCE  │              │ LIMITED / NOT       │
        │ for declared    │              │ CLEARED PENDING /   │
        │ sport at        │              │ NOT CLEARED         │
        │ declared level  │              │                     │
        └─────────────────┘              └─────────────────────┘
```

**Four dispositions; the form ships in exactly one of these states.**

### Disposition A — FULL CLEARANCE

> **CLEARED for full participation in soccer at varsity school + club U17 level for the 2026–2027 season.** No restrictions. Next PPE due in 13 months or sooner if injury, illness, or new symptom develops. *This disposition is invoked when the history is negative across all 14 AHA items, MSK screen is negative, and exam is benign.*
>
> **This athlete does not qualify for Disposition A.** Family-history items 8 and 10 are YES (Section 3). See Disposition C.

### Disposition B — LIMITED CLEARANCE (sport or position restriction)

> **CLEARED for participation in named sport(s) with the following restrictions:** [restriction]. Athlete and parent counselled on the basis of the restriction. Restriction reviewed at [interval] or upon change in condition. *This disposition is invoked when a confirmed condition (e.g., well-controlled exercise-induced bronchoconstriction; isolated single kidney with contact-sport counselling) is compatible with participation in restricted form.*
>
> **This athlete does not qualify for Disposition B at this visit.** No confirmed condition warranting restriction has been established; the family-history workup is pending. See Disposition C.

### Disposition C — NOT CLEARED PENDING WORKUP (the conditional hold)

> **NOT CLEARED for participation pending completion of cardiology workup.** The family-history red flags (Section 3, items 8 and 10) trigger the HCM-until-proven-otherwise branch (Maron 2014; ACC/AHA HCM Guideline 2020). Pediatric cardiology referral placed at this visit. Workup will include:
>
> 1. **12-lead ECG** with assessment for LVH (Sokolow-Lyon, Cornell criteria), pathologic Q waves, repolarization abnormalities, pre-excitation, QTc, and the Seattle / international consensus criteria for athlete ECG (Sharma S et al., *Eur Heart J* 2017;38:1466-1480).
> 2. **Transthoracic echocardiogram** with assessment for maximum LV wall thickness (HCM diagnostic threshold ≥ 15 mm adults, ≥ 13 mm with positive family history or genotype; pediatric criteria sex-and-BSA-adjusted Z-score ≥ +2.5), LV outflow-tract gradient at rest and with provocation (Valsalva, standing, exercise), mitral valve and papillary-muscle morphology, septal-to-posterior-wall ratio, and global longitudinal strain.
> 3. **Genetic-counselling referral** with consideration of HCM panel testing (the proband — here, the maternal grandfather — is unavailable for testing; cascade testing of the athlete and first-degree relatives is the available approach). The genetic-counselling visit must precede testing per ASHG / NSGC standards; the consent is for the athlete (≥ 14 yrs, mature-minor consent context per state law) and the parent.
> 4. **Stress / exercise testing** with cardiology-team-determined protocol, particularly if echo shows borderline findings.
>
> **No participation in any organised soccer activity** (including non-contact practice) until workup is complete and cardiology has issued a written clearance letter that reaches this office. Until workup is complete, light recreational activity that does not approximate competitive intensity (walking, social bicycling, recreational swimming) is permitted at family discretion; counselled on warning symptoms (exertional chest pain, syncope, palpitations) that warrant immediate ED evaluation.
>
> Athlete and parent counselled extensively on the rationale at this visit; counselling documented. Cardiology evaluation scheduled within 2 weeks.

**This is the disposition for A. R. at the conclusion of this visit.**

### Disposition D — NOT CLEARED

> **NOT CLEARED for participation in named sport** at this time. *Invoked when a confirmed condition incompatible with the sport's cardiovascular load is established (e.g., confirmed obstructive HCM with high-risk markers; uncontrolled Marfan with aortic-root dilation; long-QT with prior arrhythmic event). The 36th Bethesda Conference / 2015 AHA/ACC Eligibility and Disqualification Recommendations are the operative reference for activity restrictions in specific cardiac conditions.* Disposition is not permanent; reconsidered upon change in clinical status or evidence base.
>
> **This athlete does not qualify for Disposition D at this visit.** Workup is pending, not complete; the form does not pre-judge the cardiology evaluation.

---

## Section 9 — Athlete and parent counselling

Documented at this visit:

- **The family-history finding and its significance.** Maternal-grandfather sudden cardiac death at age 38 is the canonical HCM red flag in pediatric sports cardiology. HCM is the most common cause of SCD in young athletes in the U.S. (Maron BJ, *Heart Rhythm* 2009;6:1352-1357; ~ 36% of SCD in athletes < 35 yrs in the Maron registry). The condition is autosomal dominant with variable penetrance; a 16-year-old with an affected second-degree relative carries an estimated *a priori* probability of clinically significant HCM of roughly 1-5% absent testing.
- **The rationale for hold rather than full clearance.** The cardiology workup is the standard of care in this situation; clearing the athlete before workup would deviate from PPE 5th edition / AHA / ACC HCM Guideline 2020 standards. The hold is short (≈ 2-4 weeks to complete workup), the path back to full participation is clearly defined, and the alternative (proceeding without workup) carries a small but irreducible risk of an SCD event that would be in significant part preventable.
- **Warning symptoms that warrant immediate ED evaluation, regardless of context.** Chest pain or pressure with exertion. Syncope (loss of consciousness), especially during or immediately after exertion. Palpitations associated with light-headedness or dyspnea. Sudden severe shortness of breath disproportionate to exertion.
- **Resources.** AAP Council on Sports Medicine and Fitness HCM in young athletes parent page; Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy Association (4HCM.org) family-and-athlete resources; the cardiology office's pre-visit information packet.
- **Documentation.** Counselling note included in the EHR encounter; copy provided to athlete and parent at the visit.

---

## Section 10 — Signature blocks and dispositional verdict

> **Disposition: NOT CLEARED PENDING WORKUP** (Disposition C).
>
> Cardiology referral placed 2026-05-24. School and club informed by parent (consent to share recorded). Re-evaluation by this office upon receipt of cardiology clearance letter.

# Procedure note — Diagnostic lumbar puncture

**Patient:** Maya Williams · MRN-9215 · 28yo F
**Date / time of procedure:** 2026-05-24, 14:42 (note completed 15:05)
**Service:** Internal Medicine, Team B
**Performing clinician:** Dr. Adam Khoury, PGY-2 Internal Medicine, p-4612
**Supervising clinician:** Dr. Adaeze Okonkwo, MD, attending, p-3102 (present at bedside throughout)
**Witnessing nurse:** RN Lisa Cruz, BSN

---

## Indication

New-onset severe headache (worst-ever, sudden onset eight hours ago), meningismus on exam (nuchal rigidity, positive Kernig sign), fever to 38.5 °C, and leukocytosis (WBC 18.4) — workup for bacterial meningitis. Non-contrast head CT obtained at 13:30 was negative for haemorrhage, mass, or hydrocephalus, supporting safety for lumbar puncture without prior MRI. Patient meets IDSA empiric-antibiotic-while-awaiting-LP criteria and received ceftriaxone 2 g IV + vancomycin 20 mg/kg IV + dexamethasone 10 mg IV at 14:10, prior to the procedure (per 2016 IDSA Bacterial Meningitis guidelines).

---

## Pre-procedure checklist

- **Informed consent obtained:** **Yes.** Written informed consent obtained from the patient at 14:15, prior to anaesthesia. Risks discussed and acknowledged by the patient: post-LP headache (~ 10–30 %), bleeding at the site, infection at the site (rare), nerve-root irritation (rare), cerebral herniation (rare, mitigated by negative head CT), failure to obtain CSF. Alternatives discussed: lumbar puncture deferred with empiric antibiotics continued (less diagnostic information); LP under fluoroscopic guidance (escalation if bedside LP fails). Patient demonstrated decision-making capacity (alert, oriented x3, answered teach-back questions about risks and benefits). Consent witnessed by RN Cruz.
- **Pre-procedure time-out performed:** **Yes**, at 14:25, prior to anaesthesia. Confirmed by all three personnel (performing physician, supervising physician, nurse): patient identification (name + MRN + DOB matched against wristband), procedure (diagnostic lumbar puncture), site (lumbar spine, L3–L4 interspace target), positioning (left lateral decubitus), and absence of contraindications (no anticoagulation; platelet count 220, INR 1.0; head CT negative for mass effect; no skin infection at site).
- **Site marked:** **Yes**, at 14:30, with a sterile surgical marker at the L3–L4 interspace (identified by palpation along Tuffier's line — the iliac crest line crosses the L4 spinous process; the interspace immediately above is L3–L4).
- **Coagulation status:** Platelets 220, INR 1.0. Not on anticoagulation or antiplatelet therapy. Safe for LP.

---

## Procedure

**Position:** Left lateral decubitus on the gurney with knees drawn to chest and head flexed forward (fetal position), to maximise interspinous opening.

**Sterile technique:** Full sterile preparation. The lower-back skin was cleansed three times with 2 % chlorhexidine gluconate in 70 % isopropyl alcohol, allowed to dry. Sterile drape applied with fenestration over the marked site. The performing physician scrubbed and donned sterile gown and gloves.

**Anaesthesia:** Local infiltration with 5 mL of 1 % lidocaine without epinephrine, using a 25-gauge needle for skin wheal followed by a 22-gauge needle for deeper infiltration along the planned needle track. Allowed 90 seconds for onset before needle insertion.

**Technique:** A 22-gauge Quincke spinal needle (3.5-inch length, stylet in place) was introduced at the L3–L4 interspace at 14:38, in the midline, angled slightly cephalad (toward the umbilicus). A pop was appreciated at approximately 5.5 cm of needle depth (consistent with traversing the dura). The stylet was withdrawn. Clear, colourless cerebrospinal fluid was obtained on the first pass at 14:42; no blood, no traumatic tap.

**Opening pressure:** Measured with a sterile manometer attached to the spinal needle with the patient repositioned with legs extended for accurate manometry. **Opening pressure: 18 cmH2O** (reference range 6–25 cmH2O in adults; within normal limits).

**CSF collection:** Four sterile CSF tubes collected, ~ 2 mL per tube, in numbered order:

- **Tube 1 (~ 2 mL)** → cell count with differential (lab: haematology)
- **Tube 2 (~ 2 mL)** → Gram stain + bacterial culture + sensitivities (lab: microbiology)
- **Tube 3 (~ 2 mL)** → glucose + protein + lactate (lab: chemistry)
- **Tube 4 (~ 2 mL)** → hold for additional testing (HSV PCR, cryptococcal antigen, fungal culture, AFB if clinically indicated; will release on team direction; lab: microbiology, on-hold rack)

Total CSF removed: approximately 8 mL.

**Closing pressure:** Not routinely measured given normal opening pressure and uncomplicated procedure.

**Needle withdrawal:** Stylet replaced; needle withdrawn in a single smooth motion at 14:48. Pressure held over the puncture site with sterile gauze for two minutes; haemostasis confirmed. Sterile adhesive dressing applied.

---

## Estimated blood loss

**Minimal (< 2 mL).** No haemorrhage observed at the site during or after the procedure.

---

## Specimens

Four CSF tubes (Tube 1 through Tube 4) sent to the laboratory at 14:55 via the bedside tube routing system. Specimens labelled at the bedside in the presence of the patient with patient identifiers verified against the wristband. Lab notified by pager (microbiology p-2104) of urgent Gram stain processing.

---

## Complications

**None.** The procedure was uncomplicated: clear CSF on the first pass, no traumatic tap, normal opening pressure, no patient-reported pain beyond expected during anaesthesia infiltration, no post-procedure neurological changes on the immediate post-procedure exam (cranial nerves II–XII intact; lower-extremity strength 5/5 bilaterally; sensation intact to light touch; reflexes 2+ symmetric at the patellae and Achilles).

---

## Post-procedure plan

- **Patient positioning:** Patient to remain supine (flat) for 1 hour post-procedure (until 15:48); evidence for post-procedure recumbency to reduce post-LP headache is mixed, but institutional protocol recommends 1 hour flat with the patient encouraged to drink fluids.
- **Pain management for post-procedure headache prevention:** Encourage oral hydration (1 L over the next 4 hours). Acetaminophen 1 g PO q6h scheduled for the next 24 hours. Caffeine (1 cup of coffee or one 200 mg caffeine tablet) at the patient's preference; some evidence for prophylaxis of post-LP headache.
- **Monitoring:** Hourly neurological checks (cranial nerves, motor exam, mental status) for the next 4 hours. Vital signs per routine.
- **Empiric antibiotics:** **Continue** ceftriaxone 2 g IV q12h + vancomycin 20 mg/kg IV q8h + dexamethasone 10 mg IV q6h pending CSF Gram stain and culture results. Will narrow or de-escalate per the CSF profile.
- **Post-procedure escalation criteria:** Page the primary team (or cross-cover overnight) for any of:
  - Worsening headache not responsive to acetaminophen, or new-onset headache when previously resolved.
  - New neurological deficit (cranial nerve palsy, motor weakness, sensory loss, altered mental status).
  - New-onset back pain at the puncture site that is severe or progressive (concern for haematoma).
  - Fever > 38.5 °C or rigors (concern for infection at the puncture site).
  - Persistent CSF leak at the site (clear drainage).
- **Follow-up of pending results:** Sarah Chen, PGY-1 (the night-shift cross-cover, p-4471), is the named owner of the pending CSF results and will check the EHR results inbox at 18:00, 22:00, and 02:00. The primary team day shift will resume responsibility for the result follow-up at 07:00 sign-out.

---

## Disposition

Patient remained on the Internal Medicine floor, room 4-217. Patient is alert, comfortable, and tolerating the supine position. Patient was informed verbally of the procedure result (CSF obtained, will know full results in several hours), the post-procedure precautions, and the escalation criteria; her brother (present at bedside as her support person) received the same information and confirmed understanding.

---

Pager 4612 · Signed electronically 2026-05-24, 15:05

**Supervising attending:** Adaeze Okonkwo, MD — Internal Medicine, Team B
