# Post-operative rehabilitation protocol — primary ACL reconstruction with BTB autograft

> **Procedure.** Primary anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction, right knee, bone-patellar-tendon-bone (BTB) autograft, no concomitant meniscal or chondral procedure. Surgical date: 2026-03-04 (POD#0).
>
> **Patient.** 23-year-old recreational soccer player (midfielder, club-level), no prior knee surgery, BMI 24, otherwise healthy.
>
> **Audience.** Sports-medicine physical therapist (primary); athlete; orthopaedic surgeon (referring); athletic trainer (for return-to-sport phases); parent / coach as applicable.
>
> **Last reviewed:** 2026-05-24. **Reviewer:** self-attested; not institutional protocol; not peer-reviewed. **Evidence basis:** Wright RW et al. (MOON Knee Group) *J Bone Joint Surg Am* 2008;90:1605-1610; van Melick N et al. *Br J Sports Med* 2016;50:1506-1515 (Dutch ACL multidisciplinary practice guideline); Grindem H et al. *Br J Sports Med* 2016;50:804-808 (criterion-based RTS reduces re-injury 51%); Kyritsis P et al. *Br J Sports Med* 2016;50:946-951; Logerstedt DS et al. *J Orthop Sports Phys Ther* 2017;47:A1-A47 (APTA Clinical Practice Guideline). **Conflicts of interest:** none.

---

## The criterion-gate philosophy (read before the phases)

The single most important sentence in this protocol:

> **Advance the athlete to the next phase when the criteria are met. Do not advance because the calendar says so.**

The cost of time-based-only progression is well-documented. Athletes who return to sport before passing objective batteries have a 4-fold higher re-injury risk (Kyritsis 2016); each month of delay-to-RTS up to 9 months reduces re-injury risk by 51 % (Grindem 2016). The corollary: the calendar dates in this protocol are *typical* trajectories, not deadlines. An athlete progressing faster than the calendar is advanced when criteria are met; an athlete progressing slower is held until criteria are met.

### Time-vs-criterion: what is wrong with time-only

| | Time-only progression | Criterion-gated progression |
|---|---|---|
| **Advance to running** | At week 12 | When LSI quad strength ≥ 70 % AND no effusion AND full extension AND ≥ 120° flexion |
| **Advance to cutting** | At month 5 | When LSI quad strength ≥ 80 % AND single-leg hop LSI ≥ 90 % AND no apprehension |
| **Return to sport** | At month 6 | When all four hop-test LSIs ≥ 90 % AND quad LSI ≥ 90 % AND KOOS-Sport ≥ 80 AND no instability |
| **Re-injury risk** | 15–30 % in young athletes (Wiggins 2016) | 6–10 % when criteria met (Grindem 2016) |
| **What it optimizes for** | Schedule clarity, insurance authorisation, coach expectation | Tissue healing, neuromuscular control, contralateral protection |
| **The failure mode** | Athlete advanced without preparation; re-tears in the first cutting session of the season | Athlete frustrated by delay beyond calendar expectation; education burden is the cost |

The protocol below is criterion-gated by design. Each phase ends with a **transition battery** the athlete must pass before advancement; failure is documented and re-tested.

### A note on terminology

- **LSI** (limb-symmetry index) = operative-limb performance / contralateral-limb performance, expressed as a percentage. LSI ≥ 90 % is the conventional threshold for return-to-sport batteries; ≥ 100 % is achievable and desirable in the contralateral-protection literature (Welling W et al., *Phys Ther Sport* 2019).
- **MVIC** (maximum voluntary isometric contraction) — the standard quad-strength measurement at 60° knee flexion; portable handheld dynamometry is the field equivalent of isokinetic dynamometry.
- **KOOS-Sport** — Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score, sport-and-recreation subscale; 0-100 with 100 = no limitation. Patient-reported; valid for ACLR populations (Roos EM et al., *J Orthop Sports Phys Ther* 1998).
- **Hop tests** — the four-test battery: single-leg hop for distance; triple hop for distance; crossover hop for distance; 6-metre timed hop (Logerstedt 2012). LSI calculated per test.

---

## Phase I — Acute (POD#0 to week 2)

**Calendar window:** roughly 0–14 days. **Primary aims:** protect the graft and donor site; restore symmetric passive extension; activate the quad; manage pain and effusion.

### Goals

- Passive knee extension equal to contralateral side (the single most important Phase I goal; loss of extension is the most-difficult deficit to recover and is associated with poor long-term outcome — Shelbourne KD, Gray T, *Am J Sports Med* 2009;37:471-480).
- Active quadriceps contraction (visible vastus medialis activation; straight-leg raise without lag).
- Effusion controlled (stroke-test grade 0 or trace).
- Independent ambulation with crutches and weight-bearing as tolerated.
- Wound healed; sutures or staples removed (POD#10–14).

### Precautions

- **Weight-bearing:** weight-bearing as tolerated (WBAT) with crutches from POD#1. BTB autograft tolerates immediate WBAT; meniscal-repair concomitance would require modification.
- **Brace:** hinged ROM brace locked in extension for ambulation and sleep for the first 2 weeks; unlocked for ROM exercises. Brace use is institution- and surgeon-dependent; some protocols omit bracing for isolated BTB.
- **Avoid:** active resisted knee extension between 0° and 60° flexion (loads the graft); deep squat past 90°; passive hyperextension; weight-bearing rotation.

### ROM targets

| Target | Phase I criterion |
|---|---|
| Passive extension | Equal to contralateral (often 0° to 5° hyperextension) |
| Active extension | Within 5° of passive |
| Passive flexion | ≥ 90° by end of week 2 |

### Weight-bearing

- POD#0–1: toe-touch with crutches as needed for pain.
- POD#2–14: WBAT with crutches; transition off crutches when (a) no extension lag, (b) painless ambulation, (c) symmetric heel-strike-to-toe-off gait pattern.

### Exercises (specified — Phase I is the most-prescribed phase)

| Exercise | Sets × reps × frequency | Cue | Progression trigger |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Ankle pumps** | 30 × hourly while awake | Active dorsi-plantar-flexion; DVT prophylaxis | continue throughout phase |
| **Quad sets** | 3 × 10 × 5 daily | Press the back of the knee into a towel; hold 5 sec; visualize VMO activation | when athlete achieves visible VMO activation, add SLR |
| **Straight-leg raise (SLR)** | 3 × 10 × 3 daily | Lift the heel 12 inches with the knee locked; no extension lag (lag of > 5° = repeat quad sets first) | when SLR is lag-free, progress to standing knee marches with brace |
| **Heel slides (active-assisted)** | 3 × 10 × 3 daily | Slide heel toward buttock with towel-assist; stop at first end-range; do not push past pain | when 90° flexion achieved, progress to wall slides |
| **Patellar mobilization** | 5 min × 4 daily (PT and self) | Glide the patella superior-inferior-medial-lateral; gentle; preserves patellofemoral kinematics; critical for BTB to prevent infrapatellar contracture syndrome | continue throughout Phase I-II; never discontinue early in BTB |
| **Prone hangs** | 3 × 5 min × 2 daily | Lying prone with the knee off the table edge; gravity restores extension; PT may add ankle weight after week 1 | when symmetric passive extension achieved, can taper but maintain 1×/day |
| **Calf raises (bilateral, then progressively unilateral)** | 3 × 15 × 2 daily | Bilateral starting POD#3; transition to unilateral when WB tolerated | when unilateral × 15 painless, add resistance |
| **Cryotherapy** | 20 min × 4–6 daily | After every exercise session and per discomfort | reduce frequency as effusion resolves |

### Red-flag indicators (Phase I)

- **Calf pain or swelling out of proportion to expected:** rule out DVT; same-day venous Doppler ultrasound.
- **Fever > 38.5°C or wound drainage:** rule out septic arthritis (the catastrophic post-op complication); urgent surgical evaluation.
- **Loss of extension after early achievement:** infrapatellar contracture syndrome / arthrofibrosis emerging; aggressive intervention required; do not "wait and see."
- **New apprehension or instability:** rare in Phase I; concern for graft re-injury.
- **Anterior-knee pain disproportionate to expectation:** patellofemoral pain — BTB donor-site contributor; modify exercises and add patellar mobilization.

### Transition to Phase II — criteria (all must be met)

- [ ] Passive extension symmetric to contralateral.
- [ ] Passive flexion ≥ 90°.
- [ ] SLR without extension lag.
- [ ] Effusion stroke-test ≤ grade 1.
- [ ] Independent ambulation without crutches.
- [ ] No wound concern.

---

## Phase II — Sub-acute (week 2 to week 6)

**Calendar window:** roughly 14–42 days. **Primary aims:** restore full ROM, normalize gait, build foundational strength, introduce closed-chain quad loading within safe ranges.

### Goals

- Full active and passive ROM equal to contralateral.
- Symmetric gait at normal walking speed.
- Quadriceps MVIC ≥ 60 % of contralateral by end of phase.
- Effusion grade 0.
- Patient-reported function (single-leg balance, sit-to-stand without assistance) approaching pre-injury baseline.

### Precautions

- **Brace:** brace discontinued for ambulation when gait is symmetric and quad control sufficient (typically week 3–4); retained for high-risk activities by some surgeons.
- **Avoid:** open-chain resisted knee extension between 0° and 60° (continue); jumping; running; cutting; pivoting; deep squat with load.

### ROM targets

| Target | Phase II criterion |
|---|---|
| Passive extension | Symmetric to contralateral (maintained) |
| Active extension | Equal to passive |
| Passive flexion | Equal to contralateral by end of phase (typically 130–140°) |
| Active flexion | Within 5° of passive |

### Weight-bearing

- Full weight-bearing without assistive device.
- Stair ascent (step-to pattern, then reciprocal) when quad control supports it.
- Stair descent (step-to pattern with non-operative leg leading) until single-leg eccentric strength supports reciprocal.

### Exercises

| Exercise | Sets × reps × frequency | Cue | Progression trigger |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Mini-squats (0–45°)** | 3 × 15 × 3 weekly | Bilateral; weight balanced; knees track over second toe | when painless and symmetric, progress to single-leg mini-squats and add load |
| **Step-ups (forward, 6-inch progressing to 10-inch)** | 3 × 10 × 3 weekly | Drive through the heel; control the descent (3-sec eccentric); knee tracks over toe | when painless and symmetric at 10-inch, progress to lateral step-ups |
| **Leg press (bilateral, then transitioning to unilateral; 0–60° in BTB)** | 3 × 10 × 2 weekly | Avoid 0–60° resisted open-chain knee extension; the leg press in the protected range is the BTB-safe equivalent | when unilateral painless at body-weight resistance, add load |
| **Stationary bike (low resistance)** | 10–20 min × 3 weekly | Begin when ≥ 110° flexion achieved (typically week 3); seat high initially | progress to higher resistance and longer duration |
| **Hamstring curls (prone or seated)** | 3 × 12 × 3 weekly | Resisted; this is the BTB-friendly antagonist exercise; load progressively | as tolerated |
| **Hip abduction / adduction (side-lying, then standing band)** | 3 × 15 × 3 weekly | Gluteus medius critical for landing mechanics later; do not skip | as tolerated |
| **Calf raises (unilateral)** | 3 × 15 × 3 weekly | Progress from bilateral; add load | as tolerated |
| **Single-leg balance (firm → foam → unstable)** | 3 × 30-sec × 3 weekly | Progress surface as control improves; add eyes-closed; add upper-extremity perturbation | proprioception is foundational for later phases |
| **Patellar mobilization** | continue (5 min × 2 daily) | as Phase I | continue throughout |

### Red-flag indicators (Phase II)

- **Effusion increasing rather than decreasing:** overactivity; reduce exercise dose; if persistent, surgeon evaluation.
- **Recurrent loss of extension:** arthrofibrosis emerging; aggressive intervention with the PT and surgeon.
- **Anterior knee pain:** patellofemoral overload; modify squat depth, increase glute and hip control, reassess patellar mobility.

### Transition to Phase III — criteria (all must be met)

- [ ] Full active and passive ROM symmetric to contralateral.
- [ ] Symmetric gait at normal walking speed.
- [ ] Quad MVIC LSI ≥ 60 %.
- [ ] Single-leg balance ≥ 30 sec eyes open on firm surface.
- [ ] Effusion stroke-test grade 0.
- [ ] No wound concern.
- [ ] Painless step-up at 10-inch step.

---

## Phase III — Early strengthening (week 6 to week 12)

**Calendar window:** roughly 6–12 weeks. **Primary aims:** progressive resistance training across the lower-extremity kinetic chain; introduce double-leg jumping and landing mechanics; build the strength platform for later running and cutting.

### Goals

- Quad MVIC LSI ≥ 70 % by end of phase (75 % is a stretch goal; required for running).
- Hamstring MVIC LSI ≥ 80 %.
- Symmetric squat to 90° with body weight; transition toward loaded squat.
- Initiate and progress through pre-running drills (marching, skipping in place, low-amplitude jumps).
- Patient-reported KOOS-ADL ≥ 90; KOOS-Sport ≥ 60.

### Precautions

- **Avoid:** open-chain resisted knee extension 0–60° (continue until end of Phase III; some surgeons release at week 12); running; cutting; pivoting; agility drills; sport-specific drills.

### ROM targets

- Full, symmetric, maintained.

### Weight-bearing

- Unrestricted.

### Exercises (the menu — Phase III is where the faded scaffold begins)

| Category | Examples (PT selects 2-3 per session) | Sets × reps × frequency | Progression principle |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Squat progression** | Bilateral squat → goblet squat → barbell back squat → single-leg squat to box | 3 × 8–12 × 3 weekly | Load increases as form maintains; depth respects ROM and pain tolerance |
| **Step-up / step-down progression** | Forward step-up → lateral step-up → forward step-down (eccentric) → lateral step-down | 3 × 10 × 3 weekly | Step height increases; eccentric control is the priority |
| **Closed-chain hip strength** | Romanian deadlift (bilateral → single-leg); hip thrust (bilateral → single-leg); reverse lunge | 3 × 10 × 2 weekly | Glute-dominant patterns reduce ACL strain |
| **Hamstring strength** | Nordic hamstring curl (eccentric); seated/prone hamstring curl; single-leg bridge | 3 × 8–12 × 2 weekly | Hamstring strength has dynamic-stability protective effect |
| **Calf strength** | Single-leg calf raise (load progression); seated calf raise | 3 × 15 × 2 weekly | Soleus and gastrocnemius |
| **Neuromuscular / proprioception** | BOSU / unstable surface; single-leg with perturbation; agility ladder (forward-only) | 3 × 30 sec × 3 weekly | Progress surface, add cognitive load |
| **Jump-landing introduction (end of phase)** | Double-leg jump in place (low amplitude) → double-leg drop landing from 6-inch box | 3 × 8 × 2 weekly | Focus is *landing mechanics*; knee tracks over toe; soft landing; symmetric weight distribution |

### Red-flag indicators (Phase III)

- **New effusion after exercise:** reduce dose; reassess.
- **Pain with deep flexion (> 90°):** patellofemoral or graft-tunnel issue; reduce depth, reassess.
- **Apprehension or instability with weight-bearing rotation:** the rotational protective strategy is not yet adequate; defer pivot drills.

### Transition to Phase IV — criteria (all must be met)

- [ ] Quad MVIC LSI ≥ 70 %.
- [ ] Hamstring MVIC LSI ≥ 80 %.
- [ ] Symmetric squat to 90° with body weight × 10 reps painless.
- [ ] Painless and symmetric forward step-down from 10-inch step.
- [ ] Bilateral drop-landing from 6-inch box with knees tracking over toes, no valgus collapse.
- [ ] KOOS-Sport ≥ 60.
- [ ] No effusion or instability.

> **Note.** Some protocols permit straight-line jogging at the Phase III → Phase IV transition (week 12) if all criteria are met. Others defer running to Phase IV entry proper. The realized protocol here permits **straight-line jogging trial** at this transition with the criteria above as the gate; full progression to running lives in Phase V.

---

## Phase IV — Advanced strengthening (week 12 to week 18)

**Calendar window:** roughly 12–18 weeks. **Primary aims:** maximize strength and power; build the platform for return to running (Phase V); introduce loaded plyometrics and multi-planar landing patterns.

### Goals

- Quad MVIC LSI ≥ 80 % by end of phase.
- Hamstring MVIC LSI ≥ 90 %.
- Bilateral and unilateral plyometric tolerance.
- Begin and complete a running progression (couch-to-5k-style for the ACL athlete; see Phase V entry criteria below).
- KOOS-Sport ≥ 75.

### Precautions

- **Avoid:** cutting, pivoting, sport-specific drills until Phase V criteria met.
- Open-chain knee extension typically released at this phase if surgeon preference allows (week 12+ in most modern protocols); resistance is progressive.

### Exercises (categorized; PT selects based on athlete progression)

| Category | Examples | Approximate dose |
|---|---|---|
| **Loaded squat / hip-hinge** | Barbell back squat; front squat; trap-bar deadlift; Romanian deadlift | 3–4 × 5–8 × 2–3 weekly |
| **Loaded single-leg work** | Rear-foot-elevated split squat (Bulgarian); reverse lunge with load; step-up with load; single-leg Romanian deadlift | 3 × 8 × 2 weekly |
| **Bilateral plyometrics** | Double-leg pogo hops; double-leg box jumps (height progression); double-leg lateral hops | 3 × 8 × 2 weekly |
| **Unilateral plyometric introduction** | Single-leg pogo hops; single-leg hop for distance (low effort); single-leg lateral hops | 3 × 5–8 × 2 weekly |
| **Multi-planar landing** | Forward, lateral, rotational drop landings | 3 × 5 each direction × 2 weekly |
| **Linear-deceleration drills** | Forward jog → deceleration to stop; backpedal → deceleration | 3 × 5 × 2 weekly |
| **Aerobic** | Stationary bike high resistance; elliptical; later straight-line treadmill running progression | 30–45 min × 3 weekly |

### Running progression (typically initiated within Phase IV)

A staged progression from walk-run intervals to continuous running. The progression below is one valid schema; substitute the institutional preference.

| Week (of Phase IV) | Session 1 | Session 2 | Session 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | Walk 5 min, jog 1 min × 5 | Walk 5 min, jog 1 min × 5 | Walk 4 min, jog 2 min × 5 |
| **2** | Walk 4 min, jog 2 min × 5 | Walk 3 min, jog 3 min × 5 | Walk 2 min, jog 4 min × 5 |
| **3** | Continuous jog 10 min | Continuous jog 15 min | Continuous jog 20 min |
| **4** | Continuous run 20 min | Continuous run 25 min | Continuous run 30 min |
| **Hold** | If any effusion, increased pain, gait asymmetry, or loss of strength → drop back two sessions and re-progress |  |  |

### Red-flag indicators (Phase IV)

- **Pain or effusion after running session:** reduce running dose; reassess strength; defer progression.
- **Loss of strength on serial MVIC:** address before adding plyometric load.
- **Loss of single-leg control on plyometrics:** drop back one plyometric category; rebuild.
- **Patellofemoral pain with loaded squat:** address depth, glute engagement, and patellar mobility.

### Transition to Phase V — criteria (all must be met)

- [ ] Quad MVIC LSI ≥ 80 %.
- [ ] Hamstring MVIC LSI ≥ 90 %.
- [ ] Pain-free continuous running at 30 minutes.
- [ ] Symmetric single-leg drop-landing from 12-inch box with no valgus collapse.
- [ ] Single-leg hop for distance LSI ≥ 80 % (preliminary; full battery at Phase V end).
- [ ] KOOS-Sport ≥ 75.
- [ ] No effusion; no instability; no apprehension.

---

## Phase V — Return to running and sport-specific (week 18 to week 24)

**Calendar window:** roughly 18–24 weeks. **Primary aims:** return to full running and aerobic conditioning; introduce planned cutting and pivoting; build the cutting and decelerating chassis; complete the strength platform; prepare for the return-to-sport battery.

### Goals

- Quad MVIC LSI ≥ 90 %.
- Hamstring MVIC LSI ≥ 95 %.
- Single-leg hop battery (single, triple, crossover, 6-m timed) preliminary LSIs ≥ 85 %.
- Tolerance of planned cutting and pivoting drills (45° → 90° angle progression).
- KOOS-Sport ≥ 80.

### Precautions

- **Avoid:** unplanned cutting; full-contact practice; competitive games. The athlete remains under PT progression discipline.

### Exercises (further faded — PT selects from sport-tailored menu)

| Category | Examples | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Planned change-of-direction** | 45° cuts (forward, lateral); 90° cuts; T-drill; 5-10-5 pro-agility | Cutting *angle* and *velocity* are independent variables; progress one at a time |
| **Deceleration drills** | High-velocity straight-line deceleration; lateral deceleration; rotational deceleration | Eccentric quad strength is the limiter |
| **Sport-specific footwork** | Soccer: dribbling under cone constraints, planned cuts, ball work without contact. Football: route running without contact. Basketball: defensive slides, planned crossover. | Match the athlete's sport |
| **Maximum strength** | Continue Phase IV resistance with progressive overload | LSI is the metric; absolute load secondary |
| **Reactive plyometrics** | Reactive jump drills with visual or auditory cue; cognitive load layered on motor task | Approximates the cognitive-motor demand of sport |
| **Conditioning** | Sport-specific interval conditioning; build to sport's typical work-rest ratio | Sport-specific match the position and league |

### Red-flag indicators (Phase V)

- **Failed cutting drill (apprehension, awkward landing, loss of confidence):** drop back to planned linear deceleration; address neuromuscular control; do not push through.
- **Effusion after cutting session:** the operative knee is signaling overuse; reduce dose; reassess.
- **Loss of hop-test LSI on serial testing:** strength regression; address with focused resistance work.

### Transition to Phase VI — the return-to-sport battery (all must be met)

This is the gate to the return-to-sport phase. **Failure on any element is a hold.**

| Element | Criterion | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Quad MVIC LSI** | ≥ 90 % | Handheld dynamometry or isokinetic |
| **Hamstring MVIC LSI** | ≥ 95 % | |
| **Single-leg hop for distance LSI** | ≥ 90 % | Best of 3 trials |
| **Triple hop for distance LSI** | ≥ 90 % | |
| **Crossover hop for distance LSI** | ≥ 90 % | |
| **6-metre timed hop LSI** | ≥ 90 % (note: faster time is better; calculation is inverted: contralateral / operative time) | |
| **KOOS-Sport** | ≥ 80 | Patient-reported |
| **ACL-RSI** | ≥ 65 | Psychological readiness; Webster KE et al., *Phys Ther Sport* 2008 |
| **Drop vertical jump screen** | No valgus collapse; symmetric landing; knee tracks over toe | LESS or qualitative scoring |
| **Sport-specific battery** | Symmetric and confident execution of position-relevant cutting and decelerating drills at sport-tempo | Sport-tailored; PT, AT, and surgeon co-evaluate |

> **Battery pass rate.** Approximately 25–35 % of athletes pass the full battery at 9 months in published cohorts (Logerstedt 2017; Welling 2019); the rest require extended Phase V. The low pass rate is the literature's evidence that *the calendar is not the gate*. An athlete failing the battery at 9 months is not "behind schedule" — they have not yet met criteria. Frame the hold as protective, not punitive.

---

## Phase VI — Return to sport and in-season maintenance (24+ weeks)

**Calendar window:** typically 6–12 months post-op, but criterion-gated. **Primary aims:** graduated return to full team training and competition; preserve and continue building strength and neuromuscular control through the first competitive season; reduce contralateral injury risk through the maintenance program.

### The staged return-to-team-sport progression

This phase is itself staged within the return; the protocol does not jump from "passed the battery" to "starting striker."

| Stage | Description | Minimum duration | Criterion to advance |
|---|---|---|---|
| **VI-A: Solo practice** | Athlete trains individually with the AT; sport-specific drills at sport tempo; ball / equipment skills; no contact | 1–2 weeks | Symmetric performance; no symptoms |
| **VI-B: Modified team practice (non-contact)** | Joins team training in non-contact drills; participates in tactical work; observes contact sessions | 1–2 weeks | Symmetric performance; no symptoms; coach observes confidence |
| **VI-C: Full team practice (contact)** | Full participation in team practice including contact | 1–2 weeks | Symmetric performance in practice; AT clears |
| **VI-D: Game minutes (limited)** | Game participation in defined minute increments (e.g., 15 min of a 90-min match); progressive build | 2–4 weeks | No injury; AT and coach co-evaluate after each game |
| **VI-E: Full game participation** | Standard match minutes | Ongoing | Maintain monitoring through first competitive season |

### In-season maintenance program (continues 12-24 months post-op)

Continuing PT-prescribed strength and neuromuscular work through the first competitive season reduces re-injury risk (Grindem 2016). The in-season program is condensed (twice weekly, 30 minutes per session) and sport-friendly.

| Category | In-season prescription |
|---|---|
| **Strength** | Bilateral and unilateral squat / hip-hinge / lunge 2×/week; load progressively |
| **Plyometrics / landing** | Multi-planar drop landing and reactive jump 1×/week |
| **Neuromuscular** | Single-leg balance with perturbation 2×/week (warm-up integration) |
| **Hamstring** | Nordic curl 1×/week (eccentric protection) |
| **Re-test schedule** | Hop-test battery and MVIC every 3 months through first post-op year; KOOS-Sport and ACL-RSI every 3 months |

### Red-flag indicators (Phase VI)

- **Effusion after games or practices:** the operative knee is overloaded; reduce minutes; re-assess; consult surgeon.
- **New instability episode:** urgent evaluation; consider revision graft if instability confirmed.
- **Contralateral knee symptoms:** the second-ACL-injury rate in young athletes is 15–25 % on the contralateral side; an unhappy contralateral knee in this period is a real injury, not a curiosity. Evaluate.
- **Drop in serial hop-test LSI:** strength regression; protect with focused work; consider whether competition load exceeds capacity.

### Discharge from formal rehab

Discharge from PT typically occurs in the first half of the first post-op competitive season once the athlete is independently maintaining the in-season program and tolerating full game minutes. The athlete returns for periodic re-test and as needed for setbacks. The AT-physician team continues to monitor.

---

## Cross-cutting documentation: per-phase signoff

Every phase transition is documented with criteria-met checkboxes, athlete and PT signatures, and (at Phase IV and Phase V transitions) a co-signature from the referring surgeon. The artifact is bilingual: a clinician-grade version lives in the PT EHR; a plain-language version is given to the athlete and (for adolescents) the parent at each transition.

## Distinction from `clinical-pathway-stepwise.md`

`clinical-pathway-stepwise.md` (the GINA asthma example) is the **bidirectional** ladder — patients move up *and* down a single hierarchy of treatment intensity based on disease control, with step-up and step-down arrows of equal weight in the visual register. Patients can occupy any step indefinitely.

This rehab protocol is **forward-directed but regression-aware**: the phases form a unidirectional sequence (no athlete intentionally regresses from Phase IV to Phase II), but at any phase the protocol defines specific regression triggers (loss of extension; effusion increase; LSI drop; failed criterion at a later phase). Regression is not "step down to a lower phase"; it is "drop back two sessions within the same phase progression" or "return to the prior phase's criteria-met state."

The difference matters because:

- **GINA** treats step-down as a goal (minimize medication exposure while maintaining control). The ladder is genuinely bidirectional.
- **ACL rehab** treats progression as the goal (achieve return to sport). Regression is a setback to be addressed, not an outcome to be celebrated.

Both forms share the criterion-gated discipline that distinguishes them from time-only or symptom-only protocols.

## Reviewer 1 (Statistical Reviewer)

We thank Reviewer 1 for the careful statistical critique. The trial's analytic plan is materially strengthened by these comments.

### Comment 1.1

> *The sample-size justification (page 7 of the original submission, lines 118–122) is insufficient. The authors state only that "the trial was powered to detect a clinically meaningful difference"; no power calculation, no minimum clinically important difference is named, and no target N per arm is justified.*

**Response:** We agree this needed substantial clarification. We have added a power-calculation paragraph to the Methods (Statistical Considerations subsection) explicitly stating the assumptions: 80% power to detect a 4-point difference on the Children's Depression Rating Scale, Revised (CDRS-R; this is the minimum clinically important difference established by Mayes et al., 2010), at two-sided α = 0.05, assuming SD of 12 points (from the pilot work of Park et al., 2023), and a 15% loss-to-follow-up rate. The resulting target N is 400 per arm (800 total); we randomized 412 and 408. The pre-registered SAP (version 2.1, locked 14 January 2024, archived at OSF.io/XXXXX) contains the full calculation.

**Revised text** (Methods, Statistical Considerations, page 8, lines 124–132):

> *"The trial was designed to test the non-inferiority of telehealth-delivered CBT to in-person CBT, with a non-inferiority margin of 4 points on the CDRS-R — the minimum clinically important difference established by Mayes et al. (J Child Adolesc Psychopharmacol 2010; 20: 513–516). Assuming a between-group SD of 12 points (from pilot data; Park et al., 2023), two-sided α of 0.05, 80% power, and 15% loss-to-follow-up, the target sample was 400 evaluable participants per arm (800 total). We enrolled 412 in the telehealth arm and 408 in the in-person arm; the final analyzed N was 387 and 379, respectively, exceeding the powered target. The full power calculation is in the pre-registered Statistical Analysis Plan (version 2.1, locked 14 January 2024, OSF.io/XXXXX)."*

### Comment 1.2

> *The authors report p-values for eight secondary outcomes (Table 3) without any correction for multiplicity. Given that the primary outcome already establishes the trial's claim, the secondary p-values without correction are uninterpretable.*

**Response:** We thank the reviewer for catching this omission; the correction was pre-specified in the SAP but was not adequately described in the manuscript. We have added a Methods paragraph describing the pre-specified Hochberg step-up procedure (Hochberg, Biometrika 1988; 75: 800–802) applied to the eight secondary outcomes, ranked by p-value in the order pre-registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT0XXXXXXX). Three of the eight secondary outcomes (anxiety severity SCARED, parent-rated functioning, treatment-credibility composite) remain significant at the corrected threshold; five do not. We have revised Table 3 to add a corrected-p column and the Discussion paragraph on secondary outcomes accordingly.

**Revised text** (Methods, page 11, lines 198–203):

> *"Secondary outcomes were corrected for multiplicity using the Hochberg step-up procedure with family-wise α = 0.05, applied to the eight pre-specified secondary endpoints in the order registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT0XXXXXXX). Three secondary outcomes (SCARED anxiety severity; parent-rated CGAS functioning; treatment-credibility composite) remained significant at the corrected threshold and are presented in the main text; the remaining five did not meet the corrected threshold and are reported in Table 3, footnoted as not retaining significance after correction."*

### Comment 1.3

> *The missing-data approach is inadequate. The authors use complete-case analysis as the primary analysis with no formal justification, and no multiple-imputation sensitivity analysis is presented. Given the 6% loss to follow-up, this approach risks bias.*

**Response:** We appreciate the reviewer's concern about missing data. After careful consideration, we respectfully disagree that multiple imputation is required as the *primary* analysis here, because (a) the missingness rate is 6%, below the threshold at which complete-case analysis is materially biased under MAR (Sterne et al., BMJ 2009; 338: b2393, Table 1), and (b) the baseline covariates included in the analytic model (baseline CDRS-R, age, sex, site) predict missingness in our data (logistic regression of missingness on baseline covariates: c-statistic 0.71), supporting the MAR assumption. We have, however, added a multiple-imputation sensitivity analysis as a robustness check (m = 20 imputations, chained equations including baseline covariates and post-baseline outcome measurements). The results are consistent with the primary analysis (treatment effect 4.2 CDRS-R points in MI; 4.0 in complete-case; both within the non-inferiority margin). The sensitivity analysis is shown in Supplementary Table S4 and discussed in the Methods.

**Revised text** (Methods, Missing Data subsection, page 12, lines 234–244):

> *"The primary analysis was complete-case under the missing-at-random (MAR) assumption, justified by (a) the 6% loss-to-follow-up rate, below the threshold at which complete-case is materially biased under MAR (Sterne et al., 2009); and (b) baseline covariates included in the analytic model predicted missingness (logistic regression of missingness indicator on baseline covariates: c-statistic 0.71), supporting MAR. As a pre-specified sensitivity analysis (SAP §6.3), we conducted multiple imputation (m = 20, chained equations; baseline covariates and post-baseline outcome assessments as predictors). The MI estimate of the treatment effect was 4.2 CDRS-R points (95% CI 2.8 to 5.6), consistent with the complete-case estimate of 4.0 (95% CI 2.6 to 5.4); both are within the pre-specified 4-point non-inferiority margin. Detailed results are in Supplementary Table S4."*

### Comment 1.4

> *No per-protocol analysis is presented. For a non-inferiority trial, both ITT and per-protocol analyses are typically required, and the manuscript should justify why only ITT is presented.*

**Response:** We agree; the reviewer is correct that non-inferiority trials require both ITT and per-protocol analyses concordant (CONSORT extension for non-inferiority trials; Piaggio et al., JAMA 2012; 308: 2594–2604). The per-protocol analysis was pre-specified in the SAP but was inadvertently omitted from the original submission. We have added a per-protocol analysis (defined as participants who attended ≥ 8 of 12 scheduled sessions, the pre-specified minimum exposure threshold) to the Results. The per-protocol treatment effect (3.8 CDRS-R points; 95% CI 2.3 to 5.3) is concordant with the ITT estimate (4.0 points), supporting the non-inferiority conclusion. We have added text to the Methods and Results, and updated the CONSORT flow diagram (Figure 1) to show per-protocol exclusions.

**Revised text** (Methods, page 13, lines 256–262, and Results, page 15, lines 312–321):

> *"As pre-specified in the SAP (§6.4), we conducted a concordant per-protocol analysis, defined as participants who attended ≥ 8 of 12 scheduled sessions (the minimum exposure threshold pre-specified). The per-protocol analytic N was 342 (telehealth) and 339 (in-person). The per-protocol treatment effect was 3.8 CDRS-R points (95% CI 2.3 to 5.3), within the 4-point non-inferiority margin and concordant with the ITT estimate of 4.0 points (95% CI 2.6 to 5.4). Both analyses support the non-inferiority conclusion."*

### Comment 1.5

> *The effect-size confidence interval interpretation in the Discussion overreaches. The authors describe the result as showing "no clinically meaningful difference" but the upper bound of the 95% CI for the difference (5.4 CDRS-R points) exceeds the 4-point MCID — meaning the trial cannot exclude a clinically meaningful inferiority of telehealth.*

**Response:** We thank the reviewer for this important correction; the original Discussion phrasing was indeed imprecise. We have revised the Discussion paragraph to state the correct interpretation: the trial demonstrated non-inferiority against the pre-specified 4-point margin (the upper bound of the 95% CI for the telehealth-minus-in-person difference is 5.4 points, but the trial was powered against the 4-point margin and the *lower* bound of the relevant non-inferiority test does not cross the margin in the conventional one-sided framing). We have also moderated the Abstract conclusion accordingly.

**Revised text** (Discussion, page 18, lines 401–409):

> *"The CONNECT trial demonstrated non-inferiority of telehealth-delivered CBT to in-person CBT for adolescent depression against the pre-specified 4-point CDRS-R margin. The upper bound of the two-sided 95% CI for the telehealth-minus-in-person difference (5.4 points) exceeds the MCID; the trial therefore cannot rule out a clinically meaningful inferiority of telehealth at the upper extreme of the effect-size distribution. This is a feature of the non-inferiority margin chosen and the trial's power, and warrants caution in interpretation: telehealth is non-inferior on the pre-specified test, but it is not equivalent."*

---

## Reviewer 2 (Clinical Reviewer)

We thank Reviewer 2 for the depth of the clinical critique. Several of the revisions below were prompted by these comments alone.

### Comment 2.1

> *The trial was conducted in three academic medical centers with dedicated study coordinators and protocolized therapist training. The findings may not generalize to community mental-health settings, where therapist turnover is high and infrastructure for telehealth varies widely.*

**Response:** We agree this is an important limitation and have addressed it partially; the reviewer is correct that the academic-center setting is a generalizability constraint. We have added a Limitations paragraph naming the academic-center setting and identifying the specific infrastructure (dedicated coordinators, protocolized supervision, EHR-integrated telehealth platform) that may not be available in community mental-health centers. We have, however, *respectfully retained* the framing that the findings support broader telehealth deployment, because two of the three sites included a community-academic partnership clinic (Site 2: Northeast Community Health) with therapist turnover representative of the field (annual turnover 22%, comparable to community-clinic averages reported by SAMHSA, 2023). We have added a sentence noting that the partnership-clinic subgroup (n = 218) yielded a treatment effect (3.9 CDRS-R points) consistent with the academic-only sites, suggesting some generalizability beyond purely academic settings. A community-clinic implementation study (CONNECT-COMM) is planned as our next trial; we have added a sentence flagging this.

**Revised text** (Discussion, Limitations, page 19, lines 426–438):

> *"The trial was conducted in three academic medical centers, two of which include community-academic partnership clinics, with dedicated study coordinators and protocolized therapist training and supervision. Generalizability to fully community-based settings, with higher therapist turnover and variable telehealth infrastructure, is not directly supported by these data. The partnership-clinic subgroup (n = 218; therapist turnover 22%, comparable to community-clinic averages reported by SAMHSA, 2023) yielded a treatment effect (3.9 CDRS-R points; 95% CI 1.9 to 5.9) consistent with the academic-only sites, suggesting some support for broader generalizability. A community-clinic implementation trial (CONNECT-COMM, NCT0YYYYYYY) is in planning to address this directly."*

### Comment 2.2

> *Adverse-event ascertainment in the telehealth arm may be systematically lower than in-person, because clinical signs (e.g., new self-injury, weight changes, signs of agitation) may not be visible on video.*

**Response:** We thank the reviewer for raising this important safety-ascertainment concern. We have added a Methods paragraph describing the active safety ascertainment used in both arms: weekly self-report symptom checks via study app (administered identically in both arms), monthly study-coordinator phone check-ins (administered identically), and end-of-session therapist safety-assessment templates (administered identically with the addition, in the telehealth arm, of a brief structured visual assessment for new self-injury). Adverse-event ascertainment rates were similar between arms (telehealth 1.42 AE per participant-year; in-person 1.51 AE per participant-year; rate-ratio 0.94, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.09), suggesting no systematic under-ascertainment in the telehealth arm. We have added these data to the Methods and to Table 4.

**Revised text** (Methods, Safety Monitoring, page 14, lines 282–294):

> *"Active safety ascertainment was identical between arms: weekly self-report symptom checks via the study app (validated KSADS-PL adolescent self-report extension), monthly study-coordinator phone check-ins using a structured AE screener, and end-of-session therapist safety-assessment templates. In the telehealth arm, the end-of-session template included a brief structured visual assessment (visible signs of recent self-injury on arms, hands, or face; visible signs of weight loss or agitation; therapist-rated lethality assessment per C-SSRS). AE ascertainment rates were similar across arms (telehealth 1.42 AE per participant-year, 95% CI 1.27 to 1.59; in-person 1.51, 95% CI 1.35 to 1.69; rate-ratio 0.94, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.09), supporting equivalent ascertainment."*

### Comment 2.3

> *Therapist training and fidelity monitoring should be described in detail; the published manuscript should include enough detail for a reader to assess whether the intervention is reproducible.*

**Response:** We agree. We have expanded the Methods description of therapist training (40-hour initial certification in adolescent CBT, monthly group supervision, quarterly individual supervision with audio-recorded session review against the fidelity rubric) and added a Supplementary Document (Supplement 2) reproducing the full fidelity rubric, training curriculum, and supervision schedule. Therapist fidelity scores (modified Cognitive Therapy Rating Scale, adapted for adolescents) averaged 6.2 of 7.0 across both arms (telehealth 6.1, in-person 6.3), with no significant between-arm difference.

**Revised text** (Methods, Intervention, page 10, lines 178–192):

> *"Therapists in both arms completed 40-hour initial certification in adolescent CBT, with monthly group supervision and quarterly individual supervision incorporating audio-recorded session review against the adolescent-CBT fidelity rubric (modified Cognitive Therapy Rating Scale; full rubric in Supplementary Document 2). Mean therapist fidelity across both arms was 6.2 of 7.0 (telehealth arm 6.1, 95% CI 5.9 to 6.3; in-person arm 6.3, 95% CI 6.1 to 6.5; between-arm difference 0.2, 95% CI –0.1 to 0.5). The full therapist-training curriculum, supervision schedule, and fidelity rubric are reproduced in Supplementary Document 2 to support reproducibility."*

### Comment 2.4

> *Comorbid anxiety is present in roughly 50% of adolescents with depression (Costello et al., 2003) and is a plausible moderator of treatment response. The trial should report a pre-specified moderator analysis for baseline anxiety severity.*

**Response:** We thank the reviewer for raising this question; we agree it is clinically important. A baseline-anxiety moderator analysis was pre-specified in the SAP (§7.2) as exploratory, and we have added it to the Results. Baseline SCARED total score did not significantly moderate the treatment effect on CDRS-R (interaction p = 0.31); both arms produced similar reductions in depression severity across the range of baseline anxiety. We have added text to the Results and to Supplementary Figure S5 showing the treatment effect across quartiles of baseline anxiety severity.

**Revised text** (Results, page 16, lines 348–355):

> *"As pre-specified in the SAP (§7.2), we examined baseline anxiety severity (SCARED total) as a moderator of treatment response. Baseline anxiety did not significantly moderate the treatment effect on CDRS-R (interaction p = 0.31); the treatment effect was similar across baseline anxiety quartiles (Supplementary Figure S5). This is consistent with prior evidence (Walkup et al., NEJM 2008) that CBT for adolescent depression with comorbid anxiety is similarly effective across the anxiety-severity range."*

### Comment 2.5

> *The suicidality monitoring protocol should be described in the main text, not in a supplement, given the safety-critical nature of this outcome in adolescents.*

**Response:** We agree with the reviewer's reasoning. This concern overlaps substantially with Reviewer 1's Comment 1.4 (per-protocol analysis) in that both prompted a fuller Methods presentation; we have addressed the suicidality monitoring specifically by promoting the protocol from Supplement 1 into the main-text Methods, Safety Monitoring subsection, page 14, lines 295–308. The promoted text describes the weekly C-SSRS administration, the pre-specified escalation thresholds (any active suicidal ideation with method or plan triggered same-day study-psychiatrist contact and safety planning), and the per-protocol safety outcomes (one serious adverse event of suicidal behavior in the telehealth arm, two in the in-person arm; no completed suicides; no between-arm difference).

**Revised text** (Methods, Safety Monitoring continued, page 14, lines 295–308): *(promoted from Supplement 1; see manuscript for full text)*

### Comment 2.6

> *The findings on telehealth equivalence do not address equity-of-access concerns: adolescents without reliable broadband or a private device cannot access the intervention. The Discussion should engage with this.*

**Response:** We thank the reviewer for raising the equity dimension; we agree it is essential and have addressed it partially. We have added a Discussion paragraph engaging the equity concern directly, naming the broadband-and-device prerequisites for the telehealth arm, citing FCC 2024 broadband-access data showing 7% of rural US households and 12% of US households earning < $30,000/year lack broadband sufficient for video telehealth, and noting that the CONNECT trial provided loaner devices and hotspots to 8% of telehealth-arm participants (the per-protocol availability of these supports is a feature of the trial that real-world deployment may not replicate). We have *not* added a subgroup analysis by household-income or rural-urban status because the trial was not powered for that subgroup analysis and we did not want to over-interpret an underpowered finding; we have flagged this as a question for the planned CONNECT-COMM implementation trial.

**Revised text** (Discussion, Equity Considerations, page 20, lines 461–477):

> *"The findings of non-inferiority for telehealth-delivered CBT must be interpreted against the access prerequisites: reliable broadband, a private device, and a private physical space. FCC 2024 broadband-access data indicate 7% of rural US households and 12% of US households earning < $30,000/year lack broadband sufficient for video telehealth (FCC, Communications Marketplace Report, 2024). The CONNECT trial provided loaner devices and broadband hotspots to 8% of telehealth-arm participants under a trial-funded equity-access protocol; real-world deployment may not include comparable supports. The trial was not powered for subgroup analyses by household income or rural-urban status; the planned CONNECT-COMM implementation trial is designed with sufficient enrollment in low-income and rural-community sites to address equity-of-access questions directly."*

---

## Reviewer 3 (Methodological Reviewer)

We thank Reviewer 3 for the methodological rigor of the review.

### Comment 3.1

> *The open-label nature of the psychotherapy intervention is a serious threat to internal validity. Without allocation concealment from participants and therapists, expectation effects may inflate the apparent equivalence of the two arms.*

**Response:** We appreciate Reviewer 3's concern about open-label design. After careful consideration, we respectfully disagree that the open-label design compromises internal validity in this trial, because (a) the primary outcome (CDRS-R) is rater-administered by an independent assessor masked to treatment assignment — a key safeguard recognized by the CONSORT 2010 extension for non-pharmacologic trials (Boutron et al., Ann Intern Med 2008; 148: 295–309) as the appropriate mitigation when blinding of participants and providers is not feasible in behavioral trials; and (b) the rater-blinding was verified by post-assessment query of the rater (rater guessed treatment assignment correctly in 51% of assessments, consistent with chance and indicating effective blinding). We have added a Limitations paragraph acknowledging the open-label design, naming the rater-blinding mitigation, citing the CONSORT non-pharmacologic extension, and reporting the rater-blinding verification.

**Revised text** (Discussion, Limitations, page 19, lines 442–456):

> *"As is unavoidable in trials of psychotherapy, participants and treating therapists were not blinded to treatment assignment (telehealth vs. in-person); blinding of intervention delivery is infeasible in behavioral trials. The primary outcome (CDRS-R) was administered by independent assessors masked to treatment assignment, as recommended by the CONSORT 2010 extension for non-pharmacologic trials (Boutron et al., 2008). Rater-blinding was verified post-hoc: raters were asked to guess treatment assignment after each CDRS-R administration; 51% of guesses were correct, consistent with chance and indicating effective rater-blinding. Participant expectation effects on self-report secondary outcomes (e.g., treatment-credibility composite) may have been operative; the primary CDRS-R outcome and the rater-blinded SCARED total are less subject to this concern."*

### Comment 3.2

> *The CDRS-R is validated for in-person administration. Remote administration via video introduces a measurement-validity question: are the rater observations of facial affect, psychomotor signs, and engagement reliable on video?*

**Response:** We thank the reviewer for this measurement-validity concern, which we agree is important. We have added a Methods paragraph describing the rater training for video-administered CDRS-R and the inter-rater reliability data from the trial. Raters completed a video-CDRS-R certification (10 standardized video cases, scored against a gold-standard consensus; certification threshold ICC ≥ 0.85). Inter-rater reliability across paired video-administered CDRS-R assessments (n = 80 paired ratings) was ICC = 0.91 (95% CI 0.86 to 0.94), comparable to published in-person CDRS-R inter-rater reliability (ICC 0.92, Mayes et al., 2010). A separate cross-modality reliability substudy (n = 40 participants assessed via both video and in-person within 7 days) yielded a cross-modality ICC of 0.88 (95% CI 0.79 to 0.93), supporting the validity of remote CDRS-R administration.

**Revised text** (Methods, page 11, lines 215–229):

> *"All CDRS-R raters completed a video-administered CDRS-R certification (10 standardized video cases, scored against a multi-rater consensus gold standard; certification threshold ICC ≥ 0.85 against consensus). Inter-rater reliability within the trial (n = 80 paired video-administered CDRS-R assessments) was ICC = 0.91 (95% CI 0.86 to 0.94), comparable to the published in-person CDRS-R inter-rater reliability (ICC 0.92; Mayes et al., 2010). A pre-specified cross-modality reliability substudy (n = 40 participants assessed via both video and in-person within 7 days, with rater-modality counterbalanced) yielded a cross-modality ICC of 0.88 (95% CI 0.79 to 0.93), supporting the validity of video-administered CDRS-R in this trial."*

### Comment 3.3

> *The CONSORT flow diagram (Figure 1) does not match the text. The text states 412 randomized to telehealth and 408 to in-person, but the flow diagram shows 410 and 410. The numbers should be reconciled.*

**Response:** We thank the reviewer for catching this error. The text was correct (412 and 408); the flow diagram contained a transcription error from an earlier draft. We have corrected Figure 1 (CONSORT flow diagram) to show the correct enrollment numbers (412 telehealth, 408 in-person), the loss-to-follow-up (25 telehealth, 29 in-person), the per-protocol exclusions (70 telehealth, 69 in-person, primarily for fewer than 8 sessions attended), and the final analytic Ns (387 telehealth, 379 in-person ITT; 342 telehealth, 339 in-person per-protocol). The corrected Figure 1 also incorporates the CONSORT 2010 reporting elements that were previously condensed.

**Revised text** (Figure 1 caption, page 14):

> *"Figure 1. CONSORT flow diagram for the CONNECT trial. Of 1,247 adolescents assessed for eligibility, 820 were randomized (412 to telehealth CBT, 408 to in-person CBT). Loss to follow-up at the 16-week primary outcome assessment: 25 (telehealth), 29 (in-person). ITT analytic N: 387 (telehealth), 379 (in-person). Per-protocol analytic N (≥ 8 of 12 sessions): 342 (telehealth), 339 (in-person)."*

### Comment 3.4

> *The pre-registered primary outcome was the 16-week CDRS-R change score; the manuscript also presents 24-week and 52-week follow-up. The manuscript should clearly state which analyses are pre-specified and which are exploratory.*

**Response:** We agree; the reviewer is correct that the pre-specification status of each analysis should be explicit. The 16-week CDRS-R change score is the pre-specified primary outcome (SAP §5.1). The 24-week and 52-week follow-up assessments were pre-specified as secondary durability outcomes (SAP §5.2); they are not exploratory. We have revised the Methods and Results to make the pre-specification of each analysis explicit, and we have added a table footnote to Table 3 indicating the pre-specification status of every reported outcome (primary, pre-specified secondary, or exploratory).

**Revised text** (Methods, page 12, lines 247–253; and Table 3 footnote, page 17):

> *"The pre-specified primary outcome was the 16-week CDRS-R change score (SAP §5.1). Pre-specified secondary outcomes included 24-week and 52-week CDRS-R durability, SCARED anxiety severity at 16 and 52 weeks, parent-rated CGAS functioning, treatment-credibility composite, and three additional symptom and functioning measures (SAP §5.2). Exploratory analyses (SAP §7) included baseline-anxiety moderator analysis and the community-partnership-clinic subgroup analysis; both are clearly labeled as exploratory in the Results and in Table 3."*

---

## Closing

We are grateful to all three reviewers and to the editor for the depth and care of the review. The trial — and the manuscript — are materially stronger for the revision. We have addressed every comment in the response above; we have respectfully disagreed with one comment (Reviewer 1, Comment 1.3, on the primary missing-data approach) and partially agreed with two (Reviewer 2, Comments 2.1 and 2.6), with the specific reasoning given in each response. The revised manuscript is submitted with this letter; the tracked-changes version is provided separately for the editor's and reviewers' convenience.

We look forward to the editor's decision.

Sincerely,

**Sarah Park, MD, PhD** *(corresponding author)*
on behalf of the CONNECT Investigators
Department of Psychiatry, [Institution]

                under stress" (cardiac arrest, cervical spine) to "you
                know what to do; here are the gotchas" (fracture). The
                AT's clinical reasoning is matched to the time-criticality
                of the condition.
Pair with: references/medium-playbooks/cross-cluster/operating-manual.md
           (the parent playbook for declarative-imperative artifacts);
           references/medium-playbooks/clinical-algorithm.md (the
           algorithm register; each condition block is a mini-algorithm);
           references/libraries/medical-artifacts.md §20 (sports-medicine
           sideline genres); templates/scat6-interactive.tsx (Wave 13
           sibling — the concussion-specific instrument referenced under
           "Other emergencies" in this EAP); templates/ppe-form.md
           (Wave 13 sibling — pre-season ID of athletes with chronic
           conditions that change EAP response, e.g., known anaphylaxis,
           known seizure disorder, known prior concussion).
================================================================================

Why this subject:
  Friday-night high-school football is the canonical sideline-medicine
  context in U.S. sports medicine literature. The catastrophic events
  documented in this setting — sudden cardiac death, exertional
  heat stroke, cervical spine injury, anaphylaxis to a sting at a stadium
  insect swarm — drive most NATA position-statement writing on sideline
  emergency response. Memorial Stadium is the archetypal Friday-night
  venue: 4,000-seat capacity, AT-staffed home games only, ALS ambulance
  on-site under contract during games, one AED on the home sideline +
  one in the press box + one in the locker-room hallway. The realized
  scenario allows the EAP to demonstrate every required element of the
  NATA recommendation (Andersen JC et al., J Athl Train 2002;37:99-104;
  reaffirmed 2012, 2022) without relying on a fictional venue.

CUSTOMIZE — slots to swap when adapting this scaffold to another venue:

  1. Venue. Replace the Memorial Stadium specifics: address, gate
     identification, AED locations, communication infrastructure
     (radio channels, hardline phones, cell coverage status),
     trauma-center destination, ambulance staging location.
     The address-to-911 script depends on the exact street address;
     do not paraphrase.
  2. Sport season. Football is the realized example. Same-form EAPs
     are required for soccer, lacrosse, hockey, basketball, wrestling,
     gymnastics, swimming, track. Sport-specific event-mechanism
     additions: hockey adds neck-laceration / carotid injury;
     gymnastics adds catastrophic fall mechanism; track adds heat
     stroke as the dominant mechanism; swimming adds drowning /
     submersion. The five core conditions remain; the sport adds
     one or two condition-specific sections.
  3. Level. High-school is the realized example. NCAA / professional
     venues add additional personnel (independent neurotrauma
     consultant; spotter; multi-personnel ALS team; team-physician
     subspecialty roster), denser equipment inventory, and more
     formal communication infrastructure. The form scales; the
     discipline of single-glance readability survives.
  4. Personnel roster. The realized example names AT (K. Patel, ATC),
     team physician (Dr. M. Singh on-call), school nurse (RN J. Liu),
     head coach (Coach R. Foster). Replace with the real names; role
     assignments are the load-bearing element, not the names. Vacant
     roles must be filled or the EAP must explicitly state the
     workaround.
  5. EMS contract. Memorial Stadium has ALS ambulance on-site during
     football games (under a 2026 contract with County EMS). Venues
     without on-site EMS require a different timeline: dispatch to
     arrival typically 6-12 minutes; the EAP must specify the
     response time and the bridging plan (AED + AT + MD until EMS
     arrives).
  6. Trauma center. Central Trauma Center is the realized destination
     (Level II trauma center, 6 miles from the venue, 12 minutes by
     ambulance). Replace with the institutional trauma-center
     destination and confirm the destination annually (trauma-center
     designations change). The destination must be communicated by
     EMS, not by the school.
  7. Annual rehearsal. Per NATA standard, the EAP must be rehearsed
     annually. The rehearsal log lives at the bottom of the artifact;
     update with each rehearsal date and participating personnel.
================================================================================

# Sideline Emergency Action Plan — Memorial Stadium, Friday-night football

> **THE WALL DOCUMENT BELOW IS THE EAP.** This template renders it in markdown; the institutional production version is printed at A2 (594 × 420 mm), oversized type, color-coded by condition severity, laminated, posted on the locker-room wall, the AT-room wall, the press-box wall, and the gate-access shed wall. A folded laminated copy travels in the AT's medical bag.
>
> **Review.** Last rehearsed 2026-08-15 (pre-season). Next rehearsal due 2027-08. **Last reviewed:** 2026-05-24. **Reviewer:** self-attested by school athletic trainer; co-signed by team physician. **Evidence basis:** NATA Position Statement (Andersen JC et al., *J Athl Train* 2002;37:99-104; reaffirmed 2012 and 2022); Inter-Association Task Force on Appropriate Care of the Spine-Injured Athlete (Swartz EE et al., *J Athl Train* 2009; 2015 update); NATA Position Statement Exertional Heat Illness (Casa DJ et al., *J Athl Train* 2015;50:986-1000); ACSM Consensus on the Care of the Athlete with Anaphylaxis (Sicherer SH, Simons FER, *Pediatrics* 2017;139:e20164006 — adolescent/general anaphylaxis applied to sport). **Conflicts of interest:** none.

---

## 1. Venue information

### Exact venue address (read verbatim to 911)

> **Memorial Stadium, Central High School**
> **1450 Stadium Drive, Riverside, [State] [ZIP]**
>
> Cross street: Stadium Drive at Park Avenue.

### Field-of-play identification for EMS

- The football field is on the **east side** of the stadium complex.
- The **home sideline (visiting team has the west sideline)** is the working sideline for the AT; emergencies on the field route to the home sideline.
- The **end zones** are oriented north (home) and south (visitors); use end-zone color (home blue / visitors gold) to confirm position to EMS.

### Gate access for EMS

- **Primary EMS access:** Gate 4, the south end-zone gate. Width 12 ft. **Always unlocked during home games**; key on file at maintenance office for non-game emergencies.
- **Secondary access (if Gate 4 blocked):** Gate 1, north-west, requires key (key located at the AT station; coach radio channel 1 can request).
- **Helicopter landing zone:** middle of the south parking lot, 200 ft east of Gate 4. Lit at night for evening games; communicate via 911 dispatcher if needed.

### AED locations (three on-site)

| AED | Location | Maintenance |
|---|---|---|
| **AED 1** | Home sideline, in the AT's medical bag at the bench | Checked at every game by AT; battery + pads checked monthly |
| **AED 2** | Press box, mounted on west wall, by the elevator door | Checked monthly by AD's office |
| **AED 3** | Locker-room hallway, mounted by the visiting locker-room door | Checked monthly by AD's office |

### Nearest trauma center

- **Central Trauma Center (Level II)** — 1200 Hospital Boulevard, Riverside.
- **Distance:** 6 miles from Memorial Stadium; **transport time:** 12 minutes by ambulance under lights and siren.
- **Phone (medical control):** xxx-xxx-xxxx (provided by EMS protocol, not by EAP — the EAP does *not* call medical control directly; EMS does).

### On-site EMS

- **ALS ambulance contracted on-site during all home football games** (Concord County EMS, contract 2026-2027).
- **Staging location:** north-west corner of the south parking lot, with line-of-sight to Gate 4. Ambulance idles from kickoff through 30 minutes post-final-whistle.
- **EMS crew lead (per contract):** assigned at game-day briefing; introduced to AT and team physician at the pre-game safety meeting.

## 2. Personnel and role assignments

### Names and primary roles

| Role | Name | Where to find at game | Primary EAP role |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Athletic Trainer (AT)** | K. Patel, ATC | Home sideline, bench area | **Lead** — initiates assessment, runs the response, hands off to EMS |
| **Team Physician (MD)** | Dr. M. Singh | Press box (or sideline by request) | Co-leads cardiac / cervical-spine / anaphylaxis response; final clinical decision-maker before EMS hand-off |
| **School Nurse (RN)** | RN J. Liu | Sideline at home games (cardiac and medical response); locker-room at half-time | Supports AT on cardiac arrest (CPR rotation, AED setup, IV access if trained); manages chronic-condition athletes in season file |
| **Head Coach** | Coach R. Foster | Sideline | Crowd / sideline / player management during emergency; coordinates team while AT works on injured player |
| **Assistant Coach (Safety Officer)** | Coach D. Garcia | Sideline | Designated 911 caller; meets EMS at Gate 4; clears non-medical personnel from injury site |
| **Assistant Coach (Sideline AED Runner)** | Coach P. Thompson | Sideline | On AED-call, retrieves AED 2 or AED 3 if AED 1 unavailable; relieves Coach Garcia at gate if needed |
| **Game Announcer (PA)** | Announcer J. Burke | Press box | Suspends game announcements; broadcasts "medical hold" call if requested; assists in directing EMS via PA if visibility is poor |
| **Game Administrator (school side)** | AD R. Lopez | Press box or sideline | Notifies parent of injured player; coordinates with school administration; documents incident; manages media-and-crowd communications post-event |
| **Game Administrator (visiting side)** | varies by visiting team | varies | Reciprocal role for visiting-team athletes |

### Pre-game safety meeting (every game, 30 minutes before kickoff)

The AT, team physician, EMS crew lead, both head coaches, and the school AD meet at the home sideline. Topics:

- Personnel present and role confirmation (any vacant roles addressed).
- Equipment check (AED placement, medical bag inventory, splint inventory, suction, oxygen).
- Communication check (radio channels, AT cell phone, on-site EMS radio).
- Weather and conditions (heat index, lightning forecast; lightning suspension threshold).
- Athletes with chronic medical conditions identified (asthma; anaphylaxis with EpiPen; seizure history; prior concussion in current season; diabetes with insulin pump; sickle-cell trait).
- Visiting-team medical contacts (visiting AT, visiting team physician).

---

## 3. Communication

### Radio channels (handhelds provided to AT, coaches, AD, EMS lead)

| Channel | Used for |
|---|---|
| **Channel 1** | Game-day operations (coach-to-coach, sideline-to-press-box) |
| **Channel 2** | Medical / emergency response (AT, MD, RN, EMS, coaches with EAP role) |
| **Channel 3** | Backup / overflow |

### 911 script — read verbatim to dispatcher

```
911, this is Coach Garcia at Memorial Stadium, Central High School,
1450 Stadium Drive, Riverside.

We have a [medical emergency / cardiac arrest / spine injury / severe
allergic reaction / heat emergency / serious injury] involving a high-school
football player.

The player is [age, sex, conscious / unconscious; breathing / not breathing;
specifics of mechanism].

We have an on-site ALS ambulance from Concord County EMS at the venue;
they are responding. We need [additional EMS / a second ambulance /
helicopter EMS if requested by on-site EMS].

EMS will enter the field via Gate 4, south end-zone, where I will be
waiting. Please advise responding units to enter via Gate 4.

I will stay on the line until EMS arrives or you release me.

Repeat the venue address: Memorial Stadium, Central High School,
1450 Stadium Drive, Riverside.
```

### Communication infrastructure check (pre-game)

- AT carries a charged cell phone with 911 saved; backup is the coach's cell (Channel 2 radio is primary for non-911 sideline communication).
- AT cell phone displays at the AT station; coaches have written copy of the 911 script in laminated form on the back of every coach's playcard.
- Press-box hardline phone available as backup to cell.
