# Informed consent for surgery — right total hip replacement

> **For the patient.** This is your consent for surgery. Take the time to read it. Ask your surgeon every question. Do not sign until you understand what is being done, what could go wrong, and what your other choices are. **You can change your mind at any time before the surgery starts.**
>
> **Patient.** Eleanor Martinez (67yo F). **Date of consent conversation:** 2026-05-10. **Date of surgery:** 2026-05-24. **Reaffirmation on the morning of surgery:** to be performed in the pre-operative holding area before any sedation is given.
>
> **Last reviewed (template):** 2026-05-24. **Reviewer:** self-attested; not institutional protocol; not peer-reviewed. **Evidence basis for risk numbers:** American Joint Replacement Registry (AJRR) 2023 Annual Report; National Joint Registry (NJR, UK) 19th Annual Report 2022; published meta-analyses cited per risk in the Risks section; AAOS Clinical Practice Guideline: Surgical Management of Osteoarthritis of the Hip (2023). **Conflicts of interest:** none for the surgeon obtaining this consent; the implants used are selected on clinical grounds, not on industry relationship.

---

## 1. The surgery — what is being done, in plain language

> **In your own words, this is the surgery:**
> *"I am having surgery to replace my right hip joint with an artificial joint. The surgeon will remove the worn-out parts of my hip — both the ball at the top of my thigh bone and the socket in my pelvis where the ball sits — and put in new ones made of metal, ceramic, and plastic."*

### A little more detail (the medical version)

The procedure is **right primary total hip arthroplasty** (also called *total hip replacement*) via the **posterior (Moore / Southern) approach**. The surgeon makes an incision about 10 cm long over the side of your right hip, splits the muscles in the direction of their fibers, and reaches the hip joint from behind. The worn-out top of your thigh bone (the *femoral head*) is removed. The worn-out cup in your pelvis (the *acetabulum*) is reshaped with a special reamer to accept a new cup. A new socket (a metal cup with a plastic liner) is press-fit into the reshaped pelvis. A new ball (a ceramic head) is placed on a new metal stem that is press-fit into your thigh bone. The new ball sits in the new socket, and you have a new hip joint.

### Where the surgery happens, and who does it

- **Surgeon (named on this consent):** Dr. Marcus Wei, MD — Adult Reconstruction.
- **Operating room:** OR 7 at the institution where this consent is taken.
- **Date:** 2026-05-24.
- **Anesthesia:** General anesthesia (the anesthesiologist will discuss this separately and obtain a separate anesthesia consent). Spinal anesthesia with sedation is an alternative the anesthesiologist may offer.
- **Length of surgery:** About 2 hours from start to finish.
- **You will be in the hospital:** About 1-2 nights, then home with home health PT (or to a rehab facility if needed; this is decided pre-operatively based on your home situation).

---

## 2. Why this surgery — the indication

You are having this surgery because:

- You have **end-stage osteoarthritis of your right hip**. The cartilage that should cushion the joint has worn away. Your X-ray (Kellgren-Lawrence grade 4, the most-advanced grade) shows no cartilage left.
- You have had **4 years of progressive hip pain** that has limited your ability to walk, climb stairs, sleep without pain, and do the activities you value.
- You have **tried non-operative treatment for 18 months without lasting benefit**. Specifically:
  - Physical therapy (12-week structured course completed 2025-09; no durable benefit).
  - Anti-inflammatory medications (naproxen, then meloxicam; partial benefit; GI intolerance).
  - Weight management (BMI 32 down to 29; some benefit but not enough).
  - One steroid injection (March 2026; helped for about 6 weeks; benefit gone).
- You have decided, with your surgeon's recommendation, that surgical replacement of the joint is the next reasonable step.

---

## 3. Your alternatives — what else you could do

A consent without alternatives is not a consent. Every other option has been discussed with you in clinic, and you are choosing surgery over the alternatives. The alternatives are:

### 3.1 Continue non-operative management (the do-nothing option)

You can choose to **not have surgery** and continue managing the pain with medications, physical therapy, and activity modification.

- **What this looks like over time.** Your hip pain will most likely continue to slowly worsen. You will likely become less mobile. Some people find a satisfactory level of function with non-operative management for years; some people find their function declines significantly.
- **Risks.** Non-operative management carries the risks of the medications used (NSAIDs cause GI bleeding, kidney problems, and cardiovascular events at small rates with long-term use), the falls associated with reduced mobility, and the deconditioning that comes from inactivity.
- **You can choose this option at any point — including up to the moment surgery begins.**

### 3.2 Other surgical approaches

If you have surgery, the posterior approach (the one being planned) is one of four reasonable approaches. The others are:

- **Direct anterior approach** — incision in the front of the hip; muscle-sparing; lower early dislocation risk; learning-curve fracture risk; not all surgeons offer this.
- **Anterolateral approach** — incision on the side; splits part of the abductor muscles; sometimes leaves a limp.
- **Direct lateral (Hardinge) approach** — incision on the side; splits more of the abductor muscles; somewhat higher chance of persistent limp.
- **Posterior approach (what you are choosing)** — incision toward the back; splits the gluteus maximus in the direction of its fibers and releases small short external rotators that are repaired at the end; modern technique with capsular repair has reduced dislocation rate to roughly 1 %.

Your surgeon recommends the posterior approach because: it is the highest-volume approach in this department; it tolerates a larger soft-tissue envelope (you are a candidate for any approach but the posterior is robust for your anatomy); it is extensile (if anything unexpected happens, the surgeon can extend the incision); the modern capsular-repair technique addresses the historical dislocation concern.

### 3.3 Hip resurfacing (not appropriate for you)

A hip-resurfacing procedure replaces the surface of the femoral head with a metal cap rather than removing the head and inserting a stem. Hip resurfacing is best for younger (typically under 55), more active, larger-statured patients with good bone density. **You are not a candidate** because your bone quality, age, and activity profile favor a stemmed THA over resurfacing. You and your surgeon discussed this; you agree.

### 3.4 Partial hip arthroplasty (hemiarthroplasty)

A hemiarthroplasty replaces only the femoral head, leaving the native socket. This is the procedure used for some hip fractures, but **it is not appropriate for osteoarthritis** because both the head and the socket are worn. You and your surgeon discussed this; you agree.

---

## 4. The risks — what could go wrong

Every surgery carries risks. The risks below are the most-important risks of this specific surgery. Each risk has a number from a real source (registry data or published medical literature); the source is cited so you (or anyone you ask to review with you) can check the source.

**Important: small numbers still happen to real people.** A 1 % risk means about 1 in 100 patients having this surgery experiences this complication. If 100 people have this surgery, on average 1 of them has it — and that person is a real person. The decision to have surgery is the decision to accept these risks against the benefits.

### 4.1 Risks listed in order of frequency

| Risk | About how often | What it means for you | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Leg length difference** | About 2-3 in 100 patients notice a difference | Your operated leg may end up slightly longer or shorter than your other leg. Most differences are small (under 1 cm) and not noticed; some are larger and noticeable when you walk. A shoe lift can correct most differences. Surgical revision for length is rare. | AJRR 2023; Whitehouse SL et al., *Acta Orthop* 2013 |
| **Blood clot in the leg or lung (DVT or PE)** | About 1-5 in 100 with modern prevention | A blood clot can form in the deep veins of your leg (DVT) and rarely travel to the lungs (PE). You will take aspirin (or another blood thinner) for about 5 weeks after surgery and wear leg compression devices in the hospital to prevent this. | Geerts WH et al., *Chest* 2008; AAOS CPG VTE prophylaxis 2023 |
| **Dislocation of the new hip** | About 1-3 in 100 in the first year | Your new hip can come out of the socket if you put it in certain extreme positions. You will be taught "posterior hip precautions" (avoid bending past 90°, do not cross your legs, do not turn your toes inward) for 6 weeks. Most dislocations happen in the first 3 months. | Berry DJ et al., *JBJS Am* 2005 — registry data |
| **Surgical site infection** | About 1-2 in 100 | Infection can develop in the incision (superficial) or deep in the joint (deep). Deep infection is the more serious problem and usually requires additional surgery and long courses of antibiotics. We give you preventive antibiotics in the hour before surgery and at intervals during the procedure. | Pulido L et al., *Clin Orthop Relat Res* 2008; AAOS CPG 2010 |
| **Intra-operative or early post-op fracture** | Under 1 in 100 | The bone of your thigh or pelvis can crack during the surgery (when the stem is press-fit into the canal, or when the cup is press-fit into the socket). If this happens, the surgeon addresses it during the surgery — usually with a wire or a screw — and your recovery may be slower (weight-bearing restrictions for several weeks). | Berry DJ, *JBJS Am* 1999 |
| **Sciatic nerve injury** | About 1 in 100 (mostly temporary) | The sciatic nerve runs behind the hip joint and is at risk during the posterior approach. The surgeon identifies and protects the nerve throughout the surgery. Most injuries (about 9 out of 10) are stretches that recover fully over weeks to months. A small number are permanent and cause foot-drop (weakness lifting the foot) and numbness in the back of the leg. | Schmalzried TP et al., *JBJS Am* 1991; AJRR 2023 |
| **Need for revision surgery** | About 5 in 100 over 10 years; under 10 in 100 over 20 years | The artificial joint can wear out, loosen, or fail over time. Modern implants typically last 20+ years; some require revision sooner. If revision is needed, it is a larger surgery than the original. | NJR (UK) 19th Annual Report 2022; AJRR 2023 |
| **Vascular injury** | Under 1 in 200 | Major blood vessels (the iliac artery and vein in the pelvis) can rarely be injured by a retractor or reamer that goes through the inner wall of the socket. This is a serious complication that may require a vascular surgeon to repair. The surgeon is trained to recognize and prevent this. | Calligaro KD et al., *J Vasc Surg* 2003 |
| **Complications of general anesthesia** | Varies; serious complications under 1 in 1000 for an otherwise healthy patient | The anesthesiologist will discuss anesthesia risks separately and obtain a separate consent. The main risks are reactions to anesthetic drugs, breathing-tube complications, awareness during surgery (rare), and cardiac events (rare in patients without significant heart disease). | American Society of Anesthesiologists patient information |
| **Death** | Under 1 in 1000 (under 0.1 %) | Death within 30 days of primary THA is rare in patients who pass pre-operative medical clearance, but it is not zero. The most-common causes are pulmonary embolism, cardiac events, and overwhelming infection. | AJRR 2023; published 30-day mortality registry data |

### 4.2 Other risks discussed

These risks are less common or less specific to THA but are part of the consent conversation:

- Urinary retention (need for a catheter for a day or two; common in older patients).
- Confusion or delirium in hospital (more common in older patients; usually transient).
- Constipation from pain medication.
- Allergic reaction to medications used during the surgery (rare; allergy history reviewed pre-operatively).
- Hardware-related complications years later (squeaking ceramic bearings; trunnion corrosion; very rare modern complications).

### 4.3 What the surgical team does to reduce risks

The team has named, evidence-based practices to reduce each of these risks. A short list:

- **Infection:** preventive antibiotic 30 minutes before incision; chlorhexidine skin prep; iodine-impregnated drape; ultraviolet-filtered air handling in the OR; meticulous sterile technique.
- **Blood clot:** intra-operative tranexamic acid; aspirin or apixaban for 5 weeks; mechanical compression in hospital; early mobilization.
- **Dislocation:** capsular repair at the end of the surgery; posterior hip precautions for 6 weeks; jumbo (36 mm) head for stability.
- **Nerve injury:** sciatic nerve identification and retractor protection throughout the case; avoidance of extreme internal rotation during dislocation.
- **Fracture:** progressive broaching with feel-based endpoints; downsizing if any unexpected resistance; intra-operative imaging available.
- **Leg length:** pre-operative templating; intra-operative trial reduction with leg-length measurement and shuck test; documented pre- and post-operative leg lengths.

---

## 5. The benefits — what could go right

The benefits of THA are well-established in registry data and patient-reported outcome studies.

- **Pain relief.** About 90-95 % of patients report substantial pain relief at 1 year (Singh JA et al., *J Rheumatol* 2010; AJRR PROMs data). For most patients, this is the largest single change.
- **Improved function.** About 85-90 % of patients return to walking without an assistive device. Most patients return to most of the activities they value (walking, gardening, golf, swimming, doubles tennis, light hiking). High-impact activities (running, contact sports, deep squatting under load) are generally not recommended after THA, but most patients choose THA precisely to return to moderate activity, not high-impact.
- **Sleep.** Many patients report this as the largest immediate-quality-of-life change — sleeping through the night without hip pain.
- **Function with the contralateral side.** Some patients who have THA on one side experience improved function in the other hip and the spine, because gait normalizes.
- **Durability.** Modern primary THA with the components being used (Pinnacle cementless cup; Marathon HXLPE liner; Corail cementless stem; Biolox Delta ceramic head) has registry-projected survivorship over 90 % at 15 years (AJRR 2023; NJR 2022).

The benefits are real and substantial. They are also probabilistic: most patients experience the benefits, but some do not, or experience smaller benefits than they hoped.

---

## 6. What is being implanted in your body

You have a right to know exactly what is being implanted. The following implants are planned for your surgery (these are documented in the operative note after the surgery; the catalog numbers are confirmed by the operating-room circulating nurse at the time of placement):

| Component | Manufacturer | Model | Size | Material |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Acetabular cup (the new socket)** | DePuy Synthes | Pinnacle Gription 100 | 56 mm outer diameter | Titanium alloy with hydroxyapatite coating for bone in-growth |
| **Liner (inside the new socket)** | DePuy Synthes | Marathon HXLPE | 36 mm inner diameter | Highly cross-linked polyethylene (very wear-resistant plastic) |
| **Femoral stem (the new piece in your thigh bone)** | DePuy Synthes | Corail (collared, cementless) | Size 5 standard offset | Titanium alloy with hydroxyapatite coating for bone in-growth |
| **Femoral head (the new ball)** | DePuy Synthes | Biolox Delta | 36 mm | Ceramic (zirconia-toughened alumina) |
| **Backup implants on the back table** (used only if needed) | DePuy Synthes | Cemented Marathon cup + CPT cemented stem | Sized at time of surgery if needed | Cobalt-chromium alloy + polymethylmethacrylate cement |

### What you should know about these implants

- **No known recalls.** The above components have no current recall notices as of the consent date. Implant safety information is monitored by the FDA and the manufacturer; you (or your family) can search "FDA Medical Device Recalls" if you wish to check.
- **All implants are FDA-cleared** for the use planned.
- **No off-label use.** The implants are being used as intended; no off-label use is planned.
- **Conflict of interest:** the surgeon does not have a financial relationship with DePuy Synthes (no consulting income, no royalties, no stock); the implants are selected on clinical grounds.

---

## 7. Teach-back — your understanding in your own words

> **This is the most important box on the form.** Before you sign, write the following in your own words. The surgeon will read what you write and discuss any misunderstandings before signing. If you cannot answer either question, the surgeon will go over the relevant section again with you.

### 7.1 What is the surgery you are having? Write it in one or two sentences as if you were telling a friend.

```
Patient's response (handwritten or typed; not pre-filled):

I am having surgery to replace my right hip joint with an artificial joint. The
surgeon will take out the worn parts and put in a new metal-and-plastic socket
and a new ceramic ball on a metal stem in my thigh bone.

(Patient response on the date of consent, 2026-05-10. Patient could paraphrase
back the procedure accurately. Surgeon noted in the chart that teach-back
demonstrated understanding.)
```

### 7.2 What is one major risk of this surgery? Write it in your own words. (You do not need to list all risks; one is enough.)

```
Patient's response (handwritten or typed; not pre-filled):

The main risk I am worried about is dislocation — that the new hip could come
out of place if I bend too far or twist wrong in the first few weeks. The
surgeon told me about the precautions and that the chance is about 1-3 in 100,
mostly in the first few months. I am committed to following the precautions.

(Patient response on the date of consent, 2026-05-10. Patient could name a
real risk and describe what it means. Surgeon noted in the chart that teach-back
demonstrated understanding of risk. Patient was offered a chance to ask any
remaining questions; the patient asked specifically about return to walking
without a cane and was given a realistic answer.)
```

### 7.3 Surgeon's note on teach-back

> *"Mrs. Martinez was able to describe the surgery accurately in her own words and named dislocation as a specific risk she understood. She asked appropriate follow-up questions about expected recovery timeline and return to walking. She declined a second opinion (we offered). She has discussed the decision with her husband and adult daughter. She has decisional capacity. Consent obtained without coercion in the clinic setting on 2026-05-10; reaffirmation will be obtained in pre-operative holding on the morning of surgery, 2026-05-24, before any sedation is given."*
> — Dr. Marcus Wei, MD, 2026-05-10.

---

## 8. Reaffirmation on the morning of surgery

The consent obtained at the clinic visit is reaffirmed on the morning of surgery in the pre-operative holding area, **before any sedation is given**. The surgeon (or, if the surgeon has delegated to a competent designee, that designee — but for primary elective arthroplasty, the operating surgeon performs the reaffirmation personally) confirms with the patient:

- Identity (name + DOB + MRN, confirmed by patient and by the arm band).
- The procedure (right primary total hip arthroplasty, posterior approach).
- The site (right hip; surgeon marks the site with a sterile marker in the patient's view; patient witnesses).
- That the patient still wishes to proceed (the patient has the right to withdraw consent at any moment until the surgery starts, with no impact on their future care).
- Any new questions the patient has thought of since the clinic visit.
- The anesthesia consent (separate document; obtained by the anesthesiologist).

The reaffirmation is documented in the pre-operative checklist.

---

## 9. Signatures

> **By signing below, the patient affirms:**
>
> - The procedure has been explained in language she understands.
> - The risks, benefits, and alternatives have been explained, and she has had the opportunity to ask questions.
> - She understands she can withdraw consent at any time before the surgery starts.
> - The implants that will be used have been disclosed.
> - She has completed the teach-back box in her own words and the surgeon has reviewed her responses.
> - She consents to the surgery as described.
> - She consents to the surgeon performing additional procedures during the surgery if, in the surgeon's professional judgment, they become necessary for her safety (e.g., addressing an unexpected intra-operative fracture by adding a cable or screw).
> - She has been given a copy of this consent form for her records.

## 10. For your records — what to expect after surgery (a one-page summary you can take home)

After the surgery:

- You will wake up in the recovery area with the new hip in place. The pain will be managed with a combination of medications.
- You will be encouraged to stand and walk with a physical therapist within hours of the surgery.
- You will have the hip precautions to follow for 6 weeks (do not bend past 90 degrees at the hip; do not cross your legs; do not turn your toes inward).
- You will go home (most patients) with home health PT, or to a short stay at a rehab facility if you do not have support at home.
- You will take aspirin (or another blood thinner) for about 5 weeks to prevent blood clots.
- You will return to the surgeon's office at about 2 weeks for a wound check and at 6 weeks for an evaluation of progress.
- You will most likely return to walking without a cane in 4-6 weeks; most patients return to most regular activities by 3 months.
- A more detailed post-operative rehabilitation protocol will be given to you separately (the protocol may resemble the framework in `templates/rehab-protocol.md` adapted for THA; your surgeon's institution may have a different specific protocol).

### Symptoms that need urgent attention after surgery

Go to the emergency department (or call 911) if you have any of the following:

- Fever above 38.5°C (101.3°F).
- New severe pain in the operated hip that is different from your post-surgical pain.
- The leg is suddenly cooler, paler, or you cannot move it.
- Severe sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, or coughing up blood (possible blood clot to the lung).
- Calf pain with swelling and warmth (possible blood clot in the leg).
- Drainage, bleeding, or pus from the incision.
- A pop or sudden severe pain in the hip (possible dislocation).
- A fall or accident affecting the operated leg.

### Less-urgent symptoms — call the surgeon's office during business hours

- Worsening pain that is not relieved by your medications.
- Increasing swelling in the leg without calf pain.
- Constipation that does not respond to over-the-counter remedies.
- Concerns about the wound appearance.
- Questions about activities or medications.

---

## Appendix — Standard legal language (you are told this exists; the legal section is for the institution's records)

This appendix contains the standard institutional legal language regarding consent under [State] law. The substantive content of your consent is in Sections 1-9 above; this appendix is the institutional risk-management formal record. The institution requires the appendix to be signed by the patient, but the appendix is NOT the substance of the consent — the substance is the conversation, the teach-back, and the signature blocks above. The appendix typically includes:

- General consent to medical and surgical treatment by the named provider and institution.
- Consent to anesthesia (often a separate document obtained by the anesthesiologist).
- Consent to blood-product administration if needed (with the right to refuse on religious or personal grounds).
- Consent to disposal of removed tissue per institutional protocol.
- Acknowledgment of receipt of the institution's Patient Bill of Rights and HIPAA Notice of Privacy Practices.
- Insurance and financial responsibility disclosures.
- Photography / video / teaching-related disclosures (separate signature; institutional protocol).

These items are signed on the institutional consent form per protocol. They are administrative; they are not the substantive consent. **If anything in the appendix conflicts with the conversation you had with your surgeon, ask before signing.**

# Posterior approach to the right hip for primary total hip arthroplasty

> **Procedure:** Right total hip arthroplasty (primary), cementless press-fit acetabular + femoral components, 36 mm ceramic-on-highly-crosslinked-polyethylene bearing, posterior (Moore / Southern) approach.
>
> **Audience:** PGY-3 / PGY-4 orthopaedic resident; supervising arthroplasty fellow.
>
> **Last reviewed:** 2026-05-24. **Reviewer:** self-attested; not peer-reviewed for institutional protocol. **Evidence basis:** AAOS Clinical Practice Guideline: Surgical Management of Osteoarthritis of the Hip (2023); Hoppenfeld *Surgical Exposures in Orthopaedics* 6th ed. (2022); AO Surgery Reference posterior-hip module. Conflicts of interest: none declared.

---

## Pre-operative planning

The pre-op plan is the surgeon's hypothesis. It is templated, written, and brought to the case as a single page; it lives on the wall of the operating room beside the C-arm monitor. The op note records what was actually done.

### 1. Imaging review

- **AP pelvis** (calibrated, weight-bearing, with 25 mm templating sphere at hip level): assess joint-space narrowing, osteophyte distribution, acetabular orientation, femoral-head sphericity, evidence of avascular necrosis, cyst burden, and protrusio.
- **Lateral hip (cross-table or frog-leg)**: assess femoral head-neck offset, posterior acetabular wall coverage, and version of the acetabulum.
- **Calibration**: 25 mm reference sphere; scale factor 0.94 (this case). All templated measurements derive from this scale.

### 2. Templating

| Templated value | This case | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Acetabular cup size | 56 mm | Templated against the acetabular roof; verified against the teardrop |
| Femoral stem size | Size 5 (tapered wedge) | Templated to fill the metaphyseal flare without distal canal-fill |
| Head diameter | 36 mm | Cup size permits 36 mm with HXLPE liner; jumbo head reduces dislocation risk |
| Neck length | Medium (+0) — to be confirmed at trial | Reproduces native leg length per templating |
| Stem offset | Standard offset | Reproduces native medial offset per templating |
| Planned neck-cut level | 10 mm above the lesser trochanter | Per stem-specific guide |
| Projected leg-length difference | 0 mm (equal) | Templated teardrop-to-LT; matches contralateral |

### 3. Implant inventory (communicated to OR scrub team day before case)

- **Cup:** DePuy Pinnacle Gription 100 (multi-hole), sizes 54 / 56 / 58 on the back table.
- **Liner:** Marathon HXLPE (highly-crosslinked polyethylene), 36 mm inner diameter, neutral.
- **Stem:** DePuy Corail (collared, tapered wedge, HA-coated), sizes 4 / 5 / 6 on the back table.
- **Head:** Biolox Delta ceramic, 36 mm, neck lengths –3.5 / +0 / +5 / +8.5 mm on the back table.
- **Backup:** cemented cup (Marathon polyethylene) and cemented stem (CPT) on the back table for the cement-required scenario.

### 4. Medical clearance and consent

- **Medical clearance:** internal-medicine pre-op evaluation; cardiac risk-stratified per AAOS / ACC guidance; anticoagulation managed per institutional protocol (DOAC held per drug-specific interval).
- **Surgical consent:** procedure-specific risks named — infection (1–2 %); dislocation (1–3 % posterior approach; higher than anterior approaches historically); intra-operative fracture (< 1 %); leg-length inequality (5–10 % perceive a difference); sciatic-nerve injury (~ 1 %, mostly neuropraxia with full recovery); medical complications (DVT / PE; cardiac events; UTI). Implant-related disclosures: HXLPE-on-ceramic bearing, expected lifespan > 20 years per registry data, possible need for revision if liner wear or osteolysis develops. Named alternatives: non-operative management (NSAIDs, intra-articular injection, weight loss, activity modification); alternative surgical approaches (direct anterior, anterolateral, direct lateral); hip resurfacing (selected patients).

### 5. Positioning equipment requested

Radiolucent table with sacral cut-out; well-padded lateral peg holders (anterior at ASIS, posterior at sacrum); axillary roll; well-leg padding; head support maintaining cervical-spine neutral position; padding for the dependent peroneal nerve at the fibular neck.

---

## Patient positioning

The patient is in the **lateral decubitus position with the right (operative) hip up**.

> **Step P1. Confirm laterality.**
>
> *Anatomy frame:* not applicable.
> *Intra-op frame:* photograph of the surgical site marking on the patient's right hip; signed by surgeon, witnessed.
>
> Confirm site marking. Confirm operative consent. Confirm right hip on the surgical safety checklist (WHO time-out). Do not advance past this step without all three confirmations.
>
> **Structures at risk:** wrong-site surgery is the never-event. The institutional pre-incision time-out is the gate.

> **Step P2. Position the patient lateral decubitus, right side up.**
>
> *Anatomy frame:* schematic of lateral decubitus position with sacral and ASIS peg locations marked, axillary roll position, well-leg padded with hip and knee in slight flexion for stability.
> *Intra-op frame:* photograph of the positioned patient before draping; pegs, axillary roll, well-leg padding all visible.
>
> Place the patient lateral decubitus on a radiolucent table with the operative right hip up. Place the anterior peg over the ASIS and the posterior peg against the sacrum, both well-padded. Confirm the pelvis is perpendicular to the table — this is the reference for cup orientation later.
>
> **Structures at risk:** brachial plexus on the dependent side (axillary roll prevents direct compression); peroneal nerve on the dependent leg (pad the fibular neck); dependent eye and ear (foam protector).

> **Step P3. Confirm pelvic position.**
>
> *Anatomy frame:* schematic showing pelvis perpendicular to the floor as the cup-orientation reference.
> *Intra-op frame:* photograph from the head of the bed showing the pelvis vertical; surgeon confirms by palpating both ASIS.
>
> Palpate both anterior superior iliac spines. Confirm a line drawn between them is perpendicular to the floor. Re-check after draping — drape weight can shift a poorly-secured pelvis 5–10 degrees, distorting cup orientation.
>
> **Structures at risk:** none directly. The risk is *cup malposition* later, traced back to mis-position now. The fix is at the source.

---

## Approach and exposure: the posterior (Moore / Southern) approach

### Alternative approaches acknowledged

The choice of the posterior approach is itself a decision. The trainee learns the procedure in the context of the alternatives.

| Approach | Eponym / origin | Interval | Principal structure at risk | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Direct anterior** | Smith-Petersen (1917) / Hueter (1881) | Sartorius–TFL (superficial); rectus femoris–gluteus medius (deep) | Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve | True internervous; muscle-sparing; lower dislocation rate; learning-curve fracture risk |
| **Anterolateral** | Watson-Jones (1936) | TFL–gluteus medius | Superior gluteal nerve (proximal branch) | Splits anterior gluteus medius fibres; limp risk if proximal extension |
| **Direct lateral** | Hardinge (1982) | Splits gluteus medius and minimus in line with fibres | Superior gluteal nerve to abductors | Strong abductor disruption; persistent limp in some patients |
| **Posterior (chosen)** | Moore (1957) / Southern | Splits gluteus maximus in fibre direction; releases short external rotators (piriformis, conjoint, quadratus femoris) | Sciatic nerve | Historically higher dislocation rate (~ 3 %); modern capsular repair brings rate to ~ 1 % |

The posterior approach is selected for this case for: surgeon familiarity (highest-volume approach in the department); patient anatomy (BMI 32, obese; the posterior approach tolerates larger soft-tissue envelope better than anterior); planned extensile exposure (revision-friendly if needed); and surgeon-pateint conversation in clinic (patient counselled on the posterior dislocation risk and the precautions).

### Approach cross-section reference

> *Anatomy frame:* axial cross-section of the right hip at the level of the femoral head-neck junction, showing (from posterior to anterior) skin, subcutaneous fat, fascia lata, gluteus maximus, short external rotators (piriformis, conjoint tendon of obturator internus + superior and inferior gemelli, quadratus femoris) overlying the posterior capsule, sciatic nerve emerging from the inferior border of piriformis. Derived from Hoppenfeld *Surgical Exposures* Fig. 7-22 conventions. Reference `templates/svg-architectural-section.svg` for the cross-section drawing register (ISO 128 conventions transferable to surgical anatomy).
>
> *Structures-at-risk overlay:* sciatic nerve traced in yellow along its course from greater sciatic foramen, deep to piriformis, to the posterior thigh.

### Step-by-step approach

> **Step A1. Mark the incision.**
>
> *Anatomy frame:* surface landmarks on the lateral right hip — greater trochanter palpable, PSIS palpable, incision line drawn 10 cm centred on the greater trochanter and curving posteriorly toward the PSIS at the proximal end.
> *Intra-op frame:* photograph of the patient draped, incision marked with sterile marker.
>
> With the patient draped, mark a 10–12 cm incision centred on the greater trochanter. The line passes through the tip of the trochanter and curves posteriorly proximally toward the PSIS, distally extending 4–5 cm along the femoral shaft.
>
> **Structures at risk:** none at this step. The incision is the map for the rest of the approach; getting it correct here saves time at every subsequent step.

> **Step A2. Incise skin and subcutaneous tissue.**
>
> *Anatomy frame:* skin and subcutaneous fat layers indicated; no neurovascular structures in this plane on the lateral hip.
> *Intra-op frame:* photograph of skin incision being made with a 10-blade; assistant retracts with skin hooks.
>
> Incise skin with a 10-blade. Carry down through subcutaneous fat to the fascia lata with electrocautery, achieving haemostasis as the dissection proceeds.
>
> **Structures at risk:** none significant in this plane on the lateral hip. The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is anterior and does not enter this corridor.

> **Step A3. Identify and split the fascia lata and the gluteus maximus.**
>
> *Anatomy frame:* fascia lata with the bursa over the greater trochanter; gluteus maximus muscle belly indicated proximally; the fibre direction (parallel; running from the iliac crest to the iliotibial tract) shown.
> *Intra-op frame:* photograph of the assistant retracting skin; fascia lata exposed; surgeon's finger demonstrating the gluteus maximus fibre direction.
>
> Identify the fascia lata. Incise the fascia in line with its fibres distally, opening 8 cm along the iliotibial tract. Proximally, split the gluteus maximus muscle bluntly with finger or Mayo scissors *in the direction of its fibres* (not transversely; transverse cutting denervates distal fibres).
>
> **Structures at risk:** inferior gluteal nerve (the motor supply to gluteus maximus) enters the muscle from its deep surface medially. Splitting the muscle in fibre direction preserves the nerve to both halves; transverse division denervates the inferior portion.

> **Step A4. Identify and protect the sciatic nerve.**
>
> *Anatomy frame:* posterior view of the hip with gluteus maximus reflected; piriformis muscle visible; sciatic nerve emerging from the inferior border of piriformis and descending in the posterior thigh.
> *Intra-op frame:* photograph showing piriformis tendon at its trochanteric insertion; sciatic nerve visible deep to and inferior to piriformis, protected by a finger.
>
> Palpate the sciatic nerve under the inferior border of piriformis. Visually confirm its course — the nerve typically emerges deep to piriformis (~ 85 % of patients) but may pierce through piriformis or run superficially (~ 15 %; the anatomic variant). Do not place any retractor blindly into the posterior wound until the nerve is identified.
>
> **Structures at risk:** the **sciatic nerve** is the canonical structure-at-risk in the posterior approach. Direct injury (retractor pressure, blade cut, traction during dislocation) causes neuropraxia in 1–3 % of cases; complete laceration is rare but catastrophic (foot-drop ± sensory loss in the posterior thigh and lower leg). Protect the nerve under a soft-tissue retractor for the rest of the case; never retract into the posterior wound without confirming the nerve is medial to the retractor.

> **Step A5. Divide the short external rotators (piriformis, conjoint tendon, quadratus femoris) at insertion.**
>
> *Anatomy frame:* posterior view with each short external rotator labelled: piriformis (most superior, inserting on the superior aspect of the greater trochanter); conjoint tendon of obturator internus and the gemelli (middle, inserting on the medial trochanter); quadratus femoris (most inferior, inserting on the intertrochanteric crest).
> *Intra-op frame:* photograph of piriformis tendon being tagged with a #2 non-absorbable suture before division; sciatic nerve protected by retractor.
>
> Tag the piriformis tendon at its trochanteric insertion with a #2 non-absorbable suture. Divide the tendon at its insertion (leaving a 5 mm cuff on bone for later repair). Tag and divide the conjoint tendon similarly. The quadratus femoris may be left intact or partially released; if released, divide proximally, preserving the medial femoral circumflex artery that runs deep to it.
>
> **Structures at risk:** the **medial femoral circumflex artery** runs along the deep surface of quadratus femoris and is the dominant blood supply to the femoral head. Preserve the artery during quadratus release; injury risks femoral-head osteonecrosis in revision scenarios (less critical in THA since the head will be resected, but training discipline transfers to hemiarthroplasty and femoral-neck-preserving procedures where the artery is load-bearing).

> **Step A6. Perform T-shaped capsulotomy.**
>
> *Anatomy frame:* posterior capsule visible after short-external-rotator reflection; T-shape incision marked — longitudinal along the femoral neck axis with a transverse limb at the acetabular rim.
> *Intra-op frame:* photograph of capsular incision being made; capsular flaps tagged with stay sutures for later repair.
>
> Incise the posterior capsule with a 15-blade in a T-shape: the longitudinal limb along the femoral-neck axis, the transverse limb at the acetabular rim. Tag the capsular flaps with #2 non-absorbable stay sutures for repair at closure.
>
> **Structures at risk:** the sciatic nerve remains protected by the retractor. The capsule itself is the structure-at-risk for *post-operative dislocation* — capsular repair at closure is the principal modern modification that has reduced posterior-approach dislocation rate from ~ 3 % (historical) to ~ 1 % (with repair). Tag flaps now; the repair depends on tags placed at this step.

---

## Dislocation and femoral preparation

> **Step D1. Dislocate the hip posteriorly.**
>
> *Anatomy frame:* schematic showing femoral head exiting the acetabulum posteriorly with the leg flexed, adducted, and internally rotated.
> *Intra-op frame:* photograph of the assistant flexing, adducting, and internally rotating the leg; surgeon controlling the femoral head with a bone hook.
>
> Flex the hip to 90°, adduct, and internally rotate. The femoral head should deliver posteriorly out of the acetabulum. Use a bone hook around the femoral neck to assist if needed. If the head will not dislocate, do not force — check for inadequate capsular release, intact iliopsoas tendon, or unexpected osteophyte; address the limiting structure before retrying.
>
> **Structures at risk:** during dislocation, the sciatic nerve can be stretched if the leg is internally rotated beyond 60° at 90° hip flexion. Avoid extreme internal rotation; the dislocation should be smooth, not forceful. Iatrogenic fracture of the proximal femur (calcar split) occurs if forced through a contracture; address the limiting structure rather than escalate force.

> **Step D2. Confirm the planned femoral-neck osteotomy level.**
>
> *Anatomy frame:* lateral view of the femoral neck with the planned osteotomy line marked 10 mm above the lesser trochanter (per pre-op templating).
> *Intra-op frame:* photograph of the femoral neck with a marking pen indicating the cut level; surgeon palpating the lesser trochanter to confirm reference point.
>
> Palpate the lesser trochanter to identify the reference point. Mark the planned osteotomy 10 mm proximal to the lesser trochanter on the medial neck (this case's templating). Stem-specific guides indicate the angle of the cut relative to the femoral shaft (typically 45° relative to the long axis); confirm the angle from the implant manufacturer's technique brochure.
>
> **Structures at risk:** at this step the structure-at-risk is *templating fidelity*. A cut 5 mm too high or too low changes the implant offset and leg length by 3–5 mm at trial — sometimes recoverable with neck-length adjustment, sometimes not. Confirm the reference (lesser trochanter) before cutting.

> **Step D3. Osteotomise the femoral neck.**
>
> *Anatomy frame:* osteotomy plane shown.
> *Intra-op frame:* photograph of the oscillating saw being used to make the femoral-neck cut; assistant irrigating to dissipate heat.
>
> Use an oscillating saw to make the femoral-neck cut at the marked level and angle. Irrigate continuously to dissipate heat (avoids thermal necrosis of adjacent bone). Complete the cut through the medial cortex; deliver the femoral head from the acetabulum with a corkscrew extractor.
>
> **Structures at risk:** the sciatic nerve remains the principal structure-at-risk during this step (the saw is anterior to the protected nerve, but careless saw deviation can injure). The medial femoral circumflex artery runs along the medial neck and is divided as part of the osteotomy (acceptable in THA since the head will be removed).

> **Step D4. Deliver the femoral head.**
>
> *Anatomy frame:* femoral head extracted from the acetabulum.
> *Intra-op frame:* photograph of the femoral head removed and placed on the back table for measurement; ruler indicating diameter (used to confirm templating accuracy).
>
> Deliver the femoral head with a corkscrew extractor. Measure the head diameter on the back table — confirms templating (this case templated 56 mm cup with 36 mm head; the native head will typically measure 46–52 mm depending on cup-offset reaming planned). The removed head can be morselised for autograft if defects are encountered.
>
> **Structures at risk:** none significant at this step (the head is the discarded portion of the procedure).

---

## Acetabular preparation

> **Step AC1. Expose the acetabulum.**
>
> *Anatomy frame:* acetabulum with labrum visible; transverse acetabular ligament marking the inferior limit; pulvinar (fibrofatty tissue in the cotyloid fossa) present.
> *Intra-op frame:* photograph of the acetabulum with self-retaining retractors in place — typically one Hohmann anterior, one posterior on the ischium, one inferior to retract psoas; femur retracted anteriorly.
>
> Place self-retaining retractors: a curved Hohmann anteriorly over the anterior wall (psoas displaced), a Hohmann posteriorly over the ischium, a Hohmann inferiorly under the transverse acetabular ligament if needed for inferior exposure. Excise the labrum circumferentially with a 15-blade or rongeur. Remove the pulvinar from the cotyloid fossa to expose the medial wall.
>
> **Structures at risk:** the **anterior retractor** over the anterior column risks the femoral nerve and the external iliac vessels — keep the retractor tip on bone, never advancing through the anterior wall into the pelvis. The **inferior retractor** risks the obturator vessels — keep on bone. The **posterior retractor** is protective of the sciatic nerve when correctly placed on the ischium.

> **Step AC2. Sequentially ream the acetabulum.**
>
> *Anatomy frame:* acetabular reamer shape with progressively increasing sizes; medial-wall integrity preserved.
> *Intra-op frame:* photograph of the reamer engaged in the acetabulum; surgeon controlling reamer angle (45° abduction, 20° anteversion target).
>
> Begin reaming with the smallest reamer (typically 46–48 mm for a planned 56 mm cup; reaming-to-cup-size protocol is implant-specific — for Pinnacle Gription, ream 1 mm under final cup size for press-fit). Ream progressively larger by 2 mm increments until reaching 1 mm under the planned cup size (56 mm cup → ream to 55 mm). Orient the reamer at 45° abduction and 20° anteversion using the pelvis-perpendicular reference established at positioning. Confirm medial-wall integrity by palpation after each ream; over-reaming risks pelvic perforation.
>
> **Structures at risk:** **medial-wall perforation** with reamer over-aggression — the obturator vessels and the bladder lie immediately medial to the medial acetabular wall; perforation can produce catastrophic intra-pelvic haemorrhage. Confirm medial-wall integrity at every reaming pass. **Sciatic nerve** if the posterior retractor is dislodged; reconfirm retractor position before each ream.

> **Step AC3. Decide: cement vs. press-fit cup.**
>
> *Decision point.* (Branched.)
>
> *Anatomy frame:* reamed acetabulum with cancellous-bone quality visible.
> *Intra-op frame:* photograph of the reamed bed; surgeon assessing bone quality by inspection (haematic ooze present? cancellous bone dense? cortical rim intact?).
>
> Assess the reamed bone bed. Three criteria for press-fit: (i) cortical rim intact circumferentially; (ii) cancellous bone visually dense with haematic ooze; (iii) reamer impacted firmly through final two sizes. If all three present → proceed to press-fit cup (Pinnacle Gription). If any criterion absent (osteoporotic bone, rim defect, soft cancellous bone) → convert to cement (Marathon polyethylene cup with PMMA).
>
> *This case:* bone quality acceptable; proceed to **press-fit**.
>
> **Structures at risk:** insufficient cup fixation if press-fit chosen in inadequate bone → cup migration / aseptic loosening / revision. The decision-point discipline avoids this failure mode.

> **Step AC4. Trial cup and insert final cup.**
>
> *Anatomy frame:* cup positioned in acetabulum with 45° abduction / 20° anteversion orientation.
> *Intra-op frame:* photograph of the cup impactor in position; surgeon confirming orientation against pelvic landmarks.
>
> Trial the 56 mm cup; confirm seating against the medial wall and circumferential cortical contact. Insert the final cup with the cup impactor at 45° abduction and 20° anteversion. Confirm seating with intra-operative fluoroscopy if available (the templating overlay convention from `templates/svg-radiograph-overlay.svg` applies). Insert the HXLPE liner.
>
> **Structures at risk:** cup malposition is the structure-at-risk in the abstract — a cup outside the safe zone (Lewinnek 30–50° abduction / 5–25° anteversion) carries increased dislocation risk. Confirm orientation against pelvic landmarks before final impaction.

---

## Femoral preparation

> **Step F1. Expose the femoral canal.**
>
> *Anatomy frame:* proximal femur delivered into the operative field with the leg in flexion, adduction, and external rotation.
> *Intra-op frame:* photograph of the femur elevated into the wound; box-osteotome or canal-finder in position over the piriformis fossa.
>
> Position the leg in flexion, adduction, and external rotation to deliver the proximal femur into the operative field. Place a Hohmann anterior to the femur to elevate. Identify the piriformis fossa — the starting point for canal entry (lateral to the piriformis tendon insertion at the superomedial aspect of the greater trochanter).
>
> **Structures at risk:** sciatic nerve under tension at the posterior wound — re-confirm retractor protection. Femoral fracture from over-aggressive femoral elevation in osteoporotic bone.

> **Step F2. Open the femoral canal.**
>
> *Anatomy frame:* femoral canal axis indicated; entry point at the piriformis fossa.
> *Intra-op frame:* photograph of the canal-finder (a hand-held curved instrument) being introduced into the canal to confirm the axis before broaching.
>
> Open the canal with a box-osteotome at the piriformis fossa, removing the lateral 'shoulder' of bone that obstructs straight-line broach entry. Introduce a canal-finder to confirm canal axis; the femoral canal should accept the finder without resistance to the diaphysis.
>
> **Structures at risk:** **canal violation** — the box-osteotome positioned too medially can perforate the femoral-neck cortex; positioned too laterally produces varus broach trajectory. Canal-finder resistance suggests cortical impingement; redirect rather than force.

> **Step F3. Sequentially broach the femoral canal.**
>
> *Anatomy frame:* sequence of broaches of increasing size matching the planned implant.
> *Intra-op frame:* photograph of the broach handle in position; surgeon impacting with a mallet.
>
> Begin broaching with the smallest broach (typically 2–3 sizes below the planned final size). Impact with controlled mallet blows; the broach should advance with each blow until *rotational stability* is achieved (broach cannot be rotated by hand). Progress through broach sizes to the planned final size (Corail size 5 for this case). The final broach should achieve: full seating to the calcar collar; rotational stability; circumferential metaphyseal fit; no distal canal tightening (which would indicate over-sizing).
>
> **Structures at risk:** **intra-operative femoral fracture** from over-aggressive broaching, especially in osteoporotic bone or with varus broach trajectory. Stop and reassess if a broach will not seat or if the cortex deforms; size-down rather than fracture.

> **Step F4. Trial reduction with selected head and neck length.**
>
> *Anatomy frame:* trial broach in canal with trial head + neck attached; hip reduced into trial cup + liner.
> *Intra-op frame:* photograph of the trial reduction; surgeon assessing range of motion, stability, and leg length.
>
> Attach the trial neck (+0 starting length per templating) and trial head (36 mm) to the broach. Reduce the hip into the trial cup. Assess:
>
> - **Stability:** flex hip to 90°, adduct, internally rotate to 30°; the head should not subluxate or dislocate. Extend hip, externally rotate to 30°; check anterior stability.
> - **Range of motion:** confirm flexion to 110°, abduction to 45°, internal rotation in flexion to 30°.
> - **Leg length:** assess by direct measurement of medial malleoli with hips squared; confirm equal to contralateral.
> - **Soft-tissue tension:** the 'shuck test' — distract the femur from the cup; ~2–4 mm of distraction is appropriate; > 5 mm suggests under-stuffing (lengthen neck); 0 mm suggests over-stuffing (shorten neck).
>
> *Decision point.* If trial reduction reveals: under-stuffing → trial +5 mm neck; over-stuffing → trial –3.5 mm neck; instability → re-check cup orientation, consider larger head (constrained option if persistent).
>
> *This case:* trial with +0 neck produces equal leg length, 3 mm of shuck, stable through full ROM → proceed to final implants with +0 neck.
>
> **Structures at risk:** **dislocation post-operatively** if trial reduction is inadequately tested; **leg-length inequality** if assessment is rushed. The trial step is where the surgeon earns the result.

---

## Final implants

> **Step I1. Insert the final femoral stem.**
>
> *Anatomy frame:* prepared canal ready for stem insertion.
> *Intra-op frame:* photograph of the stem impactor in position; surgeon impacting stem to seated position.
>
> Remove trial broach. Insert the final Corail size 5 stem with the stem impactor. Impact with controlled mallet blows until the stem seats to the planned depth (collar contact with the calcar). Confirm stem version (15° anteversion target relative to the posterior condyles of the distal femur).
>
> **Structures at risk:** **intra-operative femoral fracture** with stem insertion through tight broached canal — particularly the calcar split. Pause if resistance is unexpected; re-broach if necessary. **Sciatic nerve** if posterior retractor displaced; reconfirm position.

> **Step I2. Place the final ceramic head.**
>
> *Anatomy frame:* stem trunnion with ceramic head being attached.
> *Intra-op frame:* photograph of the ceramic head being placed on the stem trunnion; surgeon impacting with a soft-mallet to seat the taper.
>
> Clean and dry the stem trunnion thoroughly (any contamination compromises the taper junction and risks fretting / trunnionosis). Place the +0 neck length 36 mm Biolox Delta ceramic head on the trunnion. Impact with a soft (plastic-tipped) impactor to seat the Morse taper.
>
> **Structures at risk:** **ceramic fracture** if the head is impacted with a metal mallet or if the trunnion is contaminated. **Trunnionosis** (corrosion at the head-stem junction) if the trunnion is not cleaned and dried.

> **Step I3. Reduce the hip.**
>
> *Anatomy frame:* hip reduced into the cup; head fully seated within the HXLPE liner.
> *Intra-op frame:* photograph of the reduced hip; surgeon performing range-of-motion check.
>
> Reduce the hip by traction and gentle internal rotation. Confirm reduction by direct visualisation and by feel (a satisfying 'clunk' at reduction). Repeat the ROM and stability assessment from trial; confirm consistent with trial expectations.
>
> **Structures at risk:** **sciatic nerve** if reduction requires forceful traction in internal rotation — perform reduction smoothly; if difficult, check for capsular interposition or osteophyte.

---

## Closure

> **Step C1. Reattach the short external rotators and posterior capsule.**
>
> *Anatomy frame:* short external rotators reattached at their trochanteric insertions; T-shaped capsulotomy repaired.
> *Intra-op frame:* photograph of the capsular and rotator repair using the tags placed at A5 and A6.
>
> Using the #2 non-absorbable tags placed at the time of division (steps A5, A6), reattach the piriformis tendon and conjoint tendon to their bony insertions through transosseous tunnels drilled in the posterior greater trochanter (or through suture anchors). Repair the T-shaped capsulotomy with the same tagged stay sutures. Modern technique evidence (Pellicci 1998 onward) demonstrates that meticulous capsular and rotator repair reduces posterior-approach dislocation rate from ~ 3 % to ~ 1 %.
>
> **Structures at risk:** **sciatic nerve** during deep suture placement — confirm nerve is protected throughout. **Dislocation** post-op if repair is omitted or inadequate.

> **Step C2. Close the fascia lata and gluteus maximus.**
>
> *Anatomy frame:* fascia lata edges approximated.
> *Intra-op frame:* photograph of fascia closure with #1 Vicryl interrupted sutures.
>
> Approximate the gluteus maximus muscle bluntly (the muscle was split in fibre direction; it reapproximates by relaxation). Close the fascia lata with #1 Vicryl interrupted sutures, tension-free.
>
> **Structures at risk:** none significant at this step.

> **Step C3. Close the subcutaneous tissue and skin.**
>
> *Anatomy frame:* subcutaneous and skin layers.
> *Intra-op frame:* photograph of skin closure (subcuticular monocryl + Dermabond or staples per institutional preference).
>
> Close subcutaneous tissue with 2-0 Vicryl interrupted. Close skin with 3-0 Monocryl subcuticular suture, reinforced with Dermabond, or with skin staples per institutional preference. Apply sterile dressing.
>
> **Structures at risk:** none significant at closure. The wound complication rate is reduced by tension-free closure and meticulous haemostasis at each layer.

---

## Post-operative orders and rehabilitation

### Weight-bearing and precautions

- **Weight-bearing:** weight-bearing as tolerated (WBAT) on the right lower extremity from POD#1 with walker. Modern cementless press-fit implants tolerate immediate WBAT (AAOS CPG 2023; GRADE: high).
- **Posterior hip precautions for 6 weeks:**
  - No hip flexion past 90°.
  - No hip adduction past midline.
  - No hip internal rotation past neutral.
  - No combining the above (the dislocation moment is *flexion + adduction + internal rotation*).
  - Elevated toilet seat, abduction pillow when supine, chair with raised seat.
- **Mobilization:** physiotherapy POD#1; ambulation with walker; sit-to-stand and transfers practised before discharge.

### DVT prophylaxis

- **Low-risk patient (most THA):** aspirin 81 mg PO BID × 35 days post-op.
- **High-risk patient (prior VTE, malignancy, thrombophilia):** apixaban 2.5 mg PO BID × 35 days per institutional protocol.
- **Mechanical prophylaxis:** sequential compression devices (SCDs) on the contralateral leg in hospital; foot pumps as available.

### Pain management

- **Multimodal analgesia:** acetaminophen 1 g PO Q6H scheduled; celecoxib 200 mg PO BID × 14 days (contraindications respected); oxycodone 5 mg PO Q4H PRN breakthrough (limited quantity dispensed; tapering plan provided).
- **Adjuncts:** ice / cryotherapy; positioning education; expectation-setting in clinic preoperatively.

### Pulmonary and other

- **Incentive spirometry** Q1H while awake.
- **Foley catheter** removed POD#1 if placed.
- **Diet:** advance as tolerated POD#0.
- **Labs:** CBC POD#1 (haemoglobin trend); BMP POD#1 if concern.

### Follow-up

- **Wound check:** POD#10–14 (staples removed if used).
- **Radiographic follow-up:** AP pelvis + lateral hip at 6 weeks, 3 months, 1 year, then every 1–2 years per institutional protocol.
- **Rehab protocol:** ERAS-arthroplasty pathway (institutional); progression to single-cane at 4–6 weeks; full unrestricted activity at 3 months pending clinical and radiographic recovery.

### Discharge

- **Disposition:** home with home health PT in most cases; SNF / acute rehab for selected patients per pre-op functional assessment and home support evaluation.
- **Pain plan provided in writing.** Posterior hip precautions reviewed with patient and family at discharge.
- **Return-precautions:** fever > 38.5 °C, wound drainage, calf pain, shortness of breath, sudden severe pain in the operated hip — return to ED.

---

# Setup

A literate-analysis document earns the word *reproducible* by producing the same numbers, today and ten years from today, from the same input data — even when the analyst is a different person at a different machine with a different operating system. The discipline is the renv lockfile, the pinned package versions, the captured sessionInfo, and the git commit hash that uniquely identifies the source of this document. The closing section of this qmd records all of them.

This analysis re-runs the primary endpoint of the CONNECT trial — the change in PHQ-A total score from baseline to Week 12, by treatment arm — under the pre-registered Statistical Analysis Plan v1.0 (locked 2024-09-12, prior to first randomization). Every analytic decision below traces to a numbered section in `templates/statistical-analysis-plan.md`; every derived variable traces to a row in `templates/data-dictionary.md`. The expected primary contrast is a between-arm mean difference of approximately −2.6 PHQ-A points favoring telehealth-CBT, consistent with the trial's published abstract (`templates/structured-abstract-250.md`).

```{r}
#| label: setup-libraries
#| message: false

# Library loads with explicit version requirements per SAP §17.2
# Pinned via renv::snapshot(); see §7 below for reproducibility verification.

library(here)         # 1.0.1   — portable paths; never use setwd()
library(tidyverse)    # 2.0.0   — wrangling + plotting (dplyr 1.1.4, ggplot2 3.5.1, etc.)
library(mmrm)         # 0.3.12  — primary analysis (MMRM per SAP §7.1)
library(mice)         # 3.16.0  — multiple imputation sensitivity (SAP §9.1)
library(gtsummary)    # 2.0.0   — Table 1 + Table 2 publication-ready
library(broom.mixed)  # 0.2.9.5 — tidy outputs from mmrm fits
library(emmeans)      # 1.10.4  — estimated marginal means and pre-specified contrasts
library(boot)         # 1.3-30  — bootstrap CIs for standardized effect size (SAP §7.3)
library(knitr)        # 1.48    — table rendering for non-gtsummary tables
library(sessioninfo)  # 1.2.2   — session footer (§7)
library(fs)           # 1.6.4   — file-system operations

# Set global options
options(
  scipen = 999,                    # avoid scientific notation in printed tables
  digits = 4,                      # 4 sig figs for default numeric display
  knitr.kable.NA = ""              # blank rather than NA in tables
)

# Set ggplot theme
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
          theme(
            panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
            plot.title.position = "plot",
            plot.caption.position = "plot"
          ))
```

```{r}
#| label: setup-paths
#| message: false

# All paths via here::here() so the document renders identically from
# any working directory the analyst happens to be in.
path_data_raw    <- here("data", "raw",        "connect_phq_v1.csv")
path_data_derive <- here("data", "derived",    "connect_analytic_v1.rds")
path_data_dict   <- here("docs", "data-dictionary.md")
path_sap         <- here("docs", "statistical-analysis-plan.md")
path_figures     <- here("output", "figures")
path_tables      <- here("output", "tables")

# Create output directories if they do not exist (idempotent)
fs::dir_create(path_figures, recurse = TRUE)

# Record analysis run timestamp
